title: Conflict-Free Diamonds: What the Kimberley Process Does and Does Not Guarantee
body:
The Kimberley Process does one specific thing: it certifies that rough diamonds did not finance rebel movements opposing recognized governments. It does not certify working conditions, environmental practices, or political violence committed by those same governments.

What the Kimberley Process Is

The Origin and Scope of the Certification System

The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme (KPCS) was established in 2003 following the international focus on “blood diamonds” — rough diamonds used to fund armed rebel groups, most prominently the RUF (Revolutionary United Front) in Sierra Leone and UNITA in Angola during the civil conflicts of the 1990s. The scheme is a joint agreement between 55 participating countries, the diamond industry, and civil society organizations. It requires that rough diamond shipments between participating countries be accompanied by a certificate verifying that the stones did not originate from rebel-controlled areas.

Under the Kimberley Process, member nations agree not to trade in uncertified rough diamonds and to implement internal controls that prevent non-compliant stones from entering their supply chains. Each shipment receives a tamper-resistant certificate with a unique serial number. The system covers rough diamonds only — polished stones are not individually certified under the KPCS, though member nations’ compliance at the rough stage is intended to ensure that the polished inventory from legitimate sources is traceable.

The KPCS has achieved its stated goal in specific cases: Sierra Leone and Angola are no longer significant sources of conflict diamonds, and the rebel funding mechanism that prompted the scheme’s creation has been disrupted in those specific geographies. The system represents a genuine international coordination achievement for a specific, defined problem.

What the Kimberley Process Does Not Cover

The Documented Gaps in the Certification

The Kimberley Process defines “conflict diamond” narrowly as a stone that funds “rebel movements or their allies seeking to undermine legitimate governments.” This definition excludes several categories of concern that human rights organizations and buyers commonly associate with ethical sourcing. Violence perpetrated by recognized governments — including the governments of several major diamond-producing nations — falls outside the KPCS definition. Labor abuses, including dangerous working conditions, child labor, and exploitation of artisanal miners, are not addressed. Environmental damage from mining operations is outside the scheme’s scope.

Zimbabwe’s Marange diamond fields became the most publicized example of this gap. When government forces seized the Marange fields in 2008, documented reports from NGOs (non-governmental organizations) and journalists described killings, torture, and forced labor by Zimbabwean security forces. A 2009 decision by Kimberley Process member states allowed Zimbabwean diamonds from Marange to be certified as conflict-free because the violence was committed by the recognized government rather than a rebel movement. The KPCS definition was satisfied; the ethical concerns were not.

Civil society members of the KPCS, including Global Witness — one of the founding organizations — have resigned from the process at various points, citing the scheme’s inability to address its documented gaps. The KPCS remains the operational standard because no comprehensive alternative has been established, but buyers who understand its scope know that a Kimberley Process certificate is an answer to one specific question, not a comprehensive ethical assurance.

What Stronger Assurances Look Like

Beyond Kimberley Process: Chain of Custody and Transparency

Some mining companies and retailers have implemented chain-of-custody tracking that goes beyond the KPCS minimum. Botswana, through Debswana (a joint venture between the Botswana government and De Beers), offers one of the strongest traceability programs in the industry, with social investment programs tied to diamond revenues and documented working conditions. Canadian diamonds, produced under strict federal environmental regulations with significant First Nations consultation processes, carry strong third-party documentation for several concerns beyond the KPCS scope.

Individual retailers who have committed to specific origin traceability beyond KPCS certification — providing mine-of-origin documentation for specific stones — offer meaningfully stronger assurance than KPCS certification alone. These programs exist but are less prevalent than the industry’s general marketing around “conflict-free” would suggest, which often conflates KPCS compliance with a broader ethical standard that the KPCS does not actually represent.

Lab-grown diamonds offer a different form of ethical assurance. They bypass the mining supply chain entirely, eliminating all concerns about mining conditions, geographic origin, and government-violence exclusions from the KPCS definition. The trade-off is that the economic contribution to mining communities in producing countries is also bypassed — a choice with its own social consequences. Neither choice is free of ethical considerations; they simply carry different ones.

Making a Buying Decision

What Matters and What to Ask

Buyers who want stronger ethical assurance than the KPCS baseline should ask their jeweler specific questions rather than accepting “conflict-free” as a sufficient answer. The useful questions are: Can you provide the country of origin for this rough diamond? Is there mine-of-origin documentation beyond the Kimberley Process certificate? What percentage of your inventory comes from producers with labor practice documentation?

A dealer who can answer these questions with specifics is operating at a meaningfully higher transparency standard than the industry minimum. A dealer who responds with “all our diamonds are Kimberley Process certified” has answered a narrower question than the one you asked. Both answers tell you something about the dealer’s supply chain practices.

What People

Ask Us

Does “conflict-free” mean the diamond was ethically sourced? Not comprehensively. A conflict-free certificate under the Kimberley Process means the diamond did not finance rebel movements opposing recognized governments. It does not address labor conditions, environmental practices, or violence by governments themselves. If broader ethical assurance is important to you, ask for mine-of-origin documentation or consider lab-grown diamonds.

Are Canadian diamonds really conflict-free? Canadian diamonds are produced under federal environmental regulations, significant labor protections, and First Nations consultation frameworks that are among the strictest in the world for mining operations. They carry strong third-party documentation for several ethical dimensions that KPCS does not address. Canada is not a conflict zone, and the political conditions that generate conflict diamonds do not apply. Canadian origin is among the most reliably documented in the natural diamond market.

Is a Kimberley Process certificate the same as a GIA certificate? No. They are completely different documents. A Kimberley Process certificate accompanies rough diamond shipments at the country level and certifies conflict-free origin under the KPCS definition. A GIA certificate is a laboratory grading report for a specific polished stone, documenting its color, clarity, cut, and carat weight. Both can exist for the same stone; they certify different things.

Do lab-grown diamonds avoid all ethical issues? Lab-grown diamonds avoid all mining-related ethical concerns, including the KPCS gaps. The ethical considerations that do apply to lab-grown diamonds relate to energy consumption in the manufacturing process (which depends on the energy source used by the producer) and the economic impact on diamond mining communities in producing countries. A buyer who shifts from natural to lab-grown eliminates one category of ethical concern while accepting a different one.

What happened to conflict diamonds from the 1990s? The major rebel-funded conflicts that prompted the Kimberley Process — in Sierra Leone and Angola — ended in the early 2000s, and the specific diamond-for-arms pipelines that characterized those conflicts have been disrupted in those geographies. Conflict diamonds as defined by the KPCS represent a far smaller share of the global supply now than in the late 1990s. The ongoing concern is not a return to 1990s-scale conflict diamond flows, but the narrowness of the KPCS definition in addressing current human rights concerns in the diamond supply chain.

title: Diamond Anatomy: Crown, Pavilion, Table, Girdle, and Culet
body:
A diamond is a precision optical instrument before it is a piece of jewelry, and its anatomy is the engineering that determines whether light returns to your eye or escapes through the bottom.

The Table and Crown

The Top Half and How It Handles Incoming Light

The table is the flat, octagonal facet at the very top of a round brilliant diamond — the largest single facet on the stone. Its size, expressed as a percentage of the stone’s girdle diameter, is one of the most critical proportional variables in cut grading. A table that is too large — above roughly 65 percent for a round brilliant — collects light efficiently but returns it in a flat, undifferentiated pattern that suppresses the “fire” or spectral dispersion that separates a brilliant diamond from a piece of glass. A table that is too small leaves too much of the stone’s top surface in the crown facets, which can reduce overall brightness.

The crown is everything between the table and the girdle on the upper half of the stone. For a round brilliant, the crown includes eight star facets adjacent to the table, eight bezel facets (also called kite facets) that run to the girdle, and sixteen upper-girdle facets. The crown angle — measured between the bezel facets and the girdle plane — is one of the most important proportional variables. Crown angles between roughly 33 and 35 degrees, combined with the correct pavilion angle, produce the maximum combination of brightness and fire. A crown that is too shallow or too steep delivers more of one at the expense of the other.

The crown’s function is to refract incoming light and distribute it through the stone’s interior, and to collect light returning from the pavilion and direct it back toward the viewer’s eye. The specific geometry of the crown facets creates the “scintillation” — the flashing, sparkling pattern of light and dark areas that appears as the stone moves. A well-proportioned crown creates organized, even scintillation; a poorly proportioned one creates dead zones or an unbalanced light pattern.

The Girdle

The Equator That Defines Shape and Protects the Edge

The girdle is the narrow band around the widest point of the diamond, separating the crown above from the pavilion below. It serves multiple functions: it defines the stone’s outline shape, provides the holding point for prong settings, and protects the stone’s most vulnerable edge. The girdle can be faceted (covered in small triangular facets), polished (smooth and reflective), or bruted (matte finish from the cutting process). On modern stones, faceted and polished girdles are most common; bruted girdles are associated with older cutting methods.

Girdle thickness is reported in qualitative terms on GIA certificates — from Extremely Thin to Extremely Thick, with Thin, Medium, and Slightly Thick being most desirable. An extremely thin girdle is a brittleness risk: the very edge of the stone at the girdle has no mass to absorb impact, and chipping is more likely. An extremely thick girdle wastes carat weight in a location that contributes little to the stone’s optical performance — the weight that produces the grade is not being used to create the face-up appearance the buyer is paying for.

The girdle is also where the GIA certificate number is laser-inscribed on certified stones. The inscription is readable under 10x magnification and serves as the permanent identification link between the physical stone and its documentation.

The Pavilion and Culet

The Lower Half Where the Real Optical Work Happens

The pavilion is the lower half of the diamond, below the girdle. In a round brilliant, it contains eight pavilion main facets that run from the girdle to the culet (the point at the bottom), and sixteen lower-girdle facets that connect the pavilion mains to the girdle. The pavilion angle — the angle of the main pavilion facets relative to the girdle plane — is the single most important measurement in a diamond’s cut. Pavilion angles between approximately 40.6 and 41.0 degrees, combined with the correct crown angle, produce total internal reflection: light entering the table bounces off the pavilion facets and returns directly upward through the crown.

If the pavilion is too shallow — below about 40 degrees — light passes through the bottom of the stone rather than reflecting upward. This creates what is called a “fish-eye” effect in round brilliants, where the reflection of the girdle becomes visible as a ring inside the stone when viewed face-up, and the stone appears glassy and lifeless rather than brilliant. A pavilion that is too deep sends light bouncing to one pavilion facet and then out through the opposite side of the stone, creating dark areas called “nailheads” in the face-up view.

The culet is the point at the very bottom of the pavilion. On modern rounds, the culet is typically cut to a point (listed as “None” on GIA reports) or to a very small facet. A small culet is invisible face-up; a large culet — common in antique cuts from before standardized modern cutting — appears as a dark circular dot in the center of the stone when viewed face-up, because it allows light to pass straight through rather than reflecting back.

Proportions and Performance

How All the Parts Work Together

No single measurement in a diamond’s proportions operates independently. The crown angle and pavilion angle interact to determine whether the stone’s light performance is excellent, average, or poor. The table percentage interacts with the crown height to determine how much direct light enters the stone versus how much enters through the crown facets. The girdle thickness affects how much mass is concentrated at the equator rather than distributed usefully through the crown and pavilion.

GIA’s cut grading system for round brilliants evaluates all these measurements in combination and assigns a single Cut grade from Excellent to Poor. The top Excellent grade reflects stones whose combined proportions produce maximum brightness, fire, and scintillation as measured by optical modeling. Understanding the anatomy is what allows a sophisticated buyer to read a proportions diagram independently rather than relying on the summary grade alone — which matters most for fancy shapes, where GIA does not issue a cut grade.

What People

Ask Us

What does “table percentage” mean on a diamond certificate? Table percentage is the width of the table facet expressed as a percentage of the diamond’s girdle diameter. For a round brilliant graded 60 percent, the table is 60 percent as wide as the stone is wide. The ideal range for round brilliants is roughly 53 to 62 percent, where the balance of direct light entry and crown-facet light entry produces maximum optical performance.

Why does pavilion angle matter so much? The pavilion angle governs whether light entering the stone from above reflects back up through the crown to the viewer’s eye, or leaks out through the bottom or sides of the stone. A deviation of even one or two degrees from the ideal range dramatically reduces the amount of light returned to the eye, making the stone appear dim compared to one with correct pavilion geometry.

What is a “hearts and arrows” diamond? A “hearts and arrows” diamond is a round brilliant cut to such precise optical symmetry that, when viewed under a special gemscope that reflects the stone’s pattern, the pavilion shows eight arrows in the face-up view and eight hearts in the face-down view. This pattern requires exceptional precision in facet alignment and proportions, and reliably indicates a well-cut stone. All AGS Ideal 0 rounds and most GIA Excellent rounds from quality cutters exhibit this pattern.

Can I tell the quality of the cut without a certificate? A trained eye can evaluate cut quality by observing the stone’s light behavior in a normal viewing environment — looking for even brightness across the table, organized scintillation pattern, absence of dark areas (nailheads or fish-eye), and whether the stone appears brilliant at arm’s length. This evaluation requires experience. For buyers without that experience, the GIA Excellent or AGS Ideal 0 grade provides reliable assurance without requiring independent assessment.

What happens to a diamond with a large culet? A large culet — common in antique old mine and old European cuts — creates a dark circle visible in the center of the stone when viewed face-up. Light that enters the stone directly above the culet passes straight through rather than reflecting back up. Many buyers find this characteristic attractive in antique cuts, where it is part of the stone’s historical character. In modern cuts, a pointed culet (graded “None”) is standard because the absence of a culet maximizes light return at the center of the stone.

title: Diamond Clarity: From Flawless to Included, What Matters on the Hand
body:
Clarity grades measure what is inside a diamond; the ring wearer sees what is on top of it — and those two perspectives diverge in ways that the industry rarely explains clearly.

The GIA Clarity Scale

What Each Grade Actually Measures

GIA’s (Gemological Institute of America) clarity scale has eleven grades across six categories. Flawless (FL) and Internally Flawless (IF) contain no inclusions and no blemishes visible under 10x magnification, respectively. VVS1 and VVS2 (Very Very Slightly Included) contain inclusions that are extremely difficult to see even for an experienced grader at 10x. VS1 and VS2 (Very Slightly Included) contain inclusions that are difficult but possible to see at 10x. SI1 and SI2 (Slightly Included) contain inclusions that are noticeable at 10x and may be visible to the naked eye. I1, I2, and I3 (Included) contain inclusions clearly visible to the naked eye that may affect transparency and brilliance.

The entire grading is conducted at 10x magnification under standardized lighting. This is important to keep in mind: 10x magnification is approximately what a jeweler’s loupe provides, and it is far more powerful than naked-eye viewing. An inclusion that fills the field of view at 10x magnification may be completely invisible when the stone is viewed normally at arm’s length.

The type, size, number, position, and color of inclusions all factor into the grade. A large feather — an internal fracture — at the center of the table in a VS1 stone might have placed it in SI1 in a different position. A cluster of small, off-center crystals in an SI1 might be harder to see face-up than the feather in the VS1. The grade is a summary, not a complete picture of the stone’s visual appearance.

What Eye-Clean Means

The Standard That Actually Matters for Wearers

An “eye-clean” diamond has no inclusions visible to the unaided eye when the stone is viewed face-up from a normal viewing distance of about 12 to 15 inches. This is the practical clarity standard for any ring that will be worn and observed in daily life. A stone that is eye-clean grades no differently on the hand than a flawless stone, regardless of what the certificate says.

Flawless and Internally Flawless diamonds trade at extraordinary premiums — often 30 to 50 percent above comparable VS1 stones — for a quality improvement that no observer will detect in normal use. The premium exists because collectors value rarity and the certificate, not because the ring will look different. For clients who are buying jewelry to wear and enjoy, this is a straightforward misallocation of budget.

The eye-clean threshold by shape and size follows predictable patterns. Round brilliants are the most forgiving shape for clarity: the brilliant-cut facet pattern masks inclusions efficiently, and SI1 rounds are frequently eye-clean. In SI2 territory, round brilliants can sometimes still be eye-clean, but this requires individual evaluation — the grade alone is not sufficient assurance. Fancy shapes with large open tables — emerald and asscher cuts, specifically — reveal inclusions more directly and typically require VS2 or better to be reliably eye-clean. Ovals, pears, and marquise shapes fall between these poles.

Inclusion Types

Which Features Matter More Than Others

Not all inclusions are equal. A small, colorless cloud (a diffuse group of tiny pinpoints) in the lower pavilion of an SI1 round brilliant affects the grade but will be functionally invisible in the finished ring. A dark crystal inclusion centered under the table of a VS2 stone may be more visually apparent than the cloud and can potentially affect brilliance by creating a dark spot in the face-up view. The certificate tells you the worst thing it found; it does not tell you whether that worst thing is visually relevant.

Feathers — internal fractures — deserve attention beyond their clarity grade impact. A feather near the girdle of a stone can be a vulnerability to chipping if the stone receives a hard impact in that location. The risk is not high in normal daily wear with a protective setting, but it is worth knowing about. A grader at your jeweler can assess whether a feather’s location creates meaningful wear risk.

Inclusions that affect brilliance directly — dark crystals, heavy twinning wisps, or broad feathers running through the stone’s center — should be avoided regardless of the clarity grade assigned. Inclusions that sit in the pavilion below the main facets, or near the girdle away from the table center, rarely have any visual consequence.

Buying Strategy

Where Clarity Budget Is Well Spent

For round brilliant diamonds, the VS2 grade is a solid, reliable choice that delivers eye-clean clarity across all sizes without the premium of VS1, VVS, or Flawless grades. The savings can be redirected to cut quality or color. For step-cut shapes — emerald, asscher, baguette — VS1 is the practical floor, and VVS2 or better is worth considering in larger stones where the open table is very revealing.

SI1 round brilliants can be purchased at excellent value if each stone is evaluated individually by a qualified professional before purchase. Blanket SI1 acceptance based on grade alone is not advisable; specific SI1 stones with colorless, off-center inclusions are fine, while centrally located or dark inclusions in SI1 grade should be declined regardless of price.

What People

Ask Us

What clarity grade should I buy for an engagement ring? For round brilliants, VS2 is the standard recommendation that most clients find optimal — eye-clean, certified, and meaningfully less expensive than higher grades. For step cuts and fancy shapes, VS1 is the floor. If budget allows, VS1 for round brilliants and VVS2 for step cuts provides additional margin against any visible inclusions.

Is a flawless diamond worth buying? Only if you are collecting rather than wearing. A Flawless diamond is a rarity certificate — it means the stone was perfect under a highly trained grader’s 10x examination. On the hand, it looks identical to a VS1. The 30 to 50 percent premium buys you the certificate and the bragging rights, not a different daily experience.

Can inclusions affect a diamond’s durability? In most cases, no. The vast majority of inclusions are cosmetic — they affect appearance grades, not structural integrity. The exception is large feathers or cleavage fractures that reach the surface or traverse the stone’s center. These are rare in VS and above grades but can appear in SI2 and included diamonds. Have any large feather evaluated by a professional for position and orientation before purchase.

What is the difference between VS1 and VS2? Both grades contain inclusions that are difficult to see at 10x magnification. VS1 inclusions are slightly harder to locate than VS2 inclusions, and VS1 stones occasionally have fewer total inclusions. The practical difference in most settings is negligible. The price difference between VS1 and VS2 in a given color and cut grade is typically 10 to 15 percent — a meaningful saving that can be redirected usefully.

Do lab-grown diamonds have the same clarity grades? Yes. Lab-grown diamonds are graded on the same GIA clarity scale as natural diamonds and receive the same FL through I3 grades based on the same microscopic evaluation. Lab-grown diamonds often occur at higher clarity grades because the growth environment can be more controlled than natural geological conditions, but inclusions specific to growth methods — metallic flux inclusions in HPHT stones, for example — are also present and graded accordingly.

title: The Diamond Color Grade: What D Through Z Actually Means
body:
The diamond color scale begins at D — not A — because the GIA (Gemological Institute of America) wanted no confusion with earlier grading systems that used A, AA, and AAA to mean different things to different dealers.

The Scale Itself

How GIA Color Grading Works From D to Z

The GIA diamond color grading scale assigns letter grades to represent the degree of yellowish or brownish body color present in a polished diamond. D is colorless — the purest absence of color that a natural diamond achieves. Z marks the point at which the stone has enough yellow body color to be considered a “light yellow” diamond. Below Z, the stone enters the realm of fancy color diamonds and is graded on a separate scale.

The grades are assigned in pairs — D-E-F form the colorless range, G-H-I-J form the near-colorless range, K-L-M form the faint-yellow range, and N through Z cover the very light to light yellow range. These groupings reflect real perceptual boundaries: within each group, the difference between adjacent grades is very difficult to perceive outside a controlled grading environment. Between groups, the difference becomes more visible, particularly in larger stones viewed face-up in white metal settings.

The grading is done by placing a loose stone face-down — table-down — on a white grading tray and comparing it to master stones of known color grades under standardized daylight-equivalent lighting. The face-down orientation is critical: it reveals body color more clearly than the face-up position, where the stone’s brilliance and cutting patterns can mask body color. This is why a diamond graded H can look completely colorless when it is set in a ring and you look at it normally.

What You Actually See on the Hand

The Practical Reality of Color Grades in Settings

The relationship between a laboratory color grade and what you see in daily life is not direct. Multiple factors mediate between the grade and the visual experience. The most important is the metal setting. A D-E-F stone in a yellow gold setting will reflect warm metal into its pavilion, which makes it appear slightly warmer than the color grade suggests. The same stone in platinum or white gold will appear as neutral and colorless as possible.

A G or H stone — technically in the near-colorless range — will appear visually identical to a D stone in most practical settings. In white metal, a G is nearly impossible for an untrained eye to distinguish from a D except in direct comparison with a master D stone under controlled conditions. In yellow gold, a G often appears whiter than a D, because the slightly warm body color in the G harmonizes with the yellow metal rather than contrasting with it the way a truly colorless stone does.

This has a straightforward implication for budget allocation: the premium you pay for D over G color is paid largely to the grading certificate, not to the visual experience you will have wearing the ring. That premium is real and can be substantial — 20 to 40 percent in some size and quality brackets. Buyers who understand this fact spend that budget on cut quality instead, which produces a measurable daily benefit.

Fluorescence and Color Interaction

How Fluorescence Complicates the Color Story

Approximately 30 percent of natural diamonds exhibit fluorescence — an emission of visible light (usually blue) when the stone is exposed to ultraviolet radiation. The UV in ordinary sunlight is sufficient to trigger fluorescence in affected stones. The interaction between fluorescence and body color creates counterintuitive results.

In colorless D-E-F stones, strong blue fluorescence can make the stone appear slightly hazy or oily under UV-rich conditions like outdoor daylight or club lighting with black lights. This haziness reduces value in colorless stones with strong fluorescence, even though colorless is the most desirable body-color grade. In I-J-K range stones with noticeable warm body color, strong blue fluorescence counteracts the yellow and makes the stone appear whiter in sunlight than its color grade would predict. This effect actually adds value in near-colorless to faint-yellow stones.

The practical guidance is to be aware of the fluorescence grade on the certificate and understand which direction it works. Strong fluorescence in an H stone is often an advantage; strong fluorescence in a D stone is usually a minor deficit. GIA reports fluorescence as None, Faint, Medium, Strong, or Very Strong, and notes the fluorescence color (almost always blue).

Buying Decisions

Where the Color Budget Actually Makes Sense to Spend

For round brilliant diamonds in white metal settings, the G-H range offers the best value in the entire color spectrum. The visual result is indistinguishable from colorless to any normal observer. The price difference versus D-F is meaningful and can be redirected to cut quality or clarity or carat weight, all of which produce visible results.

For fancy shapes — ovals, pears, cushions, emerald cuts — the recommendation tightens. These shapes show body color more readily than round brilliants because their cutting style does not produce the same level of light-masking brilliance. F-G is a more practical floor for fancy shapes in white metal. In yellow gold, you can relax by one grade in either direction.

What People

Ask Us

What is the best diamond color grade to buy? For round brilliants in white or platinum settings, G is the most rational choice for most budgets — visually colorless in normal settings, meaningfully less expensive than D-F. For fancy shapes or if you prefer certainty over economy, F is the floor that I recommend across all shapes and settings.

Can you see the difference between D and G color in a ring? In isolation, in a ring, under normal lighting conditions, no — most people cannot. The difference is perceptible in a side-by-side comparison under controlled conditions. In daily wear, where the stone is set in metal and observed in varying light, the distinction effectively disappears. The GIA grade is accurate; the visual consequence of the grade difference is minimal in practice.

Does color grade matter less for colored stone rings? Diamond color grade is irrelevant for colored stones, which are graded on hue, tone, and saturation rather than the D-Z colorless scale. If you are asking whether a colorless diamond accent stone matters alongside a colored center stone, the answer is that near-colorless grades read as white in any accent or side-stone application.

Why does GIA start at D and not A? The GIA standardized their scale beginning at D intentionally, to avoid any confusion with earlier systems used by dealers and trade organizations that used A, AA, and AAA designations inconsistently. By starting fresh at D, GIA signaled a clean break from those systems and created an unambiguous standard that has since become universal.

Do lower color grades look bad in yellow gold settings? Not necessarily. A K-L range stone — faint yellow — can look appropriate and even appealing in a yellow gold setting, because the metal’s warmth reduces the contrast that would make the stone’s yellow body color apparent in white metal. Many vintage-style rings are deliberately designed around faint-yellow stones in yellow gold for exactly this reason. The aesthetic is warmer and more antique-feeling rather than worse.

title: Diamond Fluorescence: Asset, Liability, or Neither
body:
Fluorescence is the most consistently misunderstood property in diamond buying — treated as a defect by some dealers and as a feature by others, when the reality depends entirely on the stone’s color grade.

What Fluorescence Is

The Science Behind the Glow

Approximately 25 to 35 percent of gem-quality diamonds fluoresce when exposed to ultraviolet light. The UV component of natural sunlight, as well as black lights used in clubs and some retail environments, activates this response. The diamond absorbs the UV radiation and re-emits it as visible light, most commonly in the blue portion of the spectrum. The GIA (Gemological Institute of America) reports fluorescence on grading certificates as None, Faint, Medium, Strong, or Very Strong, and notes the color of the fluorescence — which is blue in about 95 percent of cases, with yellow, white, and orange occurring rarely.

The fluorescence intensity grades reflect a continuum. A “Faint” fluorescent diamond will show a barely perceptible glow under a strong UV lamp. A “Very Strong” fluorescent diamond will appear to emit a brilliant, saturated blue glow under the same light. In ordinary daylight and incandescent lighting, Faint and Medium fluorescence is essentially invisible to the unaided eye. Strong and Very Strong fluorescence may be perceptible in direct sunlight or under high-UV indoor lighting.

The fluorescence effect is caused by structural defects in the diamond’s crystal lattice — specifically by nitrogen aggregates that create energy states capable of absorbing and re-emitting UV light. These defects are separate from the clarity inclusions graded on the GIA scale. A Flawless diamond can exhibit Strong fluorescence; a heavily included stone may have none. The two properties are independent.

When Fluorescence Helps

The Color-Correcting Effect in Near-Colorless Stones

The most useful function of blue fluorescence is its color-correcting effect on near-colorless to faint-yellow diamonds. Stones in the G through M color range carry some degree of yellow or brown body color. When strong blue fluorescence is present, the emitted blue light partially cancels the yellow tint under UV-rich lighting conditions — particularly in direct sunlight, which has substantial UV content. The result is that a fluorescent H stone can appear to be closer to F color in outdoor daylight than its grade would suggest.

This effect has real market implications. Fluorescent stones in the G-J color range often trade at a slight discount to non-fluorescent stones of the same grade, even though they typically perform better in the most common outdoor lighting condition. For buyers who prioritize face-up appearance in real-world conditions over certificate purity, a Strong-fluorescence G stone can be one of the best value propositions in the market.

The effect is most valuable for buyers who will wear the ring outdoors frequently and who are in the G-I color range. If you live in a sunny climate or spend significant time outdoors, a fluorescent stone in this color range will appear whiter in those conditions than a non-fluorescent stone of the same grade.

When Fluorescence Hurts

The Haziness Problem in Colorless Stones

For D, E, and F colorless stones, the conventional market wisdom reverses: Strong and Very Strong fluorescence is considered a deficit. The logic is that a colorless stone has no yellow to cancel, so the blue emission adds an unwanted visual quality rather than correcting one. In some Strong-fluorescent colorless stones, particularly Very Strong fluorescence, the blue emission creates a milky or oily appearance in the face-up view under certain lighting. This “haziness” reduces the stone’s transparency and scintillation.

Not all colorless fluorescent stones exhibit haziness. A D-Very Strong-fluorescent stone without haziness is a normal stone that happens to glow blue under UV. The problem is that haziness cannot be predicted from the fluorescence grade alone — it requires physical examination of the stone in question. GIA has studied the phenomenon and found that it affects a minority of Very Strong fluorescent colorless stones, but that minority is large enough that the trade applies a blanket discount.

The practical guidance for colorless stones is to examine any Strong or Very Strong fluorescent D-F stone in person before purchase and verify that no haziness is present. If you cannot examine the stone in person, request a video under both normal lighting and UV to assess. A non-hazy, colorless Strong-fluorescent stone is a legitimate buy at a discount to non-fluorescent equivalents.

Market Pricing and Practical Decisions

How Fluorescence Affects What You Pay

The market pricing pattern for fluorescence is consistent: in colorless grades (D-F), Strong and Very Strong fluorescence carries a 5 to 15 percent price discount versus the same stone without fluorescence. In near-colorless grades (G-J), the discount ranges from 2 to 10 percent depending on intensity. In faint-yellow and below (K onward), fluorescence is often a neutral or positive factor with no discount, and in some markets a slight premium.

For practical buyers in the G-J range, this pricing pattern represents an opportunity. A fluorescent G stone at a discount is frequently a better visual performer in daylight than a non-fluorescent G at full price. The savings can be applied elsewhere in the purchase. The caveat, as always, is to examine the specific stone — the grade describes a statistical population, not the individual stone.

What People

Ask Us

Does fluorescence make a diamond look blue? Only under UV light sources. Under ordinary incandescent lighting, halogen, or most LED lighting, fluorescence is not visible and the stone appears exactly as its color grade describes. Under direct sunlight or near UV-emitting black lights, a Strong or Very Strong fluorescent diamond will appear to glow blue. Whether that glow looks like an asset or a peculiarity depends on the stone’s color grade.

Should I avoid fluorescent diamonds? Not as a blanket policy. For colorless stones (D-F), I recommend examining any Strong-fluorescent stone in person to confirm it has no haziness. For near-colorless stones (G-J), fluorescence is frequently a positive attribute at a discount price. Faint and Medium fluorescence at any color grade is essentially a non-issue and can be ignored for practical purposes.

Does fluorescence affect a diamond’s durability? No. Fluorescence is an optical property caused by structural features that do not affect the diamond’s hardness, toughness, or chemical stability. A fluorescent diamond is not weaker or more susceptible to damage than a non-fluorescent one.

Is fluorescence reported on all grading certificates? GIA reports fluorescence on all its diamond grading reports, including the intensity grade and the color. AGS also reports fluorescence. Some lesser grading laboratories do not report fluorescence at all, or report it inconsistently. This is one of several reasons why GIA and AGS certification is preferable to other grading services for purchase decisions.

Can I use fluorescence to identify a diamond? Fluorescence pattern under UV can be used as one identifying characteristic for a specific stone, particularly if the intensity and pattern are distinctive. It is not sufficient for formal identification — that requires the full grading report and its measurements — but it is a useful field check. Two diamonds with identical certificates but different fluorescence intensities are definitively different stones.

title: Diamond Inclusions: Types, Visibility, and What to Avoid
body:
A diamond clarity grade is a summary, not a specification — it tells you the worst inclusion GIA found, but not whether that inclusion is visible in daily wear or relevant to the ring’s performance.

The Main Inclusion Types

What Causes Each Type and What They Look Like

Crystals are mineral inclusions trapped within the diamond during its formation — typically other diamond material, garnet, or olivine. They appear as small, irregularly shaped particles inside the stone. Colorless crystals are the most benign form: they are difficult to see face-up and contribute minimally to visual concern at VS1 and VS2 grades. Dark crystals — usually appearing black, brown, or deep red — are far more visually significant. A dark crystal under the table in a VS2 stone can be more visible to the naked eye than a much larger colorless inclusion in the same position, because the contrast against the bright diamond is what the eye perceives.

Feathers are internal fractures — planes of separation within the crystal structure. They appear as white or reflective lines or planes, sometimes resembling actual feathers under magnification. Small feathers in the lower pavilion at VS2 or VS1 grades are typically invisible face-up and present no durability concern. Larger feathers that run through the stone’s center or reach the surface at the girdle can be both visible and a potential durability risk if they create a path for mechanical failure. GIA notes any feather reaching the surface; a feather described as “significant” in the clarity plot comments warrants professional evaluation.

Clouds are groups of very small pinpoint inclusions clustered together. An isolated, small cloud appears as a slightly hazy patch under magnification. Most clouds in VS1 and VS2 grade stones are invisible to the naked eye and have no impact on optical performance. However, a dense, extensive cloud can affect the stone’s transparency and brilliance — making the stone appear slightly hazy in the face-up view. Dense clouds are the one inclusion type that can genuinely affect a diamond’s optical performance rather than simply contributing to a grade.

Position and Orientation

Why Location Within the Stone Matters

The grade on a GIA certificate reflects the worst characteristic found in the stone under 10x magnification. It does not specify where that characteristic is. Two VS2 stones can appear completely different face-up depending on where their key inclusions are located. Understanding this is one of the most valuable pieces of knowledge for a practical diamond buyer.

Inclusions in the lower pavilion — below the girdle, in the bottom half of the stone — are the least visible in the face-up view. The pavilion facets reflect this region away from the direct line of sight. A large, otherwise borderline inclusion situated in the lower pavilion is frequently invisible in the finished ring despite its impact on the clarity grade. Conversely, an inclusion centered directly under the table — in the upper portion of the pavilion, directly in the face-up viewing path — is the most visible location for any inclusion of equivalent size and character.

The clarity plot on a GIA report shows inclusion positions schematically. Reading the plot to determine whether the key inclusion is centrally placed or peripheral requires practice but is entirely learnable. Any jeweler can walk you through a plot and explain the positional significance of what it shows. Asking for this explanation before purchasing a VS2 or SI1 stone is simply good buying practice.

Inclusions to Avoid Regardless of Grade

Specific Characteristics That Should Trigger a Different Stone

Several inclusion characteristics create real problems beyond their impact on the clarity grade, and stones with these characteristics should be declined or significantly discounted regardless of what grade they have received.

A large feather reaching the surface at the girdle creates a structural vulnerability that can worsen with time and impact. The feather provides a path for moisture and contaminants to enter the stone, and a hard enough blow to the girdle at the right angle can propagate the feather. If GIA notes “feather reaches surface at girdle” in the clarity plot, obtain a professional evaluation of the feather’s orientation and whether the setting configuration provides adequate protection for that position.

Dense, extensive clouds — particularly those noted in the GIA comments section rather than only in the clarity plot — can affect the stone’s transparency. GIA occasionally adds a comment noting that clarity grading is based on the grade of the internal characteristics alone and that the cloud’s effect on transparency was considered separately. This note means the stone may appear hazier than its grade suggests. It is not a common notation, but when it appears, it is meaningful.

Knots are crystals that reach the diamond’s surface. The knot intersection with the surface creates a textural difference from the polished facets surrounding it. Knots in exposed positions on the table or crown facets can be felt with the fingernail and are visible to careful examination. A knot under the table in a VS1 stone is a better characteristic choice than many SI1 inclusions, but knots on the crown facets are worth noting.

Buying Strategy

Using Inclusion Knowledge to Improve Value

The practical application of understanding inclusions is to evaluate SI1 and VS2 stones individually rather than by grade alone. The most significant value opportunities in diamond buying are in the VS2 to SI1 range for round brilliants, where a buyer who evaluates specific stones can find eye-clean examples at prices below VS1 while achieving equivalent face-up visual quality.

For step-cut shapes — emerald, asscher, baguette — this evaluation is harder because the open facet arrangement shows inclusions more directly. Step-cut buyers generally need to start at VS1 and use the grade as a more reliable proxy for eye-clean appearance. Brilliant-cut buyers, including round, oval, cushion, and pear, have more room to benefit from individual stone evaluation below VS1.

What People

Ask Us

What inclusions are most common in diamonds? Pinpoints — single tiny crystal particles, usually colorless — are the most common inclusion type across all clarity grades. They appear individually in high-clarity stones and in clusters (clouds) in lower-clarity material. Crystals of various sizes are the next most common category. Feathers (fractures) and naturals (portions of the original rough diamond surface preserved on the finished stone) are common at lower clarity grades.

Can inclusions affect how a diamond sparkles? Most inclusions have no meaningful effect on optical performance. The exception is dense, extensive clouds that create a hazy appearance, and very large feathers or fractures that disrupt the internal light reflection path. These are uncommon in VS1 and VS2 grades. In SI1 and below, where inclusions are larger and more numerous, the cumulative effect can begin to reduce transparency in some stones.

Is a needle inclusion a problem in a diamond? Needles are elongated, thin crystal inclusions that appear as fine lines under magnification. They are typically colorless and oriented along the diamond’s crystal axis. A single needle in the pavilion of a VS2 stone is rarely visible face-up and does not affect durability. Multiple needles crossing the stone’s center create a more visible pattern at certain angles. As with all inclusions, position and quantity both matter more than the type alone.

What does “twinning wisp” mean on a GIA report? A twinning wisp is a cluster of pinpoints, clouds, and small crystals arranged along a crystal growth twinning plane. The twinning plane is a structural feature where two diamond crystals grew together; the disturbance in the crystal lattice at the join can trap inclusions. Twinning wisps vary enormously in their visibility — some are subtle and positioned in low-visibility locations, others are prominent. The GIA plot and comments will indicate their extent and position.

Should I prefer no inclusions near the culet? The culet is the bottom point of the diamond, and inclusions near the culet occupy the most central position as seen through the table from above. The culet’s central position means inclusions there are potentially more visible than equivalent inclusions off-center. For modern round brilliants with a pointed culet (graded “None” on GIA reports), the central position is a mathematical point, and inclusions near the culet appear in the center of the face-up view. Off-center inclusions at the same size and character will generally be less visible.

title: Diamond Shape vs Cut: Two Different Things That Are Often Confused
body:
Shape answers the question “what does the diamond look like?” Cut answers the question “how well does the diamond work?” A round brilliant with a poor cut is a beautiful shape with mediocre performance.

Shape: The Outline

What Shape Refers to and the Available Options

Shape is the silhouette of the diamond as seen from above — the two-dimensional outline of the polished stone. The major shape categories are round, oval, pear, marquise (a pointed oval), heart, cushion, radiant, princess, emerald, and asscher. Each shape is a different starting decision about how the diamond’s mass will be distributed across the face-up surface and how the stone will read on the hand.

Round brilliants are the most common shape by volume because they combine maximum cutting efficiency in terms of light return with the most universally understood engagement ring visual language. Every other shape is classified as a “fancy shape” in the trade, regardless of how conventional or unconventional it appears. A princess cut is a fancy shape; a pear is a fancy shape; an emerald cut is a fancy shape.

Shape selection is fundamentally a matter of personal aesthetic and practical fit. Some shapes elongate the finger visually — ovals, pears, and marquise cuts extend along the finger’s length and make the hand appear longer and more slender. Square and rectangular shapes — princess, radiant, asscher, emerald — feel more architectural and geometric. Round is the most neutral option and reads as classically bridal across cultural contexts.

Shape choice also affects carat efficiency — how large a given weight appears on the hand. The oval is typically the most efficient fancy shape for face-up size per carat weight, because its elongated outline creates the impression of a larger stone than a round of the same weight. The round brilliant, by contrast, concentrates all its mass in a compact circular footprint and tends to appear slightly smaller per carat than elongated shapes.

Cut: The Quality of Execution

What Cut Grading Measures and Why It Matters

Cut refers to how precisely and skillfully the shape was executed — specifically, how the facet geometry, proportions, symmetry, and polish of the finished stone produce optical performance. Two round brilliants of identical shape, color, and clarity grades can differ dramatically in cut quality, and that difference determines whether the stone appears bright, brilliant, and alive or dull, flat, and lifeless.

GIA’s (Gemological Institute of America) cut grading for round brilliant diamonds is the industry standard evaluation. It assesses seven components: brightness (the total light reflected from the stone), fire (the dispersion of light into its spectral colors), scintillation (the pattern of light and dark areas during movement), weight ratio (the relationship between the stone’s weight and its apparent size), durability (the girdle thickness and culet size that affect resistance to damage), polish (the quality of the finished facet surfaces), and symmetry (the precision of facet alignment and proportion matching). The overall Cut grade — Excellent, Very Good, Good, Fair, or Poor — summarizes the evaluation across all these components.

For fancy shapes, GIA does not issue an overall Cut grade. This is the critical gap that creates risk for fancy-shape buyers who assume shape and cut are the same question. An oval diamond has no GIA Cut grade — it has Polish and Symmetry grades, which are necessary but not sufficient. Two GIA-certified ovals with identical Excellent Polish and Symmetry grades can still differ substantially in light performance, bow-tie effect severity, and overall visual quality. Evaluating fancy shape cut requires looking at the stone, not just the certificate.

The Bow-Tie and Other Shape-Specific Cut Issues

What to Watch for in Fancy Shapes

Several fancy shapes are prone to specific optical defects that result from poor cutting proportions. The bow-tie is the most common: a dark, butterfly-shaped shadow visible in the center of oval, pear, marquise, and sometimes elongated cushion diamonds. All diamonds with elongated outlines exhibit some degree of bow-tie because the shape’s geometry creates a zone in the center where light cannot return efficiently from the pavilion. The severity ranges from barely perceptible to dominant — a strong bow-tie that occupies most of the stone’s center is a significant visual defect that reduces the stone’s appeal and value.

The bow-tie is not listed on GIA certificates. It can only be evaluated by examining the stone in person or through high-quality video. A well-cut oval with a minor bow-tie that disappears as the stone moves is normal and acceptable. An oval where a dark tie is prominent even when the stone is still is a cutting deficiency that should be reflected in a significant price reduction.

Step-cut shapes — emerald and asscher — do not produce bow-ties but have their own cutting sensitivity. Because their parallel facets act like windows into the stone rather than reflectors, poorly proportioned step cuts show their pavilion directly and any asymmetry in pavilion depth becomes visible as uneven darkening across the stone’s face. The “Hall of Mirrors” effect in a well-cut emerald — the infinite-regress pattern of reflections down through the stone — is the result of precise pavilion parallelism. A poorly cut emerald loses this effect and appears flat.

Practical Buying Guidance

Making the Shape-Cut Decision Correctly

Shape should be chosen first, based on the wearer’s aesthetic preferences and the practical characteristics of each outline — its finger appearance, its setting options, its visual vocabulary. This is a personal decision that has no objectively correct answer.

Cut should then be maximized within the budget allocated to the chosen shape. For round brilliants, GIA Excellent or AGS (American Gem Society) Ideal 0 grades reliably identify the top tier of cutting performance. For fancy shapes, that assurance requires individual stone evaluation. The minimum acceptable standard for any fancy shape is GIA Excellent Polish and Symmetry grades, but those grades are necessary without being sufficient.

What People

Ask Us

Is “princess cut” a cut grade or a shape? Princess is a shape — a square or near-square outline with brilliant-style faceting. The cut quality of a princess-cut diamond is evaluated separately by the quality of its proportions and symmetry, not by the shape designation itself. Two princess-cut diamonds with the same GIA color and clarity grade can be cut beautifully or poorly; the shape name tells you nothing about that.

Why doesn’t GIA give cut grades to fancy shapes? GIA’s round brilliant cut grade is based on decades of optical modeling research that established specific proportion ranges that reliably produce optimal performance for that symmetrical shape. Fancy shapes vary too widely in their length-to-width ratios and silhouette nuances to be captured by a single set of ideal proportions. GIA has indicated interest in extending cut grading to oval shapes, but as of the current date, the overall cut grade applies only to round brilliants.

Does shape affect diamond price per carat? Yes, significantly. Round brilliants typically trade at a 20 to 40 percent premium over equivalent fancy shapes because they require more rough diamond to cut — more carat weight is lost in cutting a round than an oval or pear from the same rough. Among fancy shapes, marquise and pear cuts tend to be slightly less expensive per carat than ovals because demand is lower. Emerald and asscher cuts are typically priced between rounds and ovals.

Which shape is best for a small diamond? Round brilliants are forgiving of smaller sizes because their cutting pattern maximizes light return and scintillation per unit of surface area. Elongated shapes like ovals and marquise appear larger than rounds of the same weight, which can be useful at smaller sizes. Step cuts — emerald and asscher — tend to look better in larger sizes, where their open tables have enough surface area to show the depth and reflections that are their defining character.

Can the same diamond shape look different in different settings? Substantially so. An oval diamond in a simple solitaire with a thin band reads as modern and minimalist. The same oval diamond in a halo setting with a pavé band reads as elaborate and glamorous. Shape interacts strongly with setting design, and the same shape can produce very different visual outcomes depending on the mount. The best approach is to evaluate the complete ring — stone and setting together — rather than assessing the shape in isolation.

title: Carat Weight vs Face-Up Size: Why They Are Not the Same Thing
body:
A carat is a unit of mass — 0.2 grams — and a gram can be distributed across a wide table or buried in a deep pavilion, producing radically different face-up appearances for the same number on the certificate.

What Carat Weight Measures

The Mass Reality Behind the Number

A carat is exactly 200 milligrams, or one-fifth of a gram. This is a measure of mass — how much the stone weighs on a precise scale. It says nothing about where that mass is located in the stone’s three-dimensional geometry. A carat of diamond in a well-cut round brilliant is distributed across a diameter of approximately 6.5 millimeters and a depth of roughly 4 millimeters. A carat of diamond in a poorly proportioned stone with an excessively deep pavilion might measure 6.0 millimeters across the face-up diameter while hiding the additional mass below the girdle, where it contributes nothing to the stone’s appearance.

This means two GIA-certified one-carat round brilliants can have face-up diameters differing by half a millimeter or more — a difference that is directly visible when the stones are compared side by side. The deeper stone looks smaller on the hand despite weighing identical to the shallower, well-cut stone. The buyer who focuses exclusively on the carat number on the certificate and not the actual face-up diameter is buying the weight of an object rather than the appearance of a ring.

The diamond industry has structured its pricing around carat weight because weight is objective and measurable in a way that appearance quality is harder to standardize. This structure creates a gap between what buyers pay for and what buyers see, and understanding that gap is one of the most useful things a buyer can know before shopping.

How Shape Affects Face-Up Size

The Geometry of Apparent Size Per Carat

Shape is the most powerful variable determining how large a given carat weight appears. The same mass distributed across different shape outlines produces dramatically different face-up areas. An oval diamond, because its elongated outline extends the stone’s length along the finger, typically covers more two-dimensional surface per carat than a round brilliant. A marquise cut carries this further — its elongated pointed shape maximizes length-to-width ratio and creates the greatest apparent size among the common shapes for a given carat weight.

The specific numbers: a well-cut one-carat round brilliant measures approximately 6.5 mm in diameter, giving it a face-up area of roughly 33 square millimeters. A well-cut one-carat oval typically measures about 7.7 mm by 5.7 mm, giving a face-up area of approximately 34 to 36 square millimeters. A one-carat marquise might measure 10 mm by 5 mm for a face-up area of about 39 square millimeters. The marquise appears noticeably larger than the round despite weighing the same.

This effect is compounded by how the shapes sit on the finger. An elongated stone oriented along the finger’s length creates the visual impression of a longer, narrower finger — the stone’s length runs with the finger. This creates the perception of greater finger coverage and, by visual association, greater stone size. This is why oval, pear, and marquise cuts have consistently been preferred by buyers who want maximum visual presence from a given budget.

Cut Depth and Its Impact

How Proportions Control What the Scale Doesn’t Measure

Within any shape, the depth of the cut controls what proportion of the stone’s weight is used to produce the face-up appearance. GIA’s total depth percentage — total depth divided by average girdle diameter, expressed as a percentage — is the summary measurement. For round brilliants, the optimal total depth range for maximum light performance and efficient use of mass is approximately 59 to 62.5 percent. Below 57 percent, the pavilion is too shallow for proper light reflection. Above 65 percent, the pavilion is deep, hiding mass below the girdle plane.

A stone at 63 percent total depth versus one at 67 percent of the same carat weight will differ by roughly 0.3 to 0.4 mm in face-up diameter. That difference is worth knowing about: 0.3 mm in a one-carat stone means the difference between a stone that looks like a 0.90-carat stone and one that looks like a true one-carat stone in terms of face-up diameter.

For buyers of round brilliants with GIA Excellent cut grades, this issue is largely managed by the cut grade itself — the Excellent grade excludes stones with excessive depth. For fancy shapes, where no cut grade exists, checking the actual measurements stated on the certificate and calculating the face-up area is the correct approach. The certificate lists the millimeter dimensions; use those numbers, not just the carat weight.

Buying for Appearance

A Practical Framework

A buyer optimizing for face-up appearance per dollar should: choose an elongated shape over a round, verify that the stone’s total depth percentage is within the efficient range for that shape, check the actual millimeter measurements rather than relying on carat weight alone, and compare face-up areas across multiple stones of similar weight and quality before committing.

The practical result of applying this framework is that many buyers end up with an elongated shape at slightly less carat weight than their original target — a 0.85-carat oval that appears larger than a one-carat round — at a lower total price, with money left for higher color or cut quality or a better setting. This is not a compromise; it is a better outcome produced by understanding what you are actually paying for.

What People

Ask Us

Does a deeper diamond look smaller? Yes, in practice. A stone with an excessively deep pavilion hides carat weight below the girdle plane, which contributes nothing to the face-up appearance. Two stones of the same certified carat weight but different total depths will show different face-up diameters, with the deeper stone appearing smaller on the finger.

How do I find a diamond’s face-up size on the certificate? GIA certificates list the stone’s dimensions in millimeters — for round brilliants, a single average diameter is given; for fancy shapes, the length, width, and depth are all listed. Calculate the face-up area from these measurements to compare stones of similar weight across different cuts. For rounds, the diameter directly correlates to the face-up appearance — 6.5 mm is the expected diameter for a one-carat well-cut round.

Which diamond shape looks the largest for the money? The marquise and pear cuts produce the greatest face-up area per carat weight among common shapes because their elongated, pointed outlines extend the stone’s length without adding proportionate weight. Ovals are close behind. Rounds are the most compact shape for a given carat weight. Step cuts — emerald and asscher — tend to produce smaller face-up areas per carat because their proportions often involve greater depth for optical performance.

Is a wider diamond better than a deeper one? Not categorically. Depth in the pavilion is necessary for light reflection — a stone that is too shallow will lose light through the bottom rather than reflecting it back up. The optimal depth range for each shape balances face-up area with optical performance. Outside that range, additional depth serves only to add carat weight that doesn’t appear in the face-up view, which is inefficient from a value perspective.

What happens to face-up size if a ring is resized? Resizing the shank does not change the stone’s face-up size. The center stone’s diameter is set by the stone itself and the size of the head, not by the ring’s shank size. Resizing only affects the metal band’s inner diameter. A stone that appears large or small at a size 5 will appear identical in face-up dimensions at a size 7.

title: Are Diamonds a Good Investment? An Honest Assessment
body:
A fancy-colored diamond sold at Sotheby’s Geneva is not the same category of asset as the round brilliant in your engagement ring — and conflating the two leads to expensive disappointment.

The Hard Truth

Most Retail Diamonds Lose Value Immediately

Walk out of any jewelry store with a one-carat round brilliant and try to sell it the next morning. You will recover somewhere between forty and sixty cents on every dollar you spent. The spread between retail and wholesale is structural, not accidental. Dealers buy at wholesale and sell at retail. When you buy at retail, you start in a hole.

That is not a scandal — it is how every luxury goods market works. The difference is that diamonds carry a mythology of value retention that most other luxury goods do not. A Chanel jacket does not claim to be an investment. A diamond, marketed since the 1940s with the phrase “a diamond is forever,” carries an implied promise that the industry has never fully backed up with data.

The first thing any serious buyer must do is separate the question of personal meaning from the question of financial return. A diamond can be the right choice for an engagement ring, an heirloom, a piece of wearable art — and still be a poor financial instrument. Those two things coexist without contradiction.

What Moves Price

Cut Quality and Rarity Create Long-Term Value

Among colorless diamonds, the variables that hold value best over time are rarity and cut quality. A three-carat D-Flawless round brilliant with GIA (Gemological Institute of America) certification is a rare object. There are not many of them, demand among a narrow group of buyers stays consistent, and the stone is objectively gradeable — you can compare it to another stone with precision. That specificity matters when you try to resell.

Cut quality matters because it is the one variable that separates a stone that looks alive from one that looks like glass. A superbly cut stone holds its desirability over decades. A poorly cut stone in the same color and clarity grade trades at a meaningful discount.

What does not hold value well: commercial-grade one-carat rounds in the G–H, VS1–VS2 range, regardless of what you paid. That segment is a commodity. Supply is plentiful, thousands of stones match the grade, and price is set at the margin by global diamond production, not by your particular stone.

The Exception

Fancy-Colored Diamonds Behave Differently

Fancy-colored diamonds — natural pinks, blues, greens, and reds — occupy a genuinely different market. The supply of natural fancy-colored diamonds contracted sharply when the Argyle mine in Western Australia closed in 2020 after producing the majority of the world’s natural pink diamonds. Blue and green diamonds of significant size come to market perhaps a handful of times per year globally.

These stones have demonstrated price appreciation over multi-decade periods. They are not liquid — you cannot call a broker and sell tomorrow — but patient sellers have extracted meaningful returns. The caveat is capital requirement. Entry into investment-grade fancy-colored stones starts in the hundreds of thousands of dollars and quickly reaches the millions.

For the buyer working with a more modest budget, the honest answer is this: buy a diamond because you love it, because it will be worn and cherished and passed down, not because you expect it to outperform the stock market. Approached that way, the question of return becomes secondary to the question of quality — and choosing quality, at the right price, is always the right answer.

Working the Numbers

What Price Benchmarks Actually Tell You

The Rapaport Report — known in the trade as “the Rap” — publishes weekly price grids for colorless diamonds by shape, weight, color, and clarity. It is a wholesale benchmark, not a retail price list. When dealers negotiate, they trade at discounts or premiums to Rap. Understanding where a stone’s asking price sits relative to Rap gives you signal about whether you are paying a fair price.

For fancy-colored diamonds, no equivalent universal benchmark exists. Price discovery happens at auction, in private treaty sales, and through specialized brokers. That opacity is part of why fancy-colored stones reward buyers who do their homework and work with dealers who have genuine experience in that market.

A final point: certification matters absolutely. A GIA certificate on a colorless stone confirms the grade. For fancy-colored diamonds, both the GIA and the Gübelin Gem Lab in Lucerne are the accepted authorities. Any stone offered as an investment without third-party certification from one of these labs should be declined, full stop.

What People

Ask Us

Are lab-grown diamonds a good investment?

Lab-grown diamonds are not investment vehicles by any reasonable definition. Prices have fallen sixty to seventy percent over the past three years as production has scaled, and there is no structural floor — manufacturers can produce more. If you want a beautiful stone at a lower price point, lab-grown has real advantages. If you are thinking about resale value, the answer is no.

What carat weight is large enough to hold value?

Among colorless diamonds, stones above two carats in high color and clarity grades hold up better than commercial-grade smaller stones — but “hold value” still means something different from “appreciate in value.” The market for exceptional stones is narrower but more consistent. Below one carat in standard grades, you are in full commodity territory.

Does the setting affect resale value?

The setting has almost no bearing on resale value of the diamond. Buyers purchasing a loose stone are buying the stone, not the metalwork. Custom settings are worth what the metal is worth at melt, minus the dealer’s cost to remove the stone — which is to say, very little. Separate your love for a setting from any financial calculus around the stone.

How do auction results translate to what I should pay?

Hammer prices at Christie’s or Sotheby’s reflect the best available buyers for the best available stones on a specific day. They are data points, not floor prices. Buyer’s premiums at major auction houses add fifteen to twenty-five percent on top of the hammer price, which means the effective price paid is substantially higher than the number reported in headlines.

Is a GIA certificate the only one worth having?

GIA is the global standard for colorless diamonds, and it is the one most resale buyers require. AGS (American Gem Society) grading is also well respected and uses a slightly different cut-grading methodology that some buyers prefer. For fancy-colored diamonds, GIA and Gübelin are the only labs whose color origin and grade determinations carry full weight in the high-value market.
