title: Fancy Yellow Diamond Rings: What Makes Color Diamonds Valuable
body:
A fancy yellow diamond that the color scale calls “light yellow” would be penalized at the bottom of the white diamond scale; elevated to the fancy color world, it becomes a stone worth celebrating.

How Fancy Color Diamonds Are Graded

The Departure From the D-Z Scale

The GIA (Gemological Institute of America) D-to-Z color scale measures how far a white diamond departs from colorlessness. Reaching Z — light yellow — on that scale is the bottom of the white diamond grading system and carries the lowest value premiums within the white diamond market. Everything changes at the other side of that boundary: a stone with enough color saturation to be classified as “Fancy” enters a separate grading category where saturation is an asset rather than a liability.

GIA’s fancy color grading scale for yellow diamonds assigns grades in order of increasing saturation: Fancy Light, Fancy, Fancy Intense, Fancy Vivid, and Fancy Deep. The highest commercial value belongs to Fancy Vivid — the grade indicating the maximum saturation achievable in natural yellow diamonds without the color darkening into the “Deep” category. A Fancy Vivid yellow is a pure, highly saturated yellow that shows no orange or green modifiers. It is also the rarest and most expensive yellow grade.

The hue descriptor matters as well as the saturation grade. A pure yellow — no modifiers — is the most valuable expression. Yellow diamonds with an orange modifier (often called “canary” in the trade) command slightly lower prices than pure yellows at equivalent saturation. Yellow diamonds with green modifiers — called “chameleon” effects in some stones — are in a separate specialty category. The GIA report states both the saturation grade and the hue description, and both matter to pricing.

What Drives Value in Yellow Diamonds

Saturation, Size, and the Supply Reality

The color in yellow diamonds comes primarily from structural defects involving nitrogen — specifically, the concentration of isolated nitrogen atoms dispersed through the crystal lattice. Most natural diamonds contain some nitrogen; it is the most common impurity in diamond and is responsible for the faint yellow body color that distinguishes a Z-grade stone from a D. In fancy yellow diamonds, the nitrogen concentration is high enough, and the arrangement specific enough, to produce vivid, saturated yellow rather than faint warmth.

Size amplifies color. A Fancy Vivid yellow at one carat shows the color clearly in face-up viewing; the same grade in a three-carat stone shows the color dramatically, with far more surface area for the saturation to develop. This is why the per-carat premium for large fancy yellow stones escalates steeply — you are paying for both the saturation grade and the size that lets the saturation perform.

Supply is genuinely constrained. Fancy Vivid yellow diamonds represent a small fraction of the fancy color diamond market, which itself represents less than one percent of all diamonds mined. The primary source of high-quality fancy yellows has historically been South Africa — “canary” yellows from South African kimberlite pipes have been among the finest examples — with significant production also from Australia and Russia. Each major producing location has its own color character, and experienced buyers can often identify geographic origin from hue characteristics alone.

Setting Design for Yellow Diamonds

Why Metal Choice Matters More Than Usual

A yellow diamond’s color is the center of the ring’s visual experience, and the setting must support that color rather than competing with it. Yellow gold amplifies the stone’s warmth and creates a unified color story — the stone and the metal both work in the yellow family, and the result is a ring that feels coherent and intentional. Platinum or white gold under a yellow stone creates contrast that some clients find dramatic and others find incongruous.

The conventional setting for a major fancy yellow center stone is a mix of yellow gold prongs holding the stone and a platinum or white gold band, creating contrast at the base while supporting the stone in a warm color. This combination is popular because it lets the stone read against a neutral background (the white hand) while the yellow gold prongs visually extend the stone’s color into the mount.

Cut design for fancy yellow diamonds differs from white diamond cutting practice. The goal in white diamonds is maximum light return to produce brightness and scintillation. The goal in fancy yellow diamonds is maximum color saturation as seen in the face-up view. Cutters sacrifice some brilliance to achieve this, using modified brilliant cuts and cushion shapes that distribute color evenly across the table rather than creating the light-and-dark contrast pattern that produces scintillation. The radiant cut — a rectangular brilliant — was developed specifically for fancy color diamonds and remains the most common shape because it delivers both good color face-up and reasonable light return.

Pricing and Investment

What Fancy Yellow Diamonds Cost and What They Hold

Fancy Light yellow diamonds — the entry saturation grade — begin around $2,000 to $4,000 per carat for stones in the half-to-one carat range, depending on quality of cut and secondary color characteristics. Fancy and Fancy Intense grades run $4,000 to $10,000 per carat in comparable sizes. Fancy Vivid yellows — the premium tier — cost $10,000 to $25,000 per carat for well-cut, pure yellow stones, with exceptional specimens above three carats at GIA Fancy Vivid reaching $40,000 per carat or more at auction.

These prices have historically maintained stability better than many categories of colored stones. Yellow diamonds, unlike sapphires or emeralds, do not have meaningful synthetic competition that has compressed natural prices. Lab-grown fancy yellow diamonds exist, but demand for them is more limited than for lab-grown white diamonds, and the natural stone market operates largely independently.

What People

Ask Us

What is the difference between a canary diamond and a fancy yellow diamond? “Canary” is a trade term, not a GIA grade. It describes pure, vivid yellow diamonds without the formal grading connotation. On a GIA certificate, a canary diamond would be graded Fancy Vivid or Fancy Intense yellow with no secondary color modifier. Not all fancy yellows are canary quality; the term implies a specific level of saturation and hue purity that corresponds to the top grade levels.

Are yellow diamonds rarer than white diamonds? Yes. Fancy color diamonds — all colors combined — represent roughly 0.01 to 0.05 percent of all diamonds mined. Among fancy color diamonds, yellow is the most common color, but that still places them far rarer than the D-Z range white diamonds that dominate the market. Fancy Vivid yellows specifically are genuinely uncommon in any commercial quantity.

Do fancy yellow diamonds hold value better than white diamonds? High-quality fancy yellow diamonds have historically held value well and appreciated modestly over long periods. The market is less liquid than white diamonds — there are fewer buyers for any specific fancy color stone — but the rarity and the absence of meaningful synthetic competition support stable pricing. A Fancy Vivid yellow with GIA documentation is a better long-term value retention asset than most colored stones.

Can I set a yellow diamond in white gold? You can, and some designs use white gold or platinum intentionally to create a cool-warm contrast. The practical consequence is that the white metal under and around the stone makes the stone’s yellow more vivid by contrast, which works well for highly saturated stones. For lower saturation grades, white metal can also make the slight warmth of the stone more apparent rather than more celebratory, so Fancy Light yellows typically look better in yellow gold.

What cut shapes show yellow color best in a diamond? The radiant cut and cushion cut are the two shapes most commonly used for fancy yellow diamonds precisely because their facet arrangements distribute color evenly across the face-up view. Round brilliants suppress body color through their light-return optimization, which reduces color saturation in fancy yellow material. Emerald cuts show color strongly but can exhibit uneven color distribution. Radiant and cushion remain the industry standard choices for yellow diamond cutting.

title: GIA vs AGS Diamond Certification: Which Lab Report Matters More
body:
A diamond without a GIA or AGS certificate is not uncertified — it is certified by someone you should not entirely trust, and that distinction has real money attached to it.

Why Certification Matters

The Problem of Grade Inflation

The diamond laboratory business has a structural conflict of interest: laboratories are paid by dealers and manufacturers to grade stones, and laboratories that grade generously attract more stones to grade. This dynamic has produced systematic grade inflation in most secondary laboratories. A stone graded VS1, G by a house lab or a minor independent laboratory is statistically likely to be VS2 or SI1, H or I when submitted to GIA. The grade on the certificate looks the same to a consumer; the stone’s actual quality does not.

GIA (Gemological Institute of America) and AGS (American Gem Society) have maintained grading consistency for decades, and their grades trade at premiums in dealer-to-dealer markets precisely because professional buyers trust them. This is not sentiment — it is reflected in actual market prices. A GIA-graded VS1 G stone commands meaningfully more money than an identically described stone from a lesser laboratory, because the professional market has priced the reliability premium into the GIA grade.

Any buyer who does not have the grading knowledge to independently evaluate a stone’s color and clarity should insist on GIA or AGS certification as a non-negotiable condition of purchase. This is not elitism — it is the minimum available protection against systematic misrepresentation.

GIA: The Global Standard

What GIA Certification Covers and What Sets It Apart

GIA is the largest and most recognized independent diamond grading laboratory in the world. Its grading reports cover the 4Cs — cut, color, clarity, and carat weight — along with fluorescence, symmetry, polish, and the proportions diagram showing table percentage, crown angle, pavilion depth, and girdle thickness. For round brilliant diamonds, GIA also assigns an overall Cut grade from Excellent to Poor based on a comprehensive optical modeling system.

GIA reports are available in multiple formats. The full Diamond Grading Report covers stones above 0.15 carats with complete measurements and proportions data. The Diamond Dossier is a laser-inscribed version with condensed information, used for smaller stones. The Diamond Origin Report, introduced in 2020, adds rough-stone provenance data for certain categories. For standard engagement ring purchases, the full Diamond Grading Report or Dossier is what you are looking for.

GIA does not buy or sell diamonds, does not appraise diamonds for resale, and has no financial interest in the grades it assigns. This independence is the foundation of the GIA grade’s credibility. The laboratory is funded by its grading fees and its educational programs, which creates clean separation from the dealer market.

AGS: The Cut Specialist

Where AGS Exceeds GIA’s Detail Level

AGS uses a different grading nomenclature and a different cut grading methodology. Where GIA grades color on the D-Z letter scale, AGS grades color on a 0 to 10 numeric scale — 0 is colorless (equivalent to GIA’s D) and 10 corresponds to light yellow. Where GIA grades clarity with abbreviations (FL, IF, VVS1, etc.), AGS uses numeric equivalents. The underlying standards are comparable, and the grades translate directly between systems.

The area where AGS distinctly outperforms GIA is in cut grading for fancy shapes. GIA’s Excellent cut grade applies only to round brilliant diamonds. For oval, pear, cushion, marquise, and other fancy shapes, GIA assigns Polish and Symmetry grades but offers no overall Cut grade. This is a significant gap for buyers of fancy-shape stones who want objective cut-quality assurance.

AGS’s performance-based cut grading system — called the AGS Ideal 0 grade — has been extended to certain fancy shapes including ovals and cushions through their Light Performance grading system. An AGS Ideal 0 oval diamond has been objectively evaluated for light return, leakage, and contrast patterns in a way that GIA does not provide for ovals. For fancy-shape buyers who prioritize cutting performance, an AGS certificate offers information that GIA’s report does not.

Choosing Between the Two

Which Certificate to Prioritize for Your Purchase

For round brilliant diamonds, GIA and AGS are interchangeable at the top grades — a GIA Excellent and an AGS Ideal 0 both represent the top tier of cutting performance, and both grades are graded by independent laboratories with established reliability. The choice between them for a round brilliant comes down to which certificate your dealer has available rather than a meaningful quality distinction.

For fancy shapes — oval, pear, cushion, marquise, radiant, trillion — AGS adds value through its Light Performance grading. A GIA-certified oval is adequately documented for most purposes; an AGS Ideal 0 oval is more specifically evaluated for cutting performance. If you are investing significantly in a fancy-shape center stone and cutting quality is a priority, the AGS certificate is worth seeking out specifically.

The practical reality is that GIA certificates are more widely available across the diamond inventory at most dealers, simply because GIA’s market share is larger. AGS Ideal 0 stones represent a smaller proportion of available inventory. Knowing that both are trustworthy, I advise clients not to pass on an exceptional stone with a GIA certificate in search of an AGS equivalent if the GIA certificate shows Excellent grades across cut, polish, and symmetry for a round brilliant.

What People

Ask Us

Is a GIA certificate a guarantee of value? A GIA certificate is a guarantee of grade accuracy from a trusted laboratory. It is not a guarantee of value in the financial sense. The market value of the stone depends on its quality parameters, the supply and demand for diamonds generally, and your specific negotiation. The GIA grade tells you what you have accurately; what that is worth depends on market conditions.

Are there other laboratories worth accepting? For stones from reputable dealers, GCAL (Gemological Certification and Assurance Lab) maintains a reliable grading standard and is sometimes seen on estate and auction pieces. IGI (International Gemological Institute) has historically shown grade inflation in studies, though IGI has made consistency investments and is commonly used for lab-grown diamonds, where GIA and AGS availability is more limited. For natural diamonds, GIA and AGS remain the standards I recommend without reservation.

Does the certificate number match the inscription on the stone? For GIA and AGS certified stones, yes. Both laboratories laser-inscribe the certificate number on the diamond’s girdle as part of standard documentation. This allows you to verify that the stone in your ring matches the certificate it was sold with. The inscription is visible under 10x magnification. Always verify the inscription matches the report number before accepting delivery.

What happens if a stone loses its certificate? GIA and AGS maintain electronic records of all graded stones and can reissue a report. GIA calls this a “duplicate report” service. There is a fee for the service, and the reissued report reflects the original grading data. For estate or inherited diamonds without certificates, GIA and AGS also accept stones for new grading submissions.

Should lab-grown diamonds have GIA or AGS certificates? Yes. GIA began grading lab-grown diamonds in 2019, using the same color and clarity scale but with “Laboratory-Grown” stated clearly on the report header. AGS also grades lab-grown diamonds. Buying a lab-grown diamond without a GIA or IGI certificate from a reputable dealer is inadvisable — the same grade inflation risks present in the natural market exist in the lab-grown market and are arguably more prevalent there.

title: How to Read a Diamond Grading Report
body:
Most buyers look at a diamond certificate for four numbers and stop — but the proportions diagram, clarity plot, and comments section contain the real information that separates good stones from great ones within the same grade.

The Certificate Basics

What a GIA Report Actually Contains

A GIA (Gemological Institute of America) Diamond Grading Report is a standardized document reporting the results of a professional gemological examination of a specific diamond. The report includes a GIA report number, the date of issue, the shape and cutting style, the measurements in millimeters, and the 4Cs grades — carat weight, color, clarity, and cut (for round brilliants). Beyond those headline items, the report contains a proportions diagram, a clarity plot, a laser inscription number, and additional grading information fields.

The report number is the most critical piece of information for verification. Every certified GIA stone has this number laser-inscribed on its girdle, and the GIA online report check system allows anyone to verify that the number matches the physical stone and retrieve the original grading data. Verifying the inscription against the report before accepting delivery is non-negotiable for any significant purchase.

The measurements field — listed in millimeters as diameter and depth for round stones, or length by width by depth for fancy shapes — tells you the physical dimensions of the stone before any proportional analysis. These numbers allow you to calculate the stone’s face-up area and verify that the depth is within efficient proportional ranges for the shape. A one-carat round listed as 6.3 mm rather than 6.5 mm tells you immediately that the stone is cut deep and is sacrificing face-up size for carat weight.

The Proportions Diagram

What the Numbers Under the Diamond Drawing Mean

The proportions diagram on a GIA round brilliant report is a cross-section drawing of the stone with all major proportional measurements labeled numerically. Table percentage, crown angle, crown height, girdle thickness range, pavilion angle, pavilion depth, culet size, and total depth percentage all appear here. For buyers who want to evaluate cut quality beyond the summary Cut grade, this is where the real information lives.

Table percentage — the table’s width as a percentage of the girdle diameter — should fall between 53 and 62 percent for maximum optical performance in round brilliants. Crown angle — the angle of the main crown facets relative to the girdle plane — should fall between 33.7 and 35.8 degrees. Pavilion angle — the most critical single measurement — should fall between 40.6 and 41.0 degrees for ideal light reflection. These ranges define the “ideal proportions” zone popularized by AGS (American Gem Society) research and refined by GIA’s optical modeling work.

A stone can receive a GIA Excellent cut grade while sitting slightly outside the tightest ideal proportions ranges, because the GIA Excellent encompasses a broader range of proportions that all produce high optical performance, not just the absolute narrowest ideal window. The proportions diagram allows buyers who want to verify they are within the tightest ideal range to do so without relying solely on the summary grade.

For fancy shapes — oval, pear, cushion, emerald, and others — GIA does not issue a cut grade, but the measurements are still reported. For fancy shapes, the length-to-width ratio (calculated from the reported measurements) is the primary proportional data point that buyers use to evaluate whether a stone’s outline matches their aesthetic preferences. A length-to-width ratio of 1.35 to 1.45 is considered the classic oval proportions; below 1.3 the stone reads as almost round, above 1.5 the stone is very elongated.

The Clarity Plot

What the Diagram of Inclusions Tells You

The clarity plot is a schematic diagram showing the position of all inclusions and surface characteristics within the stone. Inclusions are shown by their position in the face-up view (the table diagram) and in a side view (the pavilion diagram). The symbols used in the clarity plot correspond to specific types of characteristics — crystals, clouds, feathers, pinpoints, needles, indented naturals, extra facets, and others — each with its own symbol listed in the legend.

The clarity plot reveals something the grade alone cannot: where the inclusions are. An SI1 clarity grade tells you that inclusions are noticeable at 10x magnification but gives you no information about whether they are centrally located under the table (where they are most visible face-up) or near the girdle (where they are least visible). The plot shows you directly. A cluster of small inclusions near the girdle at the 4 o’clock position in the face-up view is fundamentally different from a large crystal centered under the table, even if both stones receive the same clarity grade.

Reading the plot requires knowing the symbol conventions. A green symbol indicates a surface-reaching blemish; a red symbol indicates an internal characteristic. The plot also shows whether inclusions are light-colored (open symbols) or dark (filled symbols). A dark crystal inclusion under the table creates a visible dark spot in the face-up view at much higher clarity grades than a colorless cloud inclusion in the same position.

Additional Report Fields

Comments, Polish, Symmetry, and Fluorescence

Polish and symmetry grades appear separately from the overall cut grade for round brilliants and are the only cut-quality grades for fancy shapes. Both are reported on the same Excellent-to-Poor scale as the overall cut grade. For round brilliants, Polish and Symmetry grades should both be Excellent or Very Good to support the best optical performance. A stone with Excellent cut but Good symmetry has a specific facet alignment deficiency that the cut grade alone does not reveal.

Fluorescence is reported with an intensity grade (None, Faint, Medium, Strong, Very Strong) and a color (almost always Blue). Understanding the fluorescence grade’s implication for the specific stone’s color grade is one of the most important contextual reads a buyer needs to make. Strong blue fluorescence in a G-I color stone is an asset in outdoor daylight; the same intensity in a D-F stone requires physical examination for potential haziness.

The comments field at the bottom of the report notes anything the grader found noteworthy that does not fit the standard data fields. This can include notation of natural inclusions preserved during cutting, treatment disclosures, or notes about unusual characteristics. Any notation in the comments field should be reviewed and understood before purchase.

What People

Ask Us

Can I trust a GIA report from any dealer? You can trust the GIA report if you verify that the stone matches it. The GIA inscription number on the girdle must match the report number, and the GIA report check website will confirm the certificate is in GIA’s database. A dealer who refuses to allow this verification is a dealer you should not buy from. The report itself is reliable; the stone being sold with it needs to be confirmed as the same stone.

What is a clarity plot used for? The clarity plot shows you where inclusions are located within the stone, which the grade alone does not tell you. Use it to determine whether the key inclusion driving the clarity grade is centrally located under the table (most visible) or near the girdle and pavilion (least visible). A well-positioned inclusion in a VS2 stone may be completely invisible face-up; a centrally placed inclusion in the same grade may be the first thing you notice.

Why does the GIA report show a range for girdle thickness? The girdle thickness varies around the circumference of a round brilliant because the facets that form the girdle alternate between thinner and thicker zones. The report shows the minimum and maximum thickness encountered during measurement, expressed as the thin-thick range (for example, Thin to Medium). The critical reading is whether either endpoint reaches “Extremely Thin” or “Extremely Thick,” both of which are problematic for different reasons.

What does “laser drilled” mean on a GIA report? Laser drilling is a treatment in which a laser beam is used to create a channel through the stone to a dark inclusion, followed by chemical treatment to bleach or dissolve the inclusion. The treatment improves the visual appearance of heavily included stones. GIA discloses laser drilling in the comments and on the clarity grade assessment. Laser drilled stones trade at a significant discount to untreated stones of the same apparent clarity because the treatment is artificial and permanent.

Should I buy a diamond without a GIA or AGS report? Not at any significant price point. Without a report from a trusted laboratory, the grade claims on the stone — color, clarity, cut — are supported only by the seller’s word or a report from a laboratory you may not be able to evaluate for reliability. The cost of GIA or AGS certification is a small percentage of any significant diamond purchase and is the most important protection the buyer has. Decline unstated-origin reports; the few dollars the certification costs the seller is not a reason to accept unverified quality claims.

title: Ideal Cut Diamonds: What the Grade Means and Whether It Matters
body:
The “ideal cut” designation does not mean the diamond is as perfect as possible within its grade category — it means the stone’s proportions fall within a range that optical research has shown produces the best combination of brightness, fire, and scintillation.

The History of Ideal Proportions

Where the Standard Came From

Marcel Tolkowsky published “Diamond Design” in 1919, presenting mathematical analysis of the proportions that maximize both brightness and fire in a round brilliant diamond. His calculations — a table percentage of 53 percent, crown angle of 35 degrees, pavilion angle of 40.75 degrees — defined what became known as the “Tolkowsky ideal.” The American Gem Society (AGS) adopted these proportions as the basis for their cut grading system, and the “Ideal 0” grade — their top cut grade — has been associated with this mathematical foundation ever since.

The practical proportions range that produces top optical performance has been refined since Tolkowsky’s work through advances in optical modeling and empirical measurement. Modern research, including GIA’s (Gemological Institute of America) extensive Facetware modeling studies, has established that excellent optical performance is achieved across a somewhat broader range of proportions than Tolkowsky specified. GIA’s Excellent cut grade encompasses this broader range; AGS’s Ideal 0 grade includes the stricter window. Both represent genuine top-tier cutting performance by any practical measurement.

The terminology “ideal cut” is used loosely in the trade. Some dealers apply the term to any round brilliant with high GIA polish and symmetry grades, regardless of overall cut assessment. Others use it specifically for AGS Ideal 0 stones. Buyers should ask what specific certification grade the “ideal cut” designation refers to, rather than accepting the term without documentation.

What Excellent and Ideal Actually Measure

The Seven Components GIA Uses for Cut Grading

GIA’s round brilliant cut grade is based on seven evaluated attributes: brightness (total light reflected from the stone, both from the crown and through the pavilion), fire (dispersion of white light into its spectral colors), scintillation (the flashing pattern of light and dark areas as the stone moves), weight ratio (how the stone’s mass is distributed relative to its diameter), durability (girdle thickness and culet size), polish (quality of facet surfaces), and symmetry (precision of facet alignment and proportion matching between equivalent facets).

The overall cut grade is a weighted summary of these components, assessed through a combination of measured proportions, polish and symmetry grades, and optical simulation. A stone reaches the Excellent grade by scoring in the top tier across all components — no single component can pull the overall grade to Excellent if others are poor.

In practical terms, an Excellent-cut round brilliant has maximum light return with efficient distribution across the full face-up area, no significant dark zones (nailheads or fish-eye effect), organized and balanced scintillation pattern, and facet symmetry precise enough that the “hearts and arrows” pattern is visible under a gemscope. These are observable qualities, not abstract grades — a well-cut stone looks visibly different from a mediocre-cut stone of equal color and clarity.

When Cut Grade Matters Most

The Contexts Where Top Cutting Makes a Measurable Difference

Cut grade has the greatest visible impact in three situations. The first is round brilliants, where the cut grade is directly assessable through GIA’s grading system and where the range between Excellent and Good cut is wide enough that the visual difference is immediately apparent even to an untrained observer. A GIA Good-cut round brilliant can appear lifeless beside a GIA Excellent-cut stone of the same color and clarity because the Good-cut’s proportions allow light to leak from the pavilion rather than reflecting back to the eye.

The second situation is smaller stones, where the face-up surface area is limited and the stone’s optical performance per unit of area matters most. A half-carat Excellent-cut stone will out-perform a half-carat Very Good-cut stone more visibly than the same comparison at two carats, because the smaller total surface makes the performance difference more apparent relative to the whole.

The third is step-cut shapes — emerald and asscher cuts — where cutting precision and pavilion flatness are the primary determinants of the stone’s characteristic depth, reflective quality, and “Hall of Mirrors” effect. These shapes do not have GIA cut grades, but the consequences of poor cutting are even more immediately visible in step cuts than in brilliant cuts, because the open table exposes the interior directly rather than breaking the view into scintillating facets.

When the Top Grade Premium Is and Is Not Worth It

A Practical Framework for the Buying Decision

For round brilliants, the GIA Excellent cut grade is the minimum I recommend across all budgets and sizes. The price difference between Excellent and Very Good cut grades at the same color and clarity is typically 10 to 20 percent; the visual difference is real and immediate. Below Very Good, the compromise becomes significant enough that the savings are not justified by the visual result.

The question of whether to target the AGS Ideal 0 specifically within the GIA Excellent category is more nuanced. The AGS Ideal 0 grade’s tighter proportions window identifies the best-performing subset of the GIA Excellent range, and AGS Ideal 0 stones consistently display the hearts-and-arrows pattern that indicates precise cutting. However, a GIA Excellent stone with proportions verified to be within the tighter ideal window — table 54-60 percent, crown angle 34-35 degrees, pavilion angle 40.6-41.0 degrees — performs equivalently to an AGS Ideal 0 for most practical purposes.

For buyers who do not have the expertise to evaluate specific proportion combinations from the GIA certificate, the AGS Ideal 0 label provides a reliable quality signal within GIA Excellent. For buyers comfortable reading a proportions diagram, the GIA Excellent grade with verified proportions within the ideal window is equally reliable and often more widely available in dealer inventory.

What People

Ask Us

Is an ideal cut diamond always worth the premium? For round brilliants, yes — the cut grade premium over Very Good is well justified by the visual result. For fancy shapes, where no ideal cut grade exists from GIA, the concept of “ideal” requires individual stone evaluation rather than a certificate grade. The premium for AGS Ideal 0 within the GIA Excellent range is a more nuanced decision that depends on whether the buyer needs the label as a quality signal or can evaluate proportions directly.

What is the difference between AGS Ideal 0 and GIA Excellent? GIA Excellent is a broad top-tier cut grade that encompasses a range of proportions that all produce excellent optical performance. AGS Ideal 0 is the top cut grade from a different laboratory using a performance-based assessment model that identifies the best-performing subset of that range. All AGS Ideal 0 stones would receive GIA Excellent grades if submitted to GIA; not all GIA Excellent stones would receive AGS Ideal 0 grades. Both represent genuinely outstanding cutting quality.

Can I find ideal cut diamonds in fancy shapes? AGS has extended its Light Performance cut grading to some fancy shapes, including oval and cushion cuts, through their optional Light Performance assessment. A stone receiving an AGS Ideal 0 Light Performance grade for an oval shape has been assessed for brightness, fire, and contrast patterns specific to that shape. This is a meaningful addition to the fancy shape evaluation toolkit, though it is available for fewer stone shapes than the GIA Excellent round grade.

Does ideal cut guarantee the diamond will sparkle? An ideal cut guarantees that the stone’s proportions are within the range that maximizes optical performance for that shape. It is the best available assurance that the stone will perform well optically. It does not guarantee that the stone will perform identically to every other ideal cut stone, because color, clarity, fluorescence, and individual stone character all interact with the proportions. But the cut grade eliminates one category of performance risk and is the most controllable variable in diamond performance.

What is a “super ideal” cut? “Super ideal” is a marketing term used by some cutters and dealers to describe round brilliants cut to the tightest possible proportions window — typically hearts-and-arrows stones cut to Tolkowsky proportions or tighter AGS-defined parameters. These stones represent the apex of round brilliant cutting precision and can be identified by the consistency and symmetry of their hearts-and-arrows pattern. They command a premium above standard AGS Ideal 0 stones and are appropriate for buyers who want absolute certainty about cutting quality and are prepared to pay the premium for it.

title: Internally Flawless Diamonds: Is the Premium Worth It
body:
An internally flawless diamond is not a better-looking diamond than a VS1 — it is a rarer diamond, and rarity and appearance are not the same thing.

What Internally Flawless Means

The Grade and Its Precise Definition

The GIA (Gemological Institute of America) clarity scale places Flawless (FL) and Internally Flawless (IF) at the top, above the VVS (Very Very Slightly Included) grades. A Flawless diamond has no inclusions and no blemishes visible to a skilled grader under 10x magnification. An Internally Flawless diamond has no inclusions visible at 10x but has insignificant surface blemishes — typically minor surface graining, small naturals on the girdle, or extra facets — that do not affect the stone’s internal purity.

The distinction between FL and IF is almost entirely academic for practical buyers. Extra facets on the pavilion or a small natural on the girdle do not affect the stone’s optical performance, its durability, or its visual appearance. The IF grade on a certificate signals internal perfection while acknowledging minor, typically invisible surface characteristics. Both FL and IF trade in the same premium tier.

The clarity grades below IF — VVS1 and VVS2 — contain inclusions that are extremely difficult to locate even for a trained grader at 10x. In practice, finding the inclusion that determines a VVS grade requires a skilled examiner, optimal lighting, and patience. The GIA clarity plot on a VVS certificate often shows the characteristic in a location near the girdle or in the lower pavilion, where it affects the grade while being entirely invisible in face-up viewing.

The Appearance Reality

What an IF Diamond Looks Like Versus a VS1

Face-up, in a ring, at normal viewing distance, an Internally Flawless diamond is visually indistinguishable from a VS1 (Very Slightly Included 1) diamond. This is not a controversial claim in gemology — it is a straightforward consequence of what the grades mean. VS1 inclusions are “difficult to see under 10x magnification.” In the face-up view at arm’s length, they are invisible to any normal observer. The IF stone has none, but the absence of something invisible produces no change in what the eye sees.

The difference becomes apparent only under magnification, in laboratory conditions, with trained evaluation. That context — laboratory examination — is not the context in which an engagement ring is worn and appreciated. A dinner in candlelight, a party under mixed lighting, everyday office wear: in all of these conditions, IF and VS1 are the same visual experience.

The premium between VS1 and IF at equivalent color and cut grades runs approximately 20 to 40 percent depending on stone size and market conditions. On a one-carat stone, this might mean $1,500 to $3,000. On a three-carat stone, it can mean $15,000 to $30,000 in stone price alone. That is a substantial sum for a quality improvement that produces no observable result in the ring’s daily visual experience.

Who Should Buy IF

The Legitimate Case for Internally Flawless

The argument for Internally Flawless is not visual — it is positional. IF diamonds occupy the apex of the natural diamond quality pyramid. For buyers who want to own the best available specimen — collectors, investors, buyers for whom the certificate is part of the ring’s meaning — IF is the correct choice. The premium exists because genuine scarcity commands it. Truly Flawless and Internally Flawless diamonds in significant sizes are rare enough that their supply is genuinely constrained.

For certified investment diamonds, IF and FL grades are preferred by sophisticated buyers because they carry the clearest quality story and retain the most value in resale markets. A GIA-certified three-carat D-IF stone is one of the most portable stores of value in the fine jewelry market, and the IF grade is part of what makes that true.

In very large stones — above three carats — IF clarity becomes more meaningful because the face-up table is large enough that VS1 inclusions, which are easily invisible in smaller stones, may be more visible. A five-carat VS1 might show its key inclusion to careful examination; a five-carat IF cannot. The grade’s practical value increases with stone size in a way that makes the premium more justifiable for major specimens.

The Budget Alternative

Where to Put the Savings From Choosing VS1

For the vast majority of clients buying engagement rings for wearing and daily enjoyment, VS1 is the correct clarity choice. It delivers eye-clean clarity across all common diamond shapes and sizes, carries GIA certification at the same reliability standard as IF, and costs meaningfully less. The difference between the IF and VS1 price at any given carat weight and color grade represents real money that can improve other aspects of the purchase.

The most rational allocation of the IF-to-VS1 savings is into cut quality for round brilliants, or into color grade, both of which produce visible improvements in the ring’s daily appearance. A D-VS1 Excellent-cut one-carat diamond will look better on the hand every day than an F-IF Excellent-cut stone at the same total price, because the color difference between D and F is perceptible under some lighting conditions, while the IF clarity premium above VS1 produces no perceptible change.

What People

Ask Us

Can you see any difference between an IF and VS1 diamond in a ring? No. Under normal viewing conditions, in a ring, at arm’s length, VS1 and IF diamonds are visually identical. The clarity difference between them is visible only under 10x magnification in laboratory conditions. The face-up appearance, brilliance, fire, and scintillation are governed by cut quality and color, not by clarity grades in the VS1-IF range.

Is an IF diamond a better investment than a VS1? For investment purposes, IF and FL grades are preferable because they represent the apex of the quality hierarchy and carry the clearest documentation story. A D-IF stone in a significant size has better liquidity in collector and investment markets than a D-VS1 stone. The investment premium is real, but it is an investment argument, not an appearance argument.

What makes a diamond lose an IF grade? Inclusions that are invisible at 10x in the rough or polished stone, surface blemishes beyond what IF permits, or grading discoveries upon resubmission. The IF grade is issued at a specific point in the stone’s history; a chip or scratch acquired during wear can reduce the effective grade if the stone were resubmitted. This is another reason to insure high-clarity diamonds: damage that seems cosmetically minor can affect the certified grade.

Do IF diamonds exist in all sizes? IF clarity occurs in diamonds of all sizes, but the proportion of stones achieving IF decreases as size increases. Finding an IF clarity specimen in a one-carat round is straightforward through major dealer networks. Finding a three-carat D-IF round is possible but significantly more time-consuming. Five-carat and above D-IF rounds are genuinely rare and may require targeted searching through international dealer networks.

Should I insure an IF diamond differently than a VS1? The replacement cost for an IF diamond is higher than for a VS1 of otherwise equivalent quality, so yes — the insured value should reflect the actual replacement cost of an IF specimen, which is higher than the VS1 replacement cost. A replacement value appraisal from a certified appraiser (not the selling jeweler) should be obtained at the time of purchase and updated periodically to reflect market changes.

title: Lab Grown vs Natural Diamond: The Complete Comparison
body:
Lab-grown diamonds and natural diamonds are the same material — carbon atoms arranged in the same cubic crystal structure, graded on the same scales, indistinguishable optically — and they are not the same thing, because identical material does not mean identical value.

The Chemistry

What Makes Lab-Grown Diamonds Actually Identical

A lab-grown diamond is diamond. Not diamond simulant, not diamond alternative — diamond. The carbon atoms are arranged in the same crystal lattice as natural diamond. The hardness is identical — 10 on the Mohs scale. The refractive index is identical — 2.417 to 2.419. The thermal conductivity is identical. The dispersion is identical. GIA (Gemological Institute of America) grades lab-grown diamonds using the same color and clarity scale it uses for natural diamonds, because the same grading criteria apply.

The two production methods used commercially are HPHT (High Pressure High Temperature) and CVD (Chemical Vapor Deposition). HPHT presses a carbon source under pressures and temperatures that replicate the geological conditions that form natural diamond — roughly 1.5 million pounds per square inch at 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit. CVD grows diamond crystals in a controlled chamber by depositing carbon vapor onto a diamond seed crystal. Both methods produce genuine diamond. Both produce stones that can appear in any color and clarity grade across the full GIA scale.

A trained gemologist using standard gemological equipment cannot distinguish a lab-grown diamond from a natural one by visual examination or standard refractive index measurement. Differentiation requires spectroscopic equipment — specifically, short-wave UV transmission and photoluminescence spectroscopy — available in gemological laboratories. GIA reports this origin on the certificate header with “Laboratory-Grown Diamond,” making documentation essential for any lab-grown purchase.

The Market Reality

What the Price Difference Actually Means

Lab-grown diamond prices have fallen dramatically over the past decade. A one-carat, E, VS1, Excellent-cut lab-grown round brilliant that traded at $5,000 in 2015 costs approximately $800 to $1,200 today. The price compression has been driven by production scale: as CVD growth technology became more efficient and more players entered the market, the cost of producing a lab-grown diamond dropped toward the cost of the energy and materials required. There is no geological scarcity to support price floors in lab-grown material.

Natural diamonds have not followed the same trajectory. Natural diamond prices fluctuate with economic conditions and supply constraints, but they have maintained value over decades in a way that lab-grown prices have not. A one-carat natural diamond in the E-VS1 range that cost $6,000 in 2015 costs $5,500 to $7,500 today depending on cutting quality and specific market conditions. The range moves; the baseline does not collapse.

The resale market reflects these dynamics directly. A lab-grown diamond sold to a dealer today typically recovers 15 to 30 percent of its retail purchase price. A comparable natural diamond recovers 40 to 70 percent depending on quality and conditions. If the ring is an asset — something you might need to convert to cash, something you intend to pass down with value intact — natural is the correct answer. If the ring is an object of beauty with no expectation of resale value, lab-grown delivers identical optical performance for a fraction of the cost, and that fraction can be invested elsewhere.

The Ethics Question

What Lab-Grown Solves and What It Does Not

The argument for lab-grown diamonds on ethical grounds is often framed around conflict diamonds — stones that fund armed conflict in producing regions. The Kimberley Process, established in 2003, certifies rough diamonds as conflict-free, but the process has documented limitations and does not address all human rights concerns in mining. For buyers whose primary concern is conflict diamond avoidance, lab-grown is a clear answer.

The more complete ethical picture is more complicated. Natural diamond mining is the primary formal-sector economic activity in several southern African nations. It employs hundreds of thousands of people in Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, and elsewhere. A shift away from natural diamonds reduces economic demand for those mining operations, which has human consequences in communities where the diamond industry is the primary path to formal employment. This does not make natural diamonds ethically superior — it means the ethical calculation is not resolved simply by choosing lab-grown.

The environmental comparison also lacks a clear winner. CVD production is energy-intensive and typically powered by grid electricity; the environmental cost depends entirely on the energy source. HPHT is similarly energy-intensive. Natural diamond mining has land disturbance and water use impacts but also operates under increasingly strict reclamation regulations in most major producing countries. Neither origin is free of environmental cost.

Who Should Buy What

The Decision Framework

Lab-grown diamonds make clear sense for buyers whose priorities are visual quality per dollar spent, a larger stone on a fixed budget, or certainty about conflict avoidance. A buyer who allocates $8,000 to an engagement ring can afford a two-carat, F, VS1 lab-grown stone where a natural stone of the same quality would cost $16,000 to $22,000. That visual difference — a two-carat versus a one-carat ring — is real and significant.

Natural diamonds make clear sense for buyers who regard the ring as an asset with long-term value, for whom rarity is part of the meaning of the object, or who want to be confident about resale recovery in the future. The natural diamond’s value is linked to something that cannot be replicated by engineering — the geological conditions and timescale that produced it — and that irreproducibility has historically commanded a price premium that persists in the market.

What People

Ask Us

Can a jeweler tell the difference between lab-grown and natural? Not by visual examination. Distinguishing the two requires spectroscopic equipment not available in a standard jewelry store. GIA, AGS, and other qualified laboratories can determine origin definitively. The certificate is the reliable source of origin information, which is why documentation is non-negotiable for any diamond purchase.

Will lab-grown diamonds hold their value? Based on current and historical market data, no — not the way natural diamonds do. Lab-grown diamond prices have fallen substantially since 2015 and continue to trend lower as production capacity increases. A lab-grown diamond purchased today is likely worth less at retail in five years than it costs today. This is not a criticism of lab-grown diamonds as objects; it is an accurate description of the resale market.

Do lab-grown diamonds look different from natural diamonds in a ring? No. The optical properties — refractive index, dispersion, brilliance — are identical. A lab-grown diamond in a ring looks exactly like a natural diamond of the same color, clarity, and cut grades. There is no visual difference observable in normal viewing conditions.

Are lab-grown diamonds better for the environment? The environmental comparison is not straightforward. CVD and HPHT production are both energy-intensive. Natural mining has significant land-use impact but also supports regulated reclamation in major producing countries. The environmental calculus depends heavily on the specific energy source used in production and the specific mining operation for comparison. Neither origin is clearly superior on environmental grounds without knowing those specifics.

What does GIA say on a lab-grown diamond certificate? GIA labels lab-grown diamond reports clearly as “Laboratory-Grown Diamond Report” and includes “Laboratory-Grown” in the header. The color, clarity, cut, and carat weight fields use the same grading criteria as natural diamonds. The certificate is fully valid as a quality document; the origin statement is simply additional information required by GIA’s disclosure standards.

title: Old Mine Cut and Old European Cut Diamonds: A Guide for Modern Buyers
body:
Old cuts were not failed attempts at the modern round brilliant — they were designed to work in candlelight and gas lamp, and in those conditions, they do something that modern brilliant cuts do not.

What Old Mine Cut Means

The Victorian Diamond and Its Distinctive Geometry

The old mine cut was the dominant diamond shape from roughly the 1700s through the early 1900s. It is recognizable by its characteristic cushion outline — a square shape with gently rounded corners rather than the perfect circle of the modern round brilliant — combined with a high crown, small table, large culet, and relatively deep pavilion. These proportions were not the result of imprecision; they were the deliberate choice of cutters working with the tools and optical goals of their time.

The small table of an old mine cut — typically 40 to 55 percent of the girdle diameter, versus 53 to 62 percent for modern rounds — means the stone collects more light through the crown facets and less through the flat table. The high crown — often 15 to 20 percent of total depth — provides a steep refractive path that disperses white light into spectral colors efficiently. The large culet, visible as a dark circle in the center of the stone when viewed face-up, was a practical choice: cutting to a perfect point risked breaking the fragile tip during the polishing process.

The result is a stone that performs beautifully in low-light conditions — the “fire” or spectral dispersion is pronounced because the steep crown angles maximize dispersive refraction, and the warm, soft patterns of colored light that old mine cuts produce in candlelight are genuinely different from what a modern brilliant delivers. Under bright daylight or fluorescent light, an old mine cut will produce less total brightness than a modern round of equal carat weight, because its proportions were optimized for warmth and spectral display rather than raw light return.

Old European Cut

The Transition Stone Between Old Mine and Modern Brilliant

The old European cut emerged in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as cutting technology improved and allowed more precise circular outlines. It is the direct predecessor of the modern round brilliant, retaining the old mine cut’s high crown, small table, and large culet while achieving a circular rather than cushion outline. The transition from old European to modern round brilliant was essentially the adoption of AGS ideal proportions in the 1919 publication of Marcel Tolkowsky’s mathematical analysis of diamond optics — “Diamond Design,” which established the ideal proportions for maximum light return in a round diamond.

Old European cuts share the visual character of old mine cuts — warm, soft, spectral fire in low light — with the advantage of the round outline that most buyers find more familiar. In terms of durability and wear, both cuts are fully adequate for ring use. The high crown and large culet do not make old cuts weaker than modern stones; the culet’s opening is microscopic at real scale despite appearing large at magnification.

Sizing differences matter for buyers considering replacement settings or resizing. Old mine cushion outlines do not fit standard modern setting configurations, which are designed for circular stones. An old mine cut set in a modern four-prong Tiffany solitaire will require custom-fabricated prongs that accommodate the cushion outline. Old European cuts, being circular, fit most modern round settings, though the higher crown height may require slightly taller prongs than a modern round of equal diameter.

The Market for Antique Cuts

Where to Find Them and What They Cost

Old mine and old European cut diamonds are found primarily through estate dealers, auction houses, and antique jewelry specialists. They are not routinely available from new jewelry retailers because they are not currently being produced — modern manufacturers cut diamonds to modern brilliant specifications, and the old cut inventory exists only in estate pieces and individual stones removed from antique settings.

Pricing for old cuts is complex. A quality old European cut of equivalent color and clarity to a modern round brilliant typically trades at a 20 to 40 percent discount, because the modern market undervalues the optical character of antique cuts relative to modern brilliant performance. The “fire” that old cuts produce is a feature that buyers educated about antique diamonds value highly; buyers unfamiliar with the aesthetic see a less bright stone and price it down accordingly.

For buyers specifically drawn to the warm, spectral quality of antique cut diamonds — and there is a genuine, devoted market for this aesthetic — the pricing discount relative to modern cuts is an opportunity. A well-preserved old mine cushion in SI1 clarity at two carats may cost significantly less than a modern round of comparable quality while offering visual qualities that the modern stone cannot reproduce. The decision is whether the aesthetic resonates, not whether the stone is objectively better or worse.

Setting Old Cuts Today

Respecting the Stone’s Character

Old cut diamonds in new settings are increasingly common, and the design language for these settings has evolved to respect the stone’s character. A vintage-style setting — milgrain beading, filigree gallery work, art deco geometric motifs — complements old cuts naturally. A stark, minimal contemporary solitaire can look incongruous with an old mine cushion because the setting’s modernism competes with the stone’s historicity.

Yellow gold is the natural partner for most old cuts, since it matches the era of the stones and amplifies their warm, spectral fire. Platinum became the dominant engagement ring metal in the Art Deco period, so old European cuts in platinum are period-correct and compelling. A modern white gold setting on an old mine cushion is a legitimate contemporary choice but requires more careful proportion work to make the stone and setting feel like a unified object rather than two eras placed together arbitrarily.

What People

Ask Us

Are old mine cut diamonds worth buying today? For buyers who respond to their visual character — warm, soft, with pronounced spectral fire in low and incandescent light — old mine cuts represent genuine value. They cost less than modern round brilliants of comparable weight and quality, and they produce a visual experience that modern cuts do not. For buyers who want maximum brightness and scintillation in all lighting conditions, a modern round brilliant is the better choice.

Can an old mine cut be recut to a modern round brilliant? Technically yes, but doing so is irreversible and reduces the stone’s carat weight, potentially by 15 to 30 percent, as material is removed to achieve modern proportions. Recutting also destroys the antique stone’s character, which is the primary reason most collectors find it valuable. I advise against recutting old cuts except in cases where the stone has damage that requires it.

How do I know if a stone is an old mine cut or a modern cushion brilliant? The distinguishing features are the culet and the table-to-crown ratio. An old mine cut has a large, open culet visible as a circle when you look straight down through the table, and a small table relative to the crown height. A modern cushion brilliant has a pointed culet (no visible circle) and a larger table with proportions closer to a modern round brilliant. Under 10x magnification, the differences are clear.

What clarity grade is acceptable in an old mine cut? Old mine cuts are more forgiving of lower clarity grades than modern rounds because the facet pattern and proportions distribute light differently, and the eye evaluates the stone’s overall warmth and fire rather than scanning for specific inclusions. SI1 and even SI2 old mine cuts can be visually appealing where the same grades in a modern round might show inclusions prominently. Evaluate each stone individually rather than applying modern clarity minimums.

Do old cuts have GIA certificates? They can if submitted for grading. GIA grades old cuts and issues certificates that note the cutting style. The proportions will be reported as they are — large culet, small table, high crown — and the cut grade, if issued, will reflect the stone’s optical performance rather than penalizing it for not conforming to modern round brilliant proportions. GIA’s cut grade for old cuts is based on the stone’s actual light performance, not its departure from modern ideal proportions.

title: Who Invented the Princess Cut Diamond? Meet Bez Ambar
body:
The Princess Cut is the second most popular diamond shape in the world. It is in millions of engagement rings, wedding bands, and fine jewelry pieces across every price point. The person who invented it works in Downtown Los Angeles. His name is Bez Ambar.

The Problem in 1979

Why Someone Needed to Invent a New Cut

The modern diamond industry in the late 1970s had a dominant shape: the round brilliant. Tolkowsky’s 1919 calculation of ideal proportions for a round diamond had been refined over sixty years into a cut so well-optimized that it became the default. If you were buying a diamond, you were almost certainly buying a round.

Square diamonds existed, the old mine cut, the emerald cut, the baguette, but none of them performed like a round brilliant. The stepped cuts produced dramatic flashes but not brilliance. The old square cuts had inconsistent faceting that left them looking dull by comparison.

Bez Ambar, then a young diamond cutter working in Los Angeles, saw the problem clearly: there was no square brilliant diamond. No square cut that matched the light performance of a round. He decided to create one.

The Development

Three Years of Cutting and Refinement

From 1976 to 1979, Bez worked on a facet arrangement that would do for a square what Tolkowsky’s proportions had done for a round: create a systematic geometry that maximized brilliance, fire, and scintillation from a square girdle.

The challenge was the corners. A round diamond has no corners, the girdle is continuous, and light reflects symmetrically in every direction. A square diamond has four sharp corners where the geometry changes abruptly. Managing how light behaves at those corners, and how the pavilion facets adjacent to them direct light back through the table, was the core technical problem.

Bez solved it with a 49-facet arrangement, crown and pavilion facets positioned to maintain high light return across the entire face of the stone, including the corners. The result was a diamond that was as brilliant as a round brilliant but distinctly square. He named it the Quadrillion Cut™.

The Award

De Beers Recognized It

The De Beers Diamond Award, the most prestigious recognition in the diamond industry, was given to Bez Ambar for the Quadrillion Cut. De Beers, at the time the world’s dominant diamond mining and marketing company, awarded the prize to innovations that materially advanced the art of diamond cutting.

Receiving the award confirmed what Bez had accomplished: not a variation on an existing cut, but a genuine invention. A new solution to a problem the industry had not previously solved.

The Name Change

From Quadrillion to Princess

Bez sold the cutting rights to the Quadrillion Cut to Lex Polished Diamonds in the early 1980s. Lex licensed the cut to manufacturers globally and rebranded it for the retail market.

The new name was the Princess Cut. Softer, more romantic, easier for a consumer to remember than “Quadrillion.” Lex was right about the marketing, the Princess Cut grew into the second most popular diamond shape in the United States within a decade, and it has held that position for over forty years.

The name changed. The cut did not. Every Princess Cut diamond sold anywhere in the world today, from a $300 solitaire to a six-figure custom piece, is cut to the geometry Bez Ambar developed in his Los Angeles studio in 1979.

After the Invention

What Bez Built Next

Bez did not stop at the Quadrillion. After establishing himself as the inventor of the world’s most successful new diamond cut, he continued developing new cuts and setting methods through the 1980s and 1990s.

The Blaze® came later, a cut optimized not for brilliance but for fire, producing color dispersion roughly ten times higher than a standard round brilliant. The Blaze® is used throughout the Bez Ambar collection, typically as a shank treatment or in halos where the color fire frames a different center stone.

The Bez Ambar studio in Downtown Los Angeles continues to manufacture to this day, custom engagement rings, wedding bands, and fine jewelry pieces all produced in the same building where the Quadrillion Cut was invented.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who invented the Princess Cut diamond? Bez Ambar invented the square brilliant diamond, originally named the Quadrillion Cut™, in 1979. De Beers recognized the invention with its Diamond Award, the most prestigious honor in the diamond industry. The name “Princess Cut” was introduced when Lex Polished Diamonds licensed the cut from Bez and rebranded it for retail sales.

Is the Quadrillion Cut the same as the Princess Cut? Yes. They are the same 49-facet square brilliant cut. Quadrillion Cut™ is Bez Ambar’s original name. Princess Cut is the trade name that became universally adopted after Lex Polished Diamonds licensed the cut in the early 1980s.

Did Bez Ambar win an award for inventing the Princess Cut? Yes. De Beers, then the most powerful institution in the diamond industry, awarded Bez the De Beers Diamond Award for the Quadrillion Cut. The award recognized genuine advances in diamond cutting technique.

Does Bez Ambar still sell Princess Cut diamonds? Yes. Bez continues to cut Quadrillion diamonds at his Downtown Los Angeles studio to the original specifications. These are not commodity princess cuts from wholesale supply, they are cut in-house to the proportions Bez developed in 1979. Contact the studio for current inventory and custom work.

What other diamond cuts did Bez Ambar develop? After the Quadrillion, Bez developed the Blaze® Cut, a proprietary faceting pattern that maximizes fire (color dispersion) rather than white light brilliance. The Blaze® is a registered trademark and is used extensively throughout the Bez Ambar collection as a design element in shanks, halos, and standalone pieces.

title: Princess Cut Diamond Rings: The Square Alternative to Round
body:
The princess cut is sometimes described as a square version of the round brilliant, which is accurate in terms of the facet system but misses the most important practical difference: those corners.

The Cut’s Identity

What Makes a Princess Cut Different From Other Square Shapes

The princess cut — developed in the 1960s and refined into its current form in the 1980s by Betzalel Ambar (no relation to this studio) and Israel Itzkowitz — is a square or near-square brilliant cut with pointed corners. Its defining visual characteristics are its sharp, 90-degree corners, its square outline, and its brilliant-cut facet arrangement that produces light return comparable to round brilliants for a given level of cutting precision.

The princess cut is distinct from the radiant cut, which shares the square shape but has truncated corners rather than sharp points, and from the asscher and emerald cuts, which use step-cut faceting rather than brilliant-cut faceting. The radiant cut looks softer and more cushioned at the corners; the princess cut looks crisp and geometric. The emerald and asscher cuts have a completely different optical character — they emphasize depth and reflection rather than brightness and scintillation.

The face-up appearance of a well-cut princess is characterized by X-shaped light patterns radiating from the center, with chevron-style facets in the quadrants and a specific arrangement of main facets that creates organized, symmetrical scintillation. The number of chevron facets — typically 2, 3, or 4 per quadrant — is a variable in princess cutting that affects the stone’s visual pattern. Two chevrons produce fewer, larger scintillation elements; four chevrons produce a more divided, detailed pattern. Neither is objectively superior; it is an aesthetic preference.

The Corner Risk

The Most Important Practical Consideration in Princess Buying

The princess cut’s pointed corners are its most significant durability vulnerability. Diamond is the hardest natural material, but hardness and brittleness are separate properties. Diamond cleaves readily along its octahedral crystal planes — meaning a sharp impact at the correct angle splits the crystal cleanly rather than scratching it. The pointed corners of a princess cut place the stone’s most acute angles at positions where edge impacts during daily wear are most likely.

A chipped corner on a princess cut is one of the most common ring damage events I see in studio. It most often results from striking the corner against a hard countertop, doorframe, or stone surface. The repair requires recutting — the chipped corner must be polished out, which removes some carat weight and changes the stone’s outline from a pointed corner to a truncated one. This effectively converts the stone from a princess cut to a radiant cut at that corner, and the combination is aesthetically incoherent.

The preventive solution is the setting. Princess cuts require corner prongs — prongs placed directly at the four corners that protect the most vulnerable points of the stone. V-shaped corner prongs, also called V-tips, are the preferred solution because they cup the corner geometry rather than simply sitting adjacent to it. The prong configuration is not optional. A princess cut in a setting that leaves corners exposed or underprotected is a maintenance problem waiting to happen.

Cut Quality in Princess Cuts

What GIA Measures and What It Does Not

GIA (Gemological Institute of America) does not issue an overall cut grade for princess cut diamonds. It reports the 4Cs — color, clarity, carat weight — plus polish, symmetry, and fluorescence, but no comprehensive cut quality assessment equivalent to the round brilliant’s Excellent grade. This is the same gap that exists for all fancy shapes and creates the same evaluation challenge.

For princess cuts, the key proportional variables are table percentage (ideal range 62 to 72 percent for princess) and total depth percentage (ideal range 64 to 75 percent). A princess cut with a table above 75 percent loses fire because the large flat surface returns light uniformly without the crown facets providing dispersive refraction. A total depth above 80 percent buries mass in the pavilion where it does not contribute to face-up appearance.

The length-to-width ratio for a princess cut determines whether it reads as square or slightly rectangular. A ratio of 1.00 to 1.05 reads as square. Above 1.08, the rectangular tendency becomes visible face-up. Most buyers targeting the princess cut prefer the squarest possible outline — anything above 1.05 should be evaluated in person to confirm whether the slight rectangle is acceptable.

Setting Options

Designing Around the Square Brilliant

The four-prong V-tip setting in white gold or platinum is the conventional princess cut mounting and remains appropriate for most contexts. Channel-set princess side stones on a princess center stone create a clean, geometric aesthetic that emphasizes the cut’s architectural quality. Baguette side stones frame a princess center differently — the parallel step-cut sides of the baguette contrast with the brilliant-cut center in a way that can be compelling or jarring depending on execution.

Halo settings for princess cuts use smaller diamonds cut to fit the straight and pointed geometry of the shape. Square halos around a princess center amplify the geometric identity of the stone. Round halos are also used but tend to soften the visual language of the cut, which may or may not be the intended effect. Channel-set bands on both sides of a princess solitaire are among the most enduring designs in the contemporary engagement ring market.

What People

Ask Us

Is a princess cut more or less expensive than a round brilliant? Princess cuts typically cost 10 to 25 percent less per carat than round brilliants of equivalent quality because they are cut more efficiently from rough diamond — less material is lost in achieving the square shape than in achieving a perfect circle. This price difference makes princess cuts attractive for buyers who want maximum visible size per dollar in a geometric format.

What is the best clarity grade for a princess cut? VS2 and above for most princess cuts. The princess cut’s brilliant facet arrangement is moderately good at masking inclusions compared to step cuts, but not as effective as round brilliants. VS2 is reliably eye-clean in princess cuts across common sizes. SI1 can work if the specific stone is examined and inclusions confirmed to be off-center and non-dark, but SI1 acceptance based solely on grade should not be automatic.

Can a princess cut be set in a bezel? A full bezel for a princess cut requires a square metal collar that covers the corners, providing excellent corner protection. The aesthetic is more modern and industrial than prong settings and is appropriate for some design intentions. Partial bezels that leave the corners exposed defeat the purpose of the bezel for corner protection. If you want a bezel, use a full bezel with metal walls that reach the corners.

How do I tell the difference between princess and radiant cuts? The corners are the reliable distinguishing feature. A princess cut has perfectly sharp, 90-degree pointed corners. A radiant cut has truncated corners — the corner is cut off to create a small diagonal facet, giving the stone an octagonal edge profile rather than a purely square one. Under magnification, the difference is immediately apparent. Face-up, the princess looks crisper and more angular; the radiant looks slightly softer.

Does a princess cut look larger than a round brilliant of the same weight? In face-up area, yes — a princess cut typically shows slightly more face-up surface per carat than a round brilliant because the square outline uses the stone’s width differently. Perceptually, though, round brilliants often appear larger to observers because the eye reads the widest dimension (diameter) rather than area. The princess cut’s square aspect reads differently on the finger than the round’s circular aspect; the comparison is less about size than about different visual footprints.
