title: Quadrillion Cut vs Princess Cut: What Is the Difference?
body:
The Quadrillion Cut and the Princess Cut are the same stone. They share the same geometry, the same facet arrangement, the same optical properties. The difference is history, and who invented it.

The Origin

Bez Ambar Invented the Square Brilliant Diamond

In 1979, Bez Ambar, then a young diamond cutter working in Los Angeles, developed a new way to cut a square diamond that maximized brilliance in a way no previous square cut had achieved. The round brilliant had dominated fine jewelry for decades; Bez set out to match its fire in a square format.

The result was the Quadrillion Cut™. It took years of development. The facet arrangement, 49 facets cut to precise angular specifications, was designed to produce the same kind of light performance that makes round diamonds so compelling: internal reflection, dispersion, and brightness working together rather than in competition with one another.

De Beers, at the time the most powerful force in the diamond industry, recognized the Quadrillion Cut with its Diamond Award, the most prestigious honor in the field. That award confirmed what Bez already knew: this was a genuinely new achievement in diamond cutting, not an iteration.

The Name Change

Where “Princess Cut” Came From

Bez sold the cutting rights to the Quadrillion Cut to Lex Polished Diamonds in the early 1980s. Lex licensed the cut to other manufacturers and began marketing it under a new name: the Princess Cut.

The name took. “Princess” was softer, more romantic, easier for retail jewelers to sell. By the mid-1980s, the Princess Cut was the second most popular diamond shape in the United States, behind only the round brilliant. It remains there today, accounting for roughly 25 to 30 percent of all diamond jewelry sales.

The Quadrillion Cut™ is the original. The Princess Cut is what everyone calls it now. Bez Ambar is the person who invented it.

What Makes It Different From Other Square Cuts

The Quadrillion Cut vs Asscher, Radiant, and Cushion

Square diamonds existed before the Quadrillion. The distinction matters because each cuts light differently.

Asscher Cut: A stepped cut developed in 1902. It produces long, parallel flashes of light, dramatic and architectural but not brilliant in the technical sense. The optical effect is deep, hall-of-mirrors reflection rather than sparkle.

Cushion Cut: A square or rectangular shape with rounded corners and a large facet pattern. It produces a soft, pillow-like sparkle. Predates the brilliant era; modern cushion cuts vary widely in faceting and quality.

Radiant Cut: Introduced in 1977, also aimed at producing brilliance in a square format. It has trimmed corners, where the Quadrillion/Princess has sharp corners. The corner geometry changes how the diamond looks in a setting.

Quadrillion/Princess Cut: Sharp corners, the defining physical feature. The facets narrow toward those corners, creating a pavilion that reflects light differently than any of the above. Under the right conditions, the corner facets produce a distinctive optical signature: a bow-tie-shaped light pattern visible when you look directly down the table. Well-cut princess/quadrillion diamonds minimize this effect while maximizing the overall brightness of the stone.

Buying a Quadrillion or Princess Cut

What to Actually Evaluate

Cut quality in princess/quadrillion diamonds is harder to assess than in rounds because GIA grades them as Excellent/Very Good/Good without a standardized cut grade equivalent to the round brilliant. A princess cut graded Excellent for polish and symmetry can still be poorly proportioned.

The proportions that matter most:

Table percentage: The flat top facet as a proportion of the total girdle diameter. Between 62 and 72 percent is the accepted range for well-cut stones. Below that, the stone looks deep and dark. Above that, it loses brilliance in the crown.

Depth percentage: Total depth from table to culet as a proportion of diameter. 64 to 75 percent is the target range. Stones cut too shallow or too deep sacrifice light return.

Length-to-width ratio: True squares are 1.00 to 1.05. Anything beyond 1.10 starts to look rectangular, which is fine if that is the intended shape.

The bow-tie: Hold the stone face-up under direct light. A well-cut stone shows high brightness across the entire table. Dark areas at the center or at the corners indicate poor proportioning.

Bez Ambar’s Quadrillion Today

Still Cut in Los Angeles

Bez continues to cut Quadrillion diamonds in the Downtown Los Angeles studio where the cut was invented. Every Bez Ambar piece set with a square diamond uses the original Quadrillion proportions, not a generic princess cut sourced from a commodity cutter.

The difference is measurable: stones cut to the original Quadrillion specifications consistently return more light than mass-market princess cuts because the facet angles are set to Bez’s original design, not to maximize yield from the rough.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Princess Cut the same as the Quadrillion Cut? Yes, they are the same facet pattern. The Quadrillion Cut™ is Bez Ambar’s original 1979 name for the square brilliant diamond he invented. The trade adopted “Princess Cut” in the early 1980s when Lex Polished Diamonds licensed the cut and rebranded it for retail sales.

Who invented the Princess Cut diamond? Bez Ambar invented the square brilliant diamond in 1979, originally called the Quadrillion Cut™. De Beers recognized the invention with its Diamond Award. The name “Princess Cut” was introduced by Lex Polished Diamonds when they licensed the cut from Bez.

Does the Quadrillion Cut look different from a standard Princess Cut? A Quadrillion cut to Bez Ambar’s original proportions will typically return more light than a commodity princess cut. The facet angles in mass-produced princess cuts are often optimized for rough yield rather than light performance. Same geometry; different execution.

What makes a Princess Cut diamond well-cut? Table percentage between 62–72%, depth between 64–75%, length-to-width ratio close to 1.00 for a square, and minimal bow-tie effect under direct lighting. GIA does not issue a cut grade for princess cuts the way it does for rounds, so these proportions must be evaluated manually or reviewed with the selling jeweler.

Can I get a Quadrillion Cut diamond from Bez Ambar? Yes. Bez continues to cut Quadrillion diamonds in his Los Angeles studio. Contact the studio directly for availability and specifications.

title: Rose Cut Diamond Rings
body:
The rose cut was designed for candlelight in the sixteenth century. Its domed profile and large flat facets captured ambient light in a way the modern brilliant cut was not designed for.

The rose cut emerged from Flemish and Dutch cutting workshops in the early to mid-1500s. The design logic was practical: a flat base, a domed top, and a relatively small number of triangular facets, typically 24, arranged to catch and reflect available light. In an era when the primary artificial light source was an open flame, the rose cut performed well because it spread light broadly across its surface rather than concentrating it into directed flashes.

The modern round brilliant, developed in the early twentieth century, was optimized for electric light: controlled and bright, making it possible to design for precisely directed reflection and refraction. The brilliant cut produces more fire and scintillation than a rose cut under equivalent conditions. But it produces a different kind of light, and different is not always better.

The Physical

Difference

A standard rose cut has a flat base and a rounded dome with 24 triangular facets meeting at an apex. The height of the dome varies: a high-dome rose cut has more depth and pronounced curvature; a low-dome or flat rose cut sits almost flush with the setting.

Because the base is flat, a rose cut diamond does not require the pointed pavilion of a brilliant-cut stone. This means it can be set directly against a surface, or held in a flat bezel, in ways a brilliant cut cannot accommodate. Tablet settings, where the stone rests flat against a gold base, are a characteristic rose cut approach.

The flat base also means that the weight of a rose cut concentrates in the dome rather than splitting between crown and pavilion. For a given carat weight, a rose cut faces up significantly larger than a brilliant cut of the same weight: more of the mass spreads horizontally across the table. A 1.00-carat rose cut can face up 10 to 20 percent larger than a 1.00-carat round brilliant.

The Light

It Produces

Under soft ambient light, a rose cut produces a gentle, distributed glow. The large facets spread light broadly across the dome rather than concentrating it into the precise points of brilliance characteristic of modern cuts. The effect is warm and even, sometimes described as romantic, though that word is an accurate description of an optical difference rather than a sentimental claim.

Under bright direct light, a rose cut can appear dimmer than a round brilliant of comparable quality because it lacks the deep pavilion that sends white light back through the table in concentrated flashes. This is physics: a different cut, optimized for different conditions.

Rose cuts perform beautifully in the lighting conditions most people actually live in: indoor light with natural window light, candlelight, soft evening light. They look the way they were designed to look in everyday environments.

Setting

Considerations

The flat base of a rose cut opens up setting options that do not work with brilliant cuts. A bezel setting that holds the dome while the flat base rests against the bezel floor is clean and secure. A collet setting, where the stone sits in a low cup of metal, is another traditional approach.

The low profile of a flat rose cut sits closer to the hand than a prong-set brilliant, which many people find more comfortable for daily wear. It is less likely to catch on fabrics and has less leverage for impact because it projects less from the finger.

Bez Ambar designs settings for rose cut diamonds that take advantage of the stone’s specific geometry: the wide face, the domed profile, the flat base. A setting designed for a rose cut makes better use of the stone than a standard brilliant-cut mounting with a flat-bottom modification.

What People

Ask Us

Does a rose cut diamond sparkle? Not in the way a modern brilliant cut does. A rose cut produces a softer, more distributed glow rather than precise points of fire and brilliance. Under candlelight and soft indoor light, many people find rose cuts as beautiful as brilliant cuts. Under very bright direct light, a rose cut appears quieter than a brilliant cut. This is a physical difference, not a quality issue.

Does a rose cut face up larger than a round brilliant? Yes, typically. Because all the weight sits in the dome rather than split between crown and pavilion, a rose cut of a given carat weight spreads more surface area than a brilliant cut of the same weight. A 1.00-carat rose cut often appears comparable to a 1.15 to 1.20-carat round brilliant when viewed face-up on the hand.

What era are rose cut diamonds from? Rose cut diamonds were the dominant cut from the 1500s through the early 1900s, when the modern round brilliant replaced them for most applications. Much antique and vintage jewelry from the Georgian, Victorian, and Edwardian periods features rose cuts. Contemporary jewelers work with both antique rose cuts sourced from old jewelry and newly cut rose cuts produced today.

Are rose cut diamonds less valuable than round brilliants? Per carat, rose cut diamonds are typically less expensive than comparable round brilliants because the market for them is smaller and because modern cutting standards favor brilliance. For buyers who prefer the aesthetic, this represents value: a larger-appearing stone for less money.

What setting works best for a rose cut diamond? Bezel and collet settings are traditional and appropriate because the flat base rests securely against the setting floor. Low-prong settings also work. High-prong settings designed for pavilioned brilliant cuts are not the right approach for a rose cut and can result in proportions that look off.

title: Round Brilliant Cut: Why Cut Quality Determines Everything
body:
The round brilliant is the most studied object in the history of gemology, and after forty years of cutting and setting diamonds, I will tell you plainly: cut is the only variable that separates a stone that commands a room from one that simply sits there.

What Cut Actually

Controls Inside a Diamond

A diamond does not generate light. It redirects it. The round brilliant’s 57 or 58 facets — arranged in a precise geometry across the crown, girdle, and pavilion — are engineered to capture rays entering from above, bounce them between the pavilion facets, and return them through the table directly to the observer’s eye. When that geometry is correct, you get three things: brilliance (the white light), fire (the spectral color flares), and scintillation (the on-off flash as the stone or the viewer moves).

When the geometry is off, even slightly, light escapes through the pavilion floor or leaks out the sides. The stone goes dark in the center — what cutters call a “fish-eye” or “nail head” — and no amount of color or clarity grade will rescue it. You can own a D Flawless diamond that looks like a piece of glass. I have seen it happen. The client paid a premium for two grades that the cut then erased.

The Numbers That

Define an Excellent Cut

The Gemological Institute of America (GIA) grades cut on round brilliants only — a decision made after decades of modeling light behavior. Their Excellent tier has specific proportional corridors: table percentage between 54 and 57 percent, total depth between 59 and 62.5 percent, crown angle between 34 and 35 degrees, pavilion angle between 40.6 and 41 degrees. The crown and pavilion angles are the most critical pairing. A crown of 34.5 degrees matched with a pavilion of 40.8 degrees produces a stone that exhibits both high brilliance and strong fire simultaneously.

The AGS (American Gem Society) laboratories use a ray-tracing model called the Performance-based system and issue grades of 0 through 10, where 0 is their equivalent of Excellent. AGS 0 and GIA Excellent overlap substantially, but AGS often applies stricter tolerances on girdle thickness and cutlet size. Either grade, from either lab, on a well-proportioned stone, will perform.

What neither grade captures fully is the human eye’s response to a specific stone under specific light. This is why I have always insisted that clients look at finalists side by side, face up, under a single overhead source. The numbers tell you the stone has the right architecture. The eye tells you which one speaks.

Polish, Symmetry, and

The Details That Amplify Performance

GIA and AGS both issue separate grades for polish and symmetry, and both should be Excellent or Very Good on any stone you are seriously considering. Polish describes the quality of each facet surface — tiny polishing lines visible only under magnification can scatter light at the surface before it even enters the stone. Symmetry describes how accurately each of the 57 facets mirrors its opposite: a heart-and-arrows pattern, visible through a special viewer, indicates that the cutter achieved near-perfect rotational symmetry. This is not cosmetic. Asymmetrical facets create unequal light path lengths and produce a stone that flashes unevenly.

The girdle — the thin band separating crown from pavilion — should be described as thin to slightly thick on the grading report. An extremely thin girdle is prone to chipping during setting. An extremely thick one adds weight without adding diameter, meaning you pay for more carats than you see from above.

The Price Penalty for

Choosing Cut Over Carat

Here is the honest math. A round brilliant cut to GIA Excellent with Excellent polish and symmetry will cost you eight to fifteen percent more than the same carat weight cut to Very Good or Good. That premium is one of the most rational spending decisions in the diamond market, because the Excellent stone will face-up larger, return more light, and hold its desirability in the secondary market far better than its underperforming sibling.

I have watched buyers go one-quarter carat heavier to save money, end up with a Good-cut stone, and then wonder six months later why the ring does not have the presence they expected. Cut is not a feature you can add later. It is set at the wheel, and it is set forever.

What People

Ask Us

Does a higher cut grade always mean more brilliance?

Within the Excellent tier, yes — but “more” is a relative term. The difference between a middling Excellent and a top-performing Excellent may be invisible to most observers under normal lighting. What the grade guarantees is that the stone meets the minimum performance threshold for that tier; exceptional stones within the tier have proportions that cluster around specific crown-and-pavilion angle combinations that cutters and gemologists track separately.

Is GIA Excellent the same thing as AGS 0?

They are functionally equivalent for most buyers, but the grading systems use different methodologies. GIA uses a proportions-based approach with empirically defined corridors; AGS uses a light-performance model that simulates ray tracing. An AGS 0 stone and a GIA Excellent stone will both perform beautifully. The difference becomes relevant only in edge cases where a stone sits at the boundary of proportional acceptability.

Can I get an Excellent cut in a size below half a carat?

Yes, though the tolerances become harder to achieve at very small sizes. GIA grades cut on rounds as small as 0.15 carats. Below that threshold, grading is not offered, but a skilled cutter working to ideal proportions can still produce a high-performing stone. Ask to see the stone face-up alongside a reference Excellent stone at the same size.

Why do some Excellent-graded diamonds look better than others?

Because the Excellent grade is a range, not a single point. Stones at the center of the range — with crown angles near 34.5 degrees and pavilion angles near 40.8 degrees — tend to show the best balance of brilliance and fire. Stones at the edges of the grade may pass the threshold but sacrifice one optical property for another. A reputable dealer will know where in the grade a specific stone falls.

Does cut grade affect the value at resale?

Meaningfully, yes. GIA Excellent stones are the preferred inventory of estate dealers, auction houses, and online secondary markets. A stone with a Fair or Poor cut grade can become functionally unsaleable at a fair price, even if the color and clarity grades are excellent, because sophisticated buyers know they would be paying for weight they cannot see.

Confidence: 92 — 40 years of direct diamond trade experience + GIA and AGS published grading criteria | Cost: ~$0.04

title: Trillion Cut Diamonds: What They Are and How They Are Used
body:
The trillion cut is not a minor variation on familiar shapes — it is a fundamentally different geometric approach to the diamond, with visual and structural consequences that buyers need to understand before choosing it.

The Shape’s Identity

What a Trillion Cut Is and Where It Comes From

The trillion cut — sometimes called trilliant, triangular brilliant, or triangle cut — is a diamond fashioned into a triangular outline with three equal sides and brilliant-style faceting that maximizes light return within the triangular geometry. The cut was developed in Amsterdam in the 1970s, with the name “Trilliant” originally trademarked by the Henry Meyer Diamond Company. The more generic “trillion” has since entered the trade lexicon and refers to any triangular brilliant cut without specific attribution.

The trillion’s triangular outline is its most immediately striking visual quality. It reads as a bold, architectural shape with no precedent in the major historical cutting styles — no antique trillion exists the way antique cushions and old European cuts do, because the precision required to cut a triangular brilliant cleanly was not achievable with pre-modern cutting tools. The shape is entirely a product of twentieth-century technology.

Trillion cuts occur in two main configurations. A curved-side trillion has slightly bowed edges rather than perfectly straight sides, which distributes mass slightly differently and softens the angular reading. A straight-side trillion has precise, flat edges that create a true equilateral triangle. Curved-side trillions are more common in contemporary cutting; straight-side trillions are associated with some older production and with very specific design applications where geometric precision is the goal.

Optical Behavior

How Trillions Handle Light Differently From Other Shapes

The triangular geometry creates optical patterns distinct from round or rectangular brilliants. Light entering a trillion distributes across three main facet groups that mirror the three-fold symmetry of the shape. The result is a distinctive, pinwheel-like scintillation pattern — light flashes rotate around the center of the stone in a pattern that does not occur in four-fold symmetric shapes. This optical signature is immediately recognizable to anyone familiar with the cut and is one of its primary aesthetic distinctions.

Trillions also exhibit more fire — spectral color dispersion — than rounds of equivalent carat weight in many cases, because the steep crown angles used in trillion cutting to maximize the triangular outline’s light return produce strong dispersive refraction. The fire-to-brightness ratio is different from round brilliants: trillions can appear more colorful and less purely white, which is a desirable quality for clients seeking a warmer, more dramatic optical performance.

The triangular outline’s three points are the same vulnerability in trillions that corners are in princess cuts. The points concentrate mechanical stress in the diamond’s most acute geometric features, and impacts at the point tips can chip the stone. Good trillion settings use V-tip prongs at all three corners, identical in function to the corner prongs used for princess cuts. Settings that leave the points exposed are invitations to damage.

Primary Uses

Center Stone and Side Stone Applications

As a center stone, the trillion creates a bold, distinctive ring that reads as unconventional without being eccentric. It works best in minimalist settings that let the shape speak without competing decorative elements. A simple three-prong solitaire — one prong per corner — in platinum is the cleanest presentation. More elaborate settings risk cluttering the clean geometric reading of the triangular outline.

The trillion’s most commercially significant use is as a side stone in three-stone rings flanking a larger center diamond. In this configuration, two trillion-cut diamonds of matched weight and quality are set on either side of the center stone, with the trillion’s flat edge facing the center. The result is a composition where the geometric contrast between the triangular flanks and the center stone (typically a round, oval, or cushion) creates visual tension and movement. This is among the most enduring three-stone ring designs in the contemporary market, and it uses the trillion’s shape advantages without asking the shape to carry the ring’s entire visual identity.

As accent stones in more complex compositions — in channel borders, as halo elements, or in the gallery of a more elaborate setting — the trillion’s triangular outline creates geometric complexity that most jewelers use sparingly. It is not a filling shape the way round brilliants or baguettes are; its distinctive geometry asserts itself wherever it appears.

Sizing and Pricing

What Trillion Cuts Cost and What Sizes to Choose

Trillion cuts in the 0.25 to 0.75 carat range are the most common sizes because they are most frequently used as matched pairs for three-stone settings. Matched pairs require both stones to be very closely matched in size, color, and cut quality — a visually obvious mismatch between two side stones is one of the most common complaints in three-stone ring service. When buying trillion side stones, always specify matched pairs from the same cutting lot and verify the match visually before purchase.

Trillion center stones above one carat are available but less common, because the triangular shape does not cut as efficiently from round diamond rough as oval or cushion shapes. The rough material required to produce a clean triangular brilliant at one carat or above is relatively wasteful in terms of carat recovery, which pushes per-carat prices for large trillions higher than equivalent-weight ovals or radiant cuts.

Color and clarity grading for trillions follows the same GIA standards as other fancy shapes. VS2 or better for eye-clean clarity; G or above for white metal settings. The triangular outline shows body color comparably to oval and cushion cuts — more readily than round brilliants, less readily than step cuts.

What People

Ask Us

Is a trillion cut durable enough for an engagement ring? The trillion’s three points are its vulnerability — they must be protected by properly placed V-tip prongs at each corner. With correct setting and reasonable daily care, a trillion center stone is a wearable choice. The shape is harder to source in very large sizes and is more specialized in its setting requirements than rounds or ovals, but these are not reasons to avoid it if the aesthetic is what you want.

Can trillion cuts be used as center stones? Yes, and with the right setting — typically a simple three-prong solitaire in platinum or white gold — a trillion center stone creates a dramatically distinctive ring. The shape is unconventional enough that it reads as a deliberate, knowledgeable aesthetic choice rather than a default selection. For clients who specifically want a non-round, non-oval ring with strong visual identity, the trillion center stone delivers that clearly.

What is the best length-to-width ratio for a trillion cut? An equilateral trillion — equal sides — is the standard and most aesthetically balanced form. Some fancy trillions have slightly elongated or asymmetric proportions; these are specialty cuts for specific design applications. For side-stone pairs, perfect equilateral proportion matching between the two stones is essential. For center stones, the equilateral form reads most cleanly in most settings.

Are trillion diamonds cheaper than round brilliants? Per carat, trillions are typically less expensive than round brilliants of equivalent quality because they do not have the same demand premium. As side stones in matched pairs, they are often priced as a pair rather than individually. For center stones above one carat, the limited supply can push per-carat prices higher than comparable oval or cushion shapes in some market conditions.

What metals work best with trillion cut diamonds? Platinum and white gold are the most neutral choices and let the diamond’s triangular outline read most clearly against the setting. Yellow gold can be used intentionally for warmth, particularly with lower color grades. The V-tip prongs protecting the corners are equally effective in any metal. The metal choice should follow the wearer’s preference and the overall design language rather than being dictated by the shape.

title: What Is an Asscher Cut Diamond?
body:
The Asscher cut was invented in 1902 and revived for Art Deco jewelry in the 1920s. Its step-cut facets produce a completely different visual experience than a brilliant cut.

Joseph Asscher of Amsterdam created this cut in 1902. The Asscher Brothers firm had already established itself as one of the leading diamond cutting houses in the world, responsible for cleaving the famous Cullinan diamond in 1908. The Asscher cut, with its octagonal outline and step-cut facets running parallel to the girdle, was a departure from the brilliant tradition and created a stone with a fundamentally different optical character.

In 2002, the Royal Asscher Diamond Company introduced a modified version with 74 facets rather than the original 58, which they trademarked as the Royal Asscher Cut. The original design, however, is in the public domain and is produced by many cutters worldwide.

Step Cuts

vs Brilliants

The difference between step-cut and brilliant-cut diamonds is fundamental, not superficial.

Brilliant-cut diamonds, including rounds, ovals, cushions, and radiant cuts, have triangular and kite-shaped facets arranged to maximize the return of light back through the table. The result is fire and scintillation: the rapid play of white and colored light as the stone or viewer moves. This is the dominant visual language of most engagement ring diamonds.

Step-cut diamonds, including Asscher and emerald cuts, have rectangular facets running parallel to the girdle. Rather than scattering light into small flashes, step cuts create a “hall of mirrors” effect: long, clean reflections of light and dark that alternate as you view the stone from different angles. The effect is less dynamic than a brilliant but more architectural, more deliberate.

This difference is real and significant. A person who loves the sparkle of a round brilliant may find an Asscher cut quiet by comparison. A person who finds brilliant cuts busy may find an Asscher cut precise and calm. Neither reaction is wrong. They reflect genuine visual preferences.

Asscher

vs Emerald Cut

Both are step-cut diamonds with rectangular facets and cropped corners. The distinction is shape: an Asscher cut is square, with a length-to-width ratio close to 1.00. An emerald cut is rectangular, with a length-to-width ratio typically between 1.30 and 1.50.

On the hand, the square Asscher reads as compact and graphic. The rectangular emerald cut has a more elongated presence that creates a lengthening effect on the finger. The choice between them is often about which geometry suits you: square precision or rectangular elegance.

Clarity is more critical in step-cut diamonds than in brilliant cuts. The large, transparent facets make inclusions and blemishes more visible than in a round brilliant of the same clarity grade. For Asscher cuts, VS2 is generally the practical minimum for a stone that reads clean to the naked eye. The specific stone always needs to be evaluated in person.

Art Deco

and Today

The Asscher cut’s association with Art Deco is not accidental. The geometric precision of step-cut facets and the octagonal outline fit naturally with Art Deco’s aesthetic of clean lines and architectural symmetry. Much of the most celebrated jewelry from the 1920s and 1930s features Asscher and emerald cut stones.

Contemporary buyers drawn to the Asscher often share a preference for this same aesthetic: precise, graphic, architectural rather than romantic. The stone reads as intentional in a way that a round brilliant, by virtue of its ubiquity, sometimes cannot.

One practical note: Asscher cuts are currently less fashionable than oval brilliants, which affects pricing. For equivalent quality, Asscher cuts are often less expensive per carat than rounds or ovals. This creates real value for buyers who genuinely prefer the cut.

What People

Ask Us

Is an Asscher cut the same as an emerald cut? No. Both are step cuts with cropped corners and rectangular facets, but an Asscher cut is square (length-to-width ratio near 1.00) and an emerald cut is rectangular (typically 1.30 to 1.50). The octagonal outline of an Asscher cut is also more pronounced than the emerald cut’s corner cropping.

Why does an Asscher cut look darker than a round brilliant? Step-cut diamonds reflect light differently. Instead of breaking light into many small flashes, they create large mirror-like reflections of light and dark. This is not a defect; it is the defining characteristic of the cut. Whether you find it beautiful or prefer a brilliant cut’s sparkle is a matter of taste.

What clarity grade do I need for an Asscher cut? For most stones, VS2 is the practical minimum for a clean-looking Asscher cut. The large, transparent facets make inclusions more visible than in brilliant cuts. Some VS2 stones are eye-clean; others are not. The only reliable way to evaluate clarity is to view the specific stone in person.

How does the Asscher perform in different lighting? Step cuts perform beautifully in varied, soft lighting where their depth and reflection pattern are most visible. In very bright, direct light, the contrast between reflections is most dramatic. In dim lighting, step cuts appear quieter than brilliant cuts because they do not scatter light in the same way. Knowing this helps set expectations for daily wear.

Is the Royal Asscher Cut worth the premium? The Royal Asscher Cut has 74 facets versus the standard 58 and typically shows stronger light return within the step-cut aesthetic. Whether the premium is worth it depends on your budget and how meaningful the visual difference is when viewed next to a standard Asscher in person.

title: Chandelier Diamond Earrings: Drama, Occasion, and Choosing Right
body:
A chandelier earring designed without attention to weight distribution is a beautiful object in a case and a burden on an ear — the engineering of the piece is as important as its visual architecture.

What Defines a Chandelier Earring

Form, Scale, and the Cascade Principle

The chandelier earring takes its name from the light fixture it resembles — a suspension point at the top from which multiple elements descend in tiers, expanding downward like a chandelier’s arms. The defining characteristics are multiple levels of pendant elements arranged so that the overall profile expands from the fitting attachment point toward the lower extremity of the earring. A simple teardrop pendant is not a chandelier. A triple-tier diamond cascade is.

Scale is inherent to the form. Chandelier earrings are necessarily large — their visual logic depends on the cascade reading as a cascade, which requires enough vertical extent and horizontal spread to show multiple tiers clearly. The minimum meaningful chandelier begins at approximately 40 millimeters of total length and expands from there. Most significant chandelier earrings run from 50 to 80 millimeters, which places them well onto the shoulder for many wearers.

The occasion context for chandelier earrings is genuinely formal. Black-tie events, galas, wedding ceremonies, significant celebrations — these are the contexts where the scale and drama of the chandelier form make sense. Wearing a serious chandelier to a business dinner or a cocktail party that does not reach the formal register creates a mismatch that the earrings cannot fix.

Managing Weight

The Engineering Problem That Separates Great Chandelier Earrings From Heavy Ones

Weight is the defining physical challenge of chandelier earrings. A full diamond chandelier with three tiers of stones and a substantial diamond count can weigh 10 to 20 grams per earring. That weight, concentrated at the earlobe over three to five hours, produces fatigue and, in extreme cases, distortion of the piercing. The engineering response to this problem determines whether a chandelier design is genuinely wearable or merely spectacular.

Several techniques reduce apparent weight without sacrificing visual impact. Open-frame construction — where the cascade is built around negative space rather than solid metal — reduces mass significantly while maintaining the visual footprint of a heavier design. Thin, articulated connections between tiers allow the lower elements to catch light more dynamically without adding structural mass. Metal choice matters too: 14k gold or titanium structural elements weigh less than platinum for identical physical dimensions.

The fitting is the first weight-management element. A sturdy post with a broad butterfly back or, better, a lever-back closure distributes the earring’s weight more evenly across the lobe and prevents the dramatic forward-tipping that heavy earrings show on a thin post. Some serious chandelier earrings use ear wire designs that loop over the upper helix, distributing weight across a larger portion of the ear structure rather than concentrating it at the lobe.

Diamond Quality in a Chandelier Context

What the Viewing Distance Allows

Chandelier earrings are viewed at a distance. The cascade elements, particularly the lower tiers, are typically at shoulder height when worn — six to ten inches below eye level and several feet from the nearest observer. At that distance, the distinction between a D-VVS1 diamond and a G-VS2 diamond is invisible. What matters at that distance is total sparkle effect — the aggregate scintillation of many stones moving together — not the individual quality characteristics of each stone.

This means chandelier earrings are an appropriate application for lower color and clarity grades in the diamonds themselves, provided the cutting quality is maintained for brilliance and fire. H-I color and SI1-SI2 clarity, executed in well-cut round brilliants or princess cuts, creates the same visual cascade effect as more expensive material at the same distance. The investment in a chandelier earring should go to design complexity, craftsmanship quality, and total diamond weight rather than to per-carat quality premiums that will not be perceived in the wearing context.

Color and Texture in Chandelier Design

When Diamonds Share the Design With Colored Stones or Metal

Chandelier earrings that mix diamonds with colored stones — sapphire, emerald, ruby, or tourmaline — occupy a specific design tradition. Victorian and Edwardian chandelier earrings often used colored stones for the upper structural elements and diamonds for the cascade, or alternated colored stations among white diamonds. This approach adds visual complexity and warmth that an all-white diamond cascade does not have, and it allows more expressive design language.

Mixed-metal chandeliers — yellow gold structural elements with white gold or platinum settings holding the diamonds — also add visual dimension. The design choice of where to use color or metal contrast should be deliberate, reinforcing the visual hierarchy of the piece rather than fragmenting it.

What People

Ask Us

How heavy is too heavy for a chandelier earring? The threshold is subjective and individual. Most wearers find earrings above 12 to 15 grams per ear — combined, over 25 to 30 grams — uncomfortable to wear for a full evening. Some clients with robust piercings and a tolerance for earring weight can manage more. The practical test is wearing a mockup or similar-weight piece for two to three hours before committing to the design. If you feel discomfort, adjust the design before production.

Can a chandelier earring be made in a clip-back version for ears without piercings? Yes. Clip-back chandeliers are made, though the clip mechanism adds weight and must be designed to distribute load carefully given the existing mass of the pendant elements. A clip-back chandelier earring is a more demanding engineering problem than a clip stud. An omega clip construction that grips the earlobe with a broad, padded surface distributes the weight better than a simple spring clip.

What necklines work with chandelier earrings? The standard guidance is that chandelier earrings and elaborate necklaces compete rather than complement — a significant chandelier is best paired with a simple neckline or a very minimal necklace. Strapless and off-shoulder gowns with a clean neckline create the maximum visual context for chandelier earrings. High necklines and stand-up collars physically constrain the earring’s movement and may obscure the lower tiers entirely.

How should I store chandelier earrings when not wearing them? Chandelier earrings should be stored flat or in a position where the cascade elements are supported, not hanging freely. Hanging storage allows gravity to stress the connector links between tiers over time. A padded tray or a fabric-lined box where each earring lies flat is appropriate. Separate them from harder pieces that might scratch or dent the delicate cascade elements.

What total diamond weight is appropriate for a significant chandelier earring? A meaningful formal chandelier earring pair typically carries between 5 and 20 total carats of diamonds. Below 5 carats, the diamond density in a multi-tier design looks sparse. Above 20 carats, weight management becomes the dominant design constraint. The range from 8 to 15 total carats produces substantial visual impact in a well-designed cascade without exceeding the practical weight limit for most wearers.

title: Choosing Your Diamond Earrings Studs
body:
Diamond studs are the one piece that works with everything and ages well with you. The question is not whether to own a pair, but which pair will serve you best across decades of wear.

Every jeweler has a client who comes in saying she wants a pair of studs, and after twenty minutes it becomes clear she has been postponing this purchase for years because the options felt overwhelming. Shapes, sizes, settings, total carat weight versus face-up appearance. There is a right way to think through all of it, and it begins with understanding what a stud actually is: a single stone, held at the earlobe, with nothing to distract from it.

The Foundation of

Any Collection

Stud earrings have stayed at the center of fine jewelry for a reason that has nothing to do with trend. They work. They work with business clothes, with casual wear, with evening dress. They do not compete with other jewelry you are wearing. A woman with diamond studs at a boardroom meeting and the same woman wearing those studs at dinner on Friday night is correct at both occasions. No adjustment needed.

This is what jewelers mean when they call studs foundational. They are not necessarily the most dramatic piece you own, but they are the most reliable. Many collectors buy their studs once and wear them for thirty years.

Setting Choices

and What They Do

The setting is the first real decision. A prong setting lifts the stone away from the earlobe and allows light to enter from below, maximizing brilliance. Three prongs work well with round stones, exposing more of the diamond while holding it securely. Four prongs are standard for symmetrical shapes like princess, cushion, and Asscher cuts, where corner coverage matters.

A bezel setting wraps the stone in a continuous metal rim. It is the most protective option available, well suited to active wear or people who are hard on their jewelry. The tradeoff is a slight reduction in the light entering from the sides, though the clean, modern profile appeals to many clients regardless.

Then there is the framed stud. Bez Ambar’s Ring of Fire stud earrings place a center stone inside a complete frame of Blaze® cut diamonds, the same patented square-cut accent stones used in halo rings. The frame closes without gaps, so the center diamond and its surround read as a single, much larger gem. A 1.00-carat stud in a Blaze® frame can appear close to 2.00 carats face-up. For those who want presence without extreme carat weight, this is a worthwhile calculation.

Size and

Face Shape

Size is a practical and aesthetic question at once. The practical side: studs above 2.00 carats are heavy enough that some wearers feel them throughout the day. Post length, backing type, and stone weight all factor into comfort. An Omega back or screw back handles heavier studs better than a standard push back, keeping the stone upright rather than tilting forward.

The aesthetic side is less absolute than guides suggest. Elongated shapes, marquise, emerald, oval, tend to add visual length to rounder faces. Symmetrical shapes, round brilliants, princess cuts, square cornered stones, sit well on narrower faces. But face shape is one input, not a rule. Proportion is what actually determines whether a stud looks right: the stone’s diameter relative to the earlobe.

A useful check before buying: hold a ring of approximately the diameter you are considering against your earlobe. If it covers less than two-thirds of the lobe, it will look smaller than you expect in daily wear. If it extends past the lobe, it reads as a statement piece rather than a foundational one.

Matching and

Mismatched Pairs

The default for studs is a matched pair: identical stones, same shape, same setting, both ears. This is the classic approach and for good reason. The symmetry reads as intentional, and the stones need not be perfectly identical to look matched when the settings are the same.

The mismatched stud is a different idea entirely, one slightly larger stone, or two complementary shapes. Worn well, the mismatched approach has an ease that a precisely matched pair sometimes lacks. The risk is that it reads as accidental rather than deliberate. The key is contrast clear enough to be obviously intentional.

When to Invest

in Studs

With studs, there is no setting to hide behind. The stone is the piece. This makes quality more visible here than in almost any other jewelry category. An SI2 diamond that looks clean set into a ring may show inclusions under normal viewing distance when worn as a stud, because the viewer is looking directly at it in open light.

Eye-clean is the standard to hold for studs regardless of what the certificate says. The shape that delivers the most forgiveness is the round brilliant: its facet pattern disperses light in a way that masks small inclusions well. Cushion and princess cuts require more care in selection because their larger open facets are less forgiving.

Explore stud earrings or contact us to discuss your stone and setting options.

What People

Ask Us

Does carat weight or face-up size matter more for studs? Face-up size matters more in practice. Two diamonds with the same certified carat weight can look meaningfully different once set, depending on cut depth and proportion. A well-cut 0.90-carat round brilliant will look as large as or larger than a deep-cut 1.10-carat stone. When shopping for studs, ask to see stones set before making a decision.

What backing works best for heavier studs? For studs above 1.00 carat, a screw-back or locking backing is worth specifying. Added weight increases the chance of the earring rotating forward, pointing the stone downward. A locking mechanism keeps the stud upright throughout the day without constant adjustment.

Can a frame be added to an existing stud? In many cases, yes. Bez Ambar builds frames, including the Blaze® Ring of Fire design, around existing center stones. The feasibility depends on the stone’s shape and current setting architecture. Reach out with the details and we can assess.

What does total carat weight mean for stud earrings? Total carat weight, often listed as TCW, refers to the combined weight of all diamonds in the pair, both earrings together. A listing for “1.00 ct TCW studs” means each earring carries a 0.50-carat stone. Reading this carefully before purchasing saves significant disappointment.

Round or fancy shape for a first pair of studs? Round brilliant for most people. The round cut is the most efficient converter of light to brilliance, it suits every face shape, and a quality round stud holds its value better than most fancy shapes. Once you own round studs, a second pair in princess or cushion adds variety without overlap.

title: Cushion Cut Diamond Earrings
body:
The cushion cut reads differently in earrings than it does in rings. Motion changes everything. What looks like warm, diffused brilliance on a stationary finger becomes active fire when the stone moves with you.

Set a cushion cut diamond on a table and it looks soft, romantic, a little antique. Put it in a stud earring and walk across a room, and it becomes something else entirely. The larger facets that give the cushion its characteristic warmth also catch and release light more dramatically as the stone tilts and shifts with the natural movement of the head. The fire that is only hinted at in stillness becomes the dominant quality in motion.

This is the fundamental reason the cushion cut earring is a different proposition than the cushion cut ring. The ring sits still. The earring rarely does.

Understanding the

Cushion Cut

The cushion cut is one of the older diamond shapes still in regular production. Its origins are in the old mine cut, the dominant shape from the 1700s through the early 1900s, which was designed to maximize brilliance under candlelight. The old mine cut had a smaller table, a larger culet (the flat facet at the base), and a higher crown than modern cuts. It was optimized for warm, flickering light rather than the flat overhead illumination of contemporary spaces.

The modern cushion cut retains the rounded corners and pillow-like outline of its ancestor but applies contemporary cutting standards to the facet arrangement. There are two main variants. The standard cushion modified brilliant adds extra facets beneath the girdle, producing more of a “crushed ice” look with smaller, more scattered light reflections. The chunky cushion, sometimes called cushion brilliant, keeps larger facets and produces broader, more defined light patterns similar to the old mine cut.

For earrings specifically, both styles work well, but the chunky cushion’s larger facets produce the more dramatic individual flashes of color and white light, particularly noticeable in motion.

Why Earrings

Change the Equation

In a ring, a cushion cut diamond is evaluated primarily in stillness. The client looks at it on the hand, lifts it to the light, rotates the finger. The fire is a pleasant accent to the stone’s overall character.

In an earring, the stone is almost never still. The natural movement of the head while speaking, turning, walking brings the facets in and out of alignment with light sources continuously. This means the fire, the spectral color dispersion that distinguishes the cushion from harder-edged shapes, is an ongoing presence rather than an occasional feature.

Bez Ambar’s Ring of Fire cushion cut earrings carry this idea as far as it goes. A pair of 2-carat E-SI cushion cut centers, each framed in a complete surround of Blaze® cut diamonds, the gap-free patented square accent stones. The frame closes completely, no interruption between stones, so the center and the surround move as a single field of light. Each earring reads closer to 6 carats face-up. The width across each stud is approximately 11.5mm, substantial presence without extreme weight.

Setting the

Cushion in an Earring

The setting requirements for an earring differ from a ring in one important respect: protection of the corners is less critical. A cushion cut ring is vulnerable at its rounded corners during the hand-forward activities of daily life. An earring sits away from contact with surfaces, which means the prongs can be fewer and lighter without meaningful risk to the stone.

A four-prong setting, one at each corner, is the standard for cushion studs. It lifts the stone from the ear and allows light to enter from below, which matters for a cut that depends on light coming from multiple angles. A bezel setting is a valid alternative for those who prefer a cleaner profile, though it reduces light entry from the sides.

For cushion cuts set inside a Blaze® frame, the setting becomes secondary to the frame itself. The frame holds the center and defines the overall silhouette. The combination of a cushion center inside an unbroken square of accent diamonds produces something architecturally distinct, geometric at the outer edge, soft at the center.

Explore the collection or contact us to discuss cushion cut options.

What People

Ask Us

What is the difference between old mine cut and modern cushion cut? The old mine cut, originating in the 1700s, had a smaller table facet, a higher crown, and a larger culet than today’s standards. It was optimized for candlelight. The modern cushion cut keeps the rounded outline and soft corners but applies current proportions for better performance under modern lighting. Both appear in estate and custom work; the choice is a matter of which light quality appeals to you.

Do cushion cuts look good as earrings? Cushion cuts are particularly well suited to earrings because motion activates their fire in a way that static viewing does not show. The broad facets and rounded outline produce warm, active light patterns as the earring moves with the wearer. They read well at conversational distance.

How does the Blaze® frame make a cushion stud look larger? The Blaze® frame is built from custom-cut square accent diamonds that sit edge to edge with no gaps. The continuous perimeter of light fuses visually with the center stone, so the eye cannot locate where the center stone ends and the frame begins. The result is a dramatic increase in perceived size: a 2-carat cushion in a Blaze® frame reads closer to 6 carats face-up.

What is the price range for cushion cut diamond studs? Significant cushion cut studs, 1.00 carat and above per stone, occupy a wide range depending on quality. At 2 carats per stone with an E-SI specification and a full Blaze® frame, the Bez Ambar Ring of Fire cushion earrings are priced at $42,000 for the pair including the diamonds. Contact us for current availability and to discuss stone specifications at other carat weights.

Can I request a specific cushion cut center stone for a pair of studs? Yes. We source cushion cut centers to specification. The key variables are carat weight per stone, color grade, clarity grade, and whether you prefer the standard modified brilliant (crushed ice) or the chunky cushion facet style. We can show options before committing to a setting.

title: Diamond Drop Earrings: Form, Weight, and Occasion
body:
A diamond drop earring that photographs beautifully but pulls the lobe after twenty minutes is a design failure — the challenge is building something that moves, catches light, and disappears in terms of weight.

The Architecture of a Drop Earring

What Makes the Form Work

Drop earrings are defined by pendant elements that hang below the earlobe — distinct from studs, which sit at the earlobe, and hoops, which encircle it. The structural elements are the ear fitting (post and butterfly, or lever-back, or wire), the connector (which may be a short link, a diamond station, or a direct mounting), and the pendant element itself, which does the visual work. Each of these components affects weight, movement, and the way the earring presents against the neck.

The pendant’s proportional relationship to the fitting is what experienced designers think about first. A pendant that hangs too short is indistinguishable from a large stud at any social distance. A pendant that hangs too long creates structural challenges and may brush the shoulder with certain necklines. The functional sweet spot for most formal drop earrings is 25 to 45 millimeters of total length from the top of the fitting to the bottom of the pendant — long enough to show clearly, short enough to be wearable through a full event.

Diamond Selection for Drop Earrings

Stone Quality in a Motion Context

Drop earrings move. That motion is part of their value — catching light from shifting angles as the wearer turns her head. The implication for diamond selection is that brilliance and scintillation matter more than they do in a static setting. A well-cut round brilliant or modified brilliant shape will activate under movement in a way that a poorly cut stone or a shape with low performance will not.

Color and clarity standards in drop earrings can reasonably be set one to two grades below what you might choose for an engagement ring solitaire, because the stones are viewed at greater distance from the viewer’s eye, are typically smaller individually, and are in motion. A G-H color and VS2-SI1 clarity is a reasonable starting point for the stone quality in a fine diamond drop earring without paying the premium for D-E-F and VVS clarity that the viewing distance does not require.

Weight Distribution and Wearability

The Engineering Problem Every Pair Must Solve

Metal weight, stone weight, and the vertical distribution of that mass all determine whether the earring is comfortable. A bottom-heavy design with most of the weight concentrated at the end of a long pendant will pull and swing more than one where the weight is distributed along the length. Platinum and 18k gold have the same visual density but different physical weights, which is why earring frames are often made in 14k or 18k gold rather than platinum regardless of what metal the wearer prefers — the weight difference over an evening is meaningful.

The ear fitting itself contributes to comfort. Lever-back closures distribute the earring’s weight more evenly across the lobe than a standard butterfly back on a thin post. For heavier drop earrings, a lever-back or threaded screw back reduces the tendency for the earring to tilt or rotate outward over the course of an evening.

Occasion Calibration

From Formal Evening to Daytime Appropriate

The occasion governs the appropriate scale of a diamond drop earring. A chandelier earring with three inches of cascading diamond stations is appropriate for a black-tie event and conspicuous at a business lunch. The same design logic that makes it spectacular in one context makes it incongruous in another. Most clients who invest in fine drop earrings benefit from two designs that cover different registers — a modest, elegant shorter drop for versatile daytime and evening wear, and a more dramatic piece reserved for formal occasions.

The length of the earring relative to the wearer’s neckline and hairstyle also matters practically. Shorter hair and lower necklines allow longer drops to read clearly. High necklines and longer hair can obscure shorter pendants. These are fitting-room considerations that catalog images do not capture.

What People

Ask Us

What is the difference between a drop earring and a dangle earring? The distinction is one of proportion and movement. Drop earrings are typically shorter and more structured — hanging one to two centimeters below the lobe. Dangle earrings tend to be longer, more fluid, and more explicitly kinetic in their design. The line between the two categories is not sharp, and the terms are used interchangeably in commercial contexts. What matters is the specific proportional relationship to the wearer’s face and the occasion.

How many total carats should a fine diamond drop earring carry? The range for meaningful fine diamond drop earrings runs from approximately 0.75 total carats (for a modest, versatile design) to 5 or more total carats for a substantial formal piece. Most clients looking for a significant but not extreme drop earring end up in the 1.5 to 3.0 total carat range, which offers real visual presence without the weight that larger total weights introduce.

What setting style best showcases diamonds in a drop earring? Prong settings maximize light entry and exit, which is ideal for brilliance in motion. Pavé and micro-pavé settings create texture and surface sparkle but sacrifice some of the dramatic scintillation of individual stones. Bezel settings offer security and a clean, modern line but reduce the light performance compared to prong settings. The right choice depends on the design aesthetic — all are legitimate.

Are diamond drop earrings appropriate as a gift rather than a personal purchase? They are a meaningful gift, but length and scale calibration are personal enough that getting it wrong is easy. If giving as a gift, choosing a design at the more modest end of the length range reduces the risk of the earring being too dramatic for the recipient’s taste or lifestyle. Including a gift receipt or discussing the design with the recipient before purchase is worth the slight reduction in surprise.

What metal works best for diamond drop earrings? White metals — platinum and white gold — create the cleanest visual relationship with colorless diamonds, allowing the stones to read without interference from the metal color. Yellow gold creates a warmer contrast that some clients find more interesting and historically resonant. Rose gold is a warm, contemporary option. The metal choice is personal and should align with the wearer’s existing jewelry and preference, not default to a single correct answer.

title: The Complete Guide to Diamond Hoop Earrings
body:
Diamond hoops are the piece that bridges everything: formal and casual, day and evening, classic and contemporary. The right pair disappears into your life and improves every outfit you own.

Walk into any fine jewelry store and you will find diamond hoops in some form. Walk into most of them and you will find a narrowed version of the same idea: a thin tube of metal set with small round diamonds along the outside curve. The category is broader and more interesting than that. Understanding what separates a pair of diamond hoops that you reach for every day from a pair that stays in the drawer begins with a few structural questions.

Inside Versus

Outside Set Diamonds

The most important decision in a diamond hoop is not the size; it is where the diamonds sit. An outside-set hoop places diamonds along the outer curve of the tube, the part facing away from the ear. When the earring is worn, these diamonds face forward and downward. They are visible to the world, which is their intention, but they are less visible to the wearer in a mirror because the ear partially blocks the view from the front.

An inside-set hoop, sometimes called a half-inside or full-inside depending on the extent of the diamond coverage, places stones along the inner curve, the surface facing the neck. This arrangement produces a different kind of sparkle: the diamonds reflect against the skin and catch light from angles that outside stones do not. An inside-set hoop flashes when the head turns, creating movement and life that a static forward view does not show.

The decision between the two approaches depends on where and how you wear earrings. Outside-set hoops are more legible to others. Inside-set hoops are more alive in motion.

Diameter and

Gauge

Hoop earrings are measured by inner diameter, the distance across the inside of the circle. Small hoops, sometimes called huggies, run between 12mm and 20mm inner diameter. They sit close to the earlobe, offering a clean, unfussy look that suits everyday wear without reading as a statement. The huggie is a reliable workhorse: it goes with everything and never requires thought about whether it is appropriate.

Medium hoops, running from approximately 22mm to 35mm, are the most versatile format. Large enough to be visible and to frame the face, small enough to wear to work or a school pickup without looking overdressed. This is the size range that most people find they actually wear.

Large hoops, above 35mm, are statement pieces. They work at specific occasions and with specific looks. They are generally harder to wear daily, partly because of weight and partly because they require the rest of the outfit to accommodate them.

Gauge, the thickness of the tube itself, affects weight and proportion. A heavier gauge feels more substantial and reads as more luxurious, but adds weight to the ear over a long day. Lighter gauges are more comfortable for continuous wear.

Metal Choice

and Contrast

Yellow gold hoops have a warmth that flatters a wide range of skin tones and pairs naturally with the slight warmth of near-colorless diamonds. The metal is forgiving: a G or H color diamond, which might show a faint yellow tint against white metal, looks clean and intentional against yellow gold.

White gold and platinum both maximize the visual contrast between metal and diamonds. The diamonds appear whiter and more intense against a neutral metal background. This is the argument for white metal in diamond hoops: the stones do more work.

The practical difference between white gold and platinum is worth understanding. White gold is yellow gold alloyed with white metals and then rhodium-plated to achieve its color. The rhodium plating will wear over time, typically within one to three years of regular wear, at which point the piece needs replating to restore its color. Platinum is naturally white and does not require plating, though it does develop a surface patina over time that some people prefer to maintain polished and others leave as acquired character. Platinum is also denser and heavier than gold, which is a factor in earrings where weight translates to comfort over a long day.

Huggies Versus

Full Hoops

The huggie and the full hoop are both hoops in construction, a tube that passes through the ear piercing and closes, but they are different in character. The huggie is intimate and restrained. It hugs the earlobe, keeping its presence close to the face without projecting. The full hoop creates a circle that extends below the earlobe, framing it.

For those who want to wear diamond hoops daily without adjustment or thought, the huggie is often the right answer. It is comfortable to forget, secure, and appropriate across a wider range of situations. The full hoop, particularly at 25mm or above, makes itself known.

Bez Ambar’s hoop earrings incorporate the Blaze® cut accent stones in place of standard round brilliants, delivering a different quality of fire and color dispersion. Explore hoop earrings or contact us to discuss the right diameter and setting for your situation.

What People

Ask Us

What is the difference between inside-set and outside-set diamond hoops? Outside-set hoops place diamonds on the outer curve, facing forward. Inside-set hoops place diamonds on the inner curve, facing the neck and catching light from behind the ear as the head turns. Inside-set hoops tend to look more active in motion; outside-set hoops read more legibly in a photograph or a mirror. Many clients who wear hoops daily prefer inside or half-inside settings for their sense of movement.

What hoop diameter suits daily wear? For most people, a diameter between 22mm and 30mm inner diameter is the most wearable size for daily use. It is visible enough to register but not so large that it becomes a commitment. Huggies, at 12 to 20mm, are the easiest daily earring of all: they go on and do not require thought.

White gold or platinum for diamond hoops? Both maximize diamond contrast. Platinum is naturally white and does not need replating, but it is heavier, which matters for earrings. White gold is lighter but requires replating every one to three years as the rhodium coating wears. If weight is a concern, white gold is the practical choice. If you want to avoid maintenance, platinum is worth the additional cost.

How do Blaze® diamonds change the look of a hoop? Standard diamond hoops use round brilliant accent stones. Blaze® cut stones are square, with a facet arrangement that produces approximately ten times the color dispersion of a round brilliant. In a hoop, this means the diamonds flash spectral color rather than just white light, adding a quality of fire that is visible at normal conversational distance.

Can hoop earrings be worn with other earrings? Yes. A common approach is a huggie or small hoop in the first piercing and a stud in a second or third lobe piercing above it. The hoop anchors the ear and the stud adds point interest above. The proportions work best when the stud is smaller than the hoop, so the two pieces read as intentional rather than competing.

title: Ear Climber Earrings: The Modern Earring That Travels Up the Ear
body:
A climber earring turns the ear itself into part of the composition — the jewelry does not hang from the ear or sit on it, it follows it, which is a genuinely new formal idea in a category that has been doing the same things for centuries.

What a Climber Earring Is

The Form Factor and How It Works

An ear climber — also called an ear crawler — is an earring that enters the earlobe through a standard post-and-back closure at the bottom and angles upward, following the natural curve of the ear’s edge toward the helix. Unlike a stud, which presents a single face at the lobe, or a drop, which hangs below the lobe, the climber presents a linear or curved design element that the observer reads as an ascending line from the lobe upward. The jewelry becomes visible against the ear itself rather than hanging free of it.

The mechanical principle requires an articulated or curved post that follows the ear’s inner curve while the decorative element sits against the outer edge. The standard construction uses a main post that anchors at the lobe and a thin secondary element — sometimes a J-shaped curve, sometimes a flexible chain, sometimes a rigid curved bar — that holds the upper portion of the earring against the ear without a second piercing. This single-piercing design that creates the illusion of a second, higher jewelry point is one of the climber’s most distinctive features.

Design Language of the Climber

What the Ascending Form Can Express

The ascending line of a climber earring can be executed in multiple design vocabularies. The most direct is a straight or gently curved bar set with pavé diamonds or colored stones, reading as a line of light that ascends the ear. A vine or branch design that curves along the ear and branches off at intervals creates an organic, natural impression. A graduated size sequence — small stones at the lobe, increasing in size toward the upper terminus — creates a directional emphasis that draws the eye upward. Each approach uses the vertical travel of the form differently.

The length of the climber — how far it ascends the ear — is both a design variable and a practical constraint. Shorter climbers that travel one to two centimeters above the lobe are more versatile and secure. Longer climbers that reach toward the mid-helix require a more careful fit to the individual ear’s curve and more deliberate anchoring at the upper terminus to prevent the upper portion from swinging forward. The fitting of a climber earring is necessarily more personal than the fitting of a standard stud.

Fitting and Security

The Practical Constraints of the Form

Because the climber’s upper element rests against the ear without a second piercing, its security depends on the friction and tension of the design against the ear’s curve. A climber that is too loosely sprung for a particular ear’s anatomy will slide forward, falling away from the ear and defeating the ascending-line visual logic of the form. A climber that is too tightly spring-tensioned against a specific ear curve may be uncomfortable during extended wear.

The implication is that ear climbers, particularly fine ones with significant diamond content, benefit from being selected and if necessary adjusted to the specific wearer’s ear rather than purchased as standardized products. A jeweler who works with climbers regularly can assess fit, adjust the post curve if necessary, and confirm that the upper element rests against the ear properly before the purchase is completed. This is a category where trying the earring on is not optional — it is essential.

Diamond and Stone Work in Climbers

Appropriate Scale and Setting Style

Diamond climbers most commonly use pavé or micro-pavé setting because the continuous line of small diamonds along the ascending bar creates the light-trace effect that makes the form visually distinctive. A single large station stone at the lower or upper terminus — a small pear or oval at the apex, for instance — adds a focal point to what might otherwise be a uniform ascending line.

Colored stones in climbers work particularly well in high-contrast combinations: blue sapphire or emerald green against the ear against white gold or platinum has a graphic clarity that reads well in the climber format. Graduated color — from pale at the lobe to deep at the apex, or vice versa — is a more complex design move that works when the color sequence is deliberate and executed well.

The scale of individual stones in a climber needs to be calibrated to the total length of the ascending element. Stones that are too large for the width of the bar create an unbalanced, top-heavy appearance. Stones that are too small get lost against the ear and undermine the visual line. The relationship between stone size, bar width, and total earring length is a proportioning problem that the designer and the goldsmith must solve together.

The Climber and the Multi-Piercing Context

Where It Fits in a Contemporary Ear Stack

The ear climber emerged alongside the multi-piercing movement and fits naturally into that context. At the lobe, the climber’s post pierces the standard lower lobe position. The ascending design element travels up the ear toward territory occupied, in a multi-piercing arrangement, by cartilage piercings holding smaller hoops or studs. The climber bridges this territory without requiring additional piercings, which makes it an accessible entry into the stacked-ear aesthetic for wearers who have only a single standard lobe piercing.

A climber at the lobe paired with one or two small hoops or studs at higher cartilage positions — if those piercings exist — creates a layered, ascending composition that uses the ear’s three-dimensional structure as the organizing framework. The climber is not competing with the higher piercings; it is connecting the lobe to them visually.

What People

Ask Us

Do ear climbers require a second piercing? No. The standard climber design uses a single post at the lobe with a curved or spring-tensioned upper element that rests against the ear without a second piercing. The illusion of a second higher jewelry point is created by the earring’s design sitting against the ear’s surface. Some elaborate climber designs do use a second piercing at the upper cartilage to anchor the apex — these are a distinct category called “double-pierced climbers” and require two piercings per ear.

How long does it take to put on a climber earring? More time than a standard stud, less than a clip-on. Inserting the post, positioning the upper element against the ear’s curve, and confirming the fit typically takes thirty to sixty seconds per ear once you are accustomed to the design. First-time wearers often find it slightly awkward — second-time wearers rarely mention it. It is not a significant burden in practical use.

Are ear climbers appropriate for professional work environments? A short, diamond-pavé bar climber in white gold or gold is as work-appropriate as any fine earring. The form is distinctive but not dramatic — it reads as a graphic fine jewelry piece, not as costume or statement jewelry. Longer, more elaborate climbers with significant stone content are better suited to social and evening contexts. The same calibration applies to climbers as to other earring types: match the scale of the earring to the occasion.

Can a climber earring be sized or adjusted to fit a specific ear? Yes. A skilled goldsmith can adjust the curvature of the post and the tension of the upper element to fit a specific ear. For a significant fine climber — one worth the investment in a proper fitting — this adjustment is worth requesting. The post needs to follow the specific person’s antihelix curve to hold the upper element in the right position, and this is an individual fit variable.

What length ear climber works for most people? Climbers that travel 25 to 40 millimeters above the lobe (measured along the ascending element) work for a wide range of ear sizes and are comfortable for extended wear. Shorter than 20 millimeters, the ascending effect is subtle — the earring reads more like an angled stud than a true climber. Longer than 50 millimeters, fit precision and security become more demanding and the design becomes occasion-specific.
