title: How to Clean Diamond Jewelry at Home Without Damaging It
body:
A diamond is the hardest natural material on earth, but the film that accumulates on its surface from daily wear — body oil, lotion, soap residue, and cooking grease — does not need to be hard to make the stone look dead.

The Problem

Why Diamond Jewelry Loses Brilliance Between Cleanings

A diamond appears brilliant because light enters through the table and crown facets, reflects off the pavilion facets, and exits back through the crown. This optical performance depends on clean, unobstructed facet surfaces. A thin film of skin oil on the diamond’s table facet does not scratch the stone — diamond’s hardness is too high for any common household substance to scratch it — but it does change the refractive behavior of light at the surface. Oil has a refractive index closer to glass than to air, and when a diamond’s facet surface is coated with oil, the light behavior that produces fire and scintillation is substantially degraded.

Body chemistry is the primary source of contamination. Your hands produce natural oils, and every time you touch your ring the stone contacts that oil. Lotion, hand cream, sunscreen, and moisturizer accelerate the contamination cycle. Soap itself, counterintuitively, leaves a film — bar soap in particular deposits a waxy residue that adheres to prong settings and lodge beneath stones where it is impossible to remove without a brush. Cooking grease and cleaning products create the most tenacious films, which is why jewelry worn in the kitchen accumulates visible residue faster than jewelry worn in other environments.

The visual test for a contaminated stone is direct comparison in bright light. Hold the piece under a single direct light source and look at the stone from above. A clean diamond returns a bright, crisp reflection of the light source from each major facet. A contaminated diamond shows a dull, diffuse surface with scattered reflections that do not resolve into clear facet patterns. The difference is dramatic, and a client who has never cleaned their ring under this test is often surprised at how much brilliance has been lost.

The Method

How to Clean Diamond Jewelry Safely at Home

The correct home cleaning method for diamond jewelry is warm water, a small amount of mild dish soap, a soft toothbrush, and adequate rinsing. This is not a simplified version of a more complex professional process — it is the actual process, and it works.

Fill a small bowl with warm water — not hot, because thermal shock can stress certain stone settings, and not cold because warm water cuts oil more effectively. Add one or two drops of mild dish soap, the type with no harsh chemical additives or bleaching agents. Place the piece in the soapy water and allow it to soak for three to five minutes. The soak softens the contamination layer.

Remove the piece and use a soft-bristled toothbrush to gently scrub the stone and setting. Pay particular attention to the areas behind and beneath the stone where the most contamination accumulates, especially in prong settings where the skin-contact areas are most active. Use short, light strokes — the point is to dislodge loosened contamination, not to scrub mechanically. Rinse thoroughly under running warm water, covering the drain with a cloth or stopper in case the piece slips. Dry with a clean lint-free cloth or allow to air dry on a soft surface.

What Not to Do

Common Cleaning Mistakes That Damage Fine Jewelry

Chlorine bleach is the most dangerous household cleaner for gold jewelry. Chlorine attacks gold alloys at the grain boundaries of the metal, weakening the structure over time in a process called stress corrosion cracking. The damage is invisible at first and catastrophic when it manifests — a prong structure weakened by chlorine exposure can fracture suddenly under normal wear stress. Remove all gold jewelry before entering a chlorinated pool or hot tub, and never use bleach or bleach-containing cleaners on gold pieces.

Ultrasonic cleaners are available for home use and are effective, but they are not appropriate for all pieces. Ultrasonic cavitation can loosen pavé stones that are not perfectly seated, and it can aggravate existing cracks in included or surface-reaching natural stones. A home ultrasonic cleaner is safe for well-set, clean diamond jewelry with no known structural issues. It is not safe for estate pieces of unknown condition, pieces with large surface-reaching inclusions, or pieces with loose stones. When in doubt, use the warm-water-and-brush method instead.

Toothpaste is a popular home remedy for jewelry cleaning and a bad one. Most toothpastes contain mild abrasives that can scratch softer stones and gold settings. The abrasive level that is too mild to scratch a diamond is sufficient to scratch a gold surface to a matte finish. Avoid toothpaste for any metal-and-stone jewelry.

What People

Ask Us

How often should I clean my diamond ring at home? For a ring worn daily, once every two weeks maintains the diamond at near-optimal brilliance. Clients who cook frequently, apply lotion regularly, or work with their hands should clean weekly. The cleaning takes ten minutes and the visual improvement is immediate. Do not wait until the diamond looks obviously cloudy — a stone cleaned regularly never reaches the worst contamination state.

Can I use hand sanitizer to clean my jewelry? Hand sanitizer — the alcohol-gel type that became ubiquitous after 2020 — is not a cleaning solution for jewelry. The gel polymer in many formulations leaves a residue on the stone and setting that is as problematic as the original contamination. Alcohol-based sanitizer in liquid form will clean the stone surface but has no detergent action to remove oils from beneath stones and inside settings. Use proper warm water and dish soap.

Is it safe to clean diamond earrings the same way as rings? Yes. The warm-water-and-brush method is safe for diamond studs and drop earrings. Remove the earring backs before cleaning so the post and backing are fully exposed. Pay attention to the area where the stone sits in its setting, which accumulates skin oil from contact with the earlobe. Rinse carefully and confirm the post and backing are fully dry before reattachment.

Will cleaning affect the rhodium plating on white gold? The warm-water-and-dish-soap method does not remove rhodium plating. Rhodium plating is a durable electroplated surface that withstands routine cleaning. Rhodium plating is degraded over time by normal wear — contact with skin, friction against surfaces, and the mechanical action of removing the piece — not by gentle cleaning. Clean your white gold diamond jewelry without concern for the plating.

What professional cleaning services do you offer? We offer professional ultrasonic and steam cleaning with inspection at our atelier. Professional cleaning differs from home cleaning in that steam cleaning reaches areas a brush cannot and ultrasonic cavitation removes contamination from inside the setting with no mechanical contact. We inspect every piece that comes in for cleaning for prong integrity, loose stones, and clasp condition before returning it. We recommend this service once a year regardless of home cleaning frequency.

title: Jewelry Appraisal: How It Works and What the Number Means
body:
The appraisal value on a jewelry document is not the price you paid, not the price you could sell it for, and not the price you would pay to replace it with an identical piece — it is a specific figure for a specific purpose, and conflating it with the others creates expensive confusion.

The Document

What an Appraisal Is and What Purpose It Serves

A jewelry appraisal is a professional opinion of value, issued in writing by a qualified appraiser, that describes the piece and assigns it a monetary figure. That figure is the appraiser’s professional opinion of the piece’s value in a defined market context. The key phrase is “defined market context” — different appraisal types are calculated for different purposes, and the same ring can legitimately receive two very different appraisal values depending on the purpose of the document.

The most common appraisal type is the insurance replacement appraisal. This figure represents the cost to replace the piece with a comparable piece of equivalent quality through a retail jewelry establishment. Retail replacement values are typically 50 to 100 percent above the price originally paid for the piece, because retail replacement assumes purchasing from a retail store at full retail price at the time of the claim — not at the price the client originally paid in a different market or at a different time. Insurance companies use this figure to calculate premiums and pay claims.

A fair market value appraisal estimates what the piece would sell for between a willing buyer and a willing seller, neither under compulsion, in the open market. Fair market value is almost always lower than insurance replacement value for fine jewelry, because the secondary market for used jewelry — even fine jewelry — prices below retail. Estate appraisals are typically fair market value appraisals. Liquidation value appraisals are lower still, assuming a forced or quick sale.

The Process

How a Qualified Appraiser Arrives at a Number

A thorough appraisal begins with physical examination of the piece. The appraiser identifies the metal type and karat through hallmark reading and, when necessary, acid testing or XRF analysis. Stones are identified by species — natural diamond, natural sapphire, synthetic, simulant — and measured using a calibrated micrometer or optical measuring device. Each stone’s dimensions translate to an estimated weight because removing and weighing stones independently would require removing them from their settings.

Diamond grading in an appraisal context uses the same 4C framework as a laboratory grading report — cut, color, clarity, and carat weight — but the appraiser’s grade is an estimate made with the stone in its setting. The accuracy of an in-setting diamond grade is lower than the accuracy of a laboratory grade on an unset stone, because the setting obscures the girdle, restricts the angle of examination, and makes accurate size measurement more difficult. Significant discrepancies between appraisal grades and laboratory grades are common and not automatically indicative of bad faith — they reflect the inherent limitation of grading a set stone.

The value conclusion comes from the appraiser’s knowledge of the current market for comparable pieces. A qualified appraiser tracks market prices through dealer contacts, auction results, and retail survey data. An appraiser who has not actively updated their market knowledge within the past twelve months should be presenting current appraisal values with caution.

The Appraiser

How to Identify Qualified Versus Unqualified Appraisers

The United States has no mandatory licensing requirement for jewelry appraisers, which means anyone can call themselves a jewelry appraiser without formal training or credential. This creates a real quality problem in the appraisal market. The professional credentials that indicate genuine qualification are the GIA Graduate Gemologist (GG) designation, the American Society of Jewelry Appraisers’ Certified Senior Member (CSM), and the American Gem Society Certified Gemologist Appraiser (CGA). Appraisers with these credentials have passed curriculum and examination requirements specific to gemological assessment and valuation methodology.

An appraiser who charges a flat fee for the appraisal — rather than a fee based on a percentage of the appraised value — has no financial incentive to inflate the value figure. Percentage-based appraisal fees create a conflict of interest: the higher the appraiser values the piece, the more they earn. Flat fee appraisals are the professional standard.

Be cautious of appraisals issued at the point of sale by the same entity selling the piece. A jeweler selling a ring and simultaneously issuing an appraisal that shows the piece is worth significantly more than the sale price has an obvious commercial interest in a high appraisal value. Independent appraisals — obtained from an appraiser who has no commercial relationship with the seller — are the appropriate standard for insurance and estate purposes.

What People

Ask Us

Why is my appraisal value much higher than what I paid? Insurance replacement appraisals are calculated at retail replacement cost — the cost of purchasing a comparable piece from a retail jewelry store at full retail price. If you purchased a piece at a discount, from a wholesale source, or in a different market condition than currently exists, the retail replacement value will be higher than your purchase price. This is normal and expected.

How often should jewelry be reappraised? Fine jewelry should be reappraised every three to five years for insurance purposes. Gold and diamond prices fluctuate, and an appraisal that was accurate in 2018 may significantly understate current replacement value. If you file an insurance claim against an outdated appraisal and the replacement cost has increased substantially, the insurance payout may not cover the actual replacement. Current appraisals protect against this gap.

Does a GIA grading report replace an appraisal? No. A GIA grading report describes the stone’s gemological characteristics — it does not provide a value opinion. An appraisal uses the stone description (which can reference the GIA report) and adds a monetary conclusion based on current market conditions. Both documents serve different purposes and neither replaces the other.

Can I appraise a piece I bought from you at Bez Ambar? Yes. We provide documentation with all pieces we make, which includes stone descriptions, metal content, and approximate weight. This documentation supports an independent appraisal by providing the factual description from the maker. An independent appraiser can then add their value conclusion. Some clients also ask us to provide a replacement value estimate at the time of purchase — we can do this, with the understanding that it represents our professional opinion, not a third-party appraisal.

Does the appraisal value affect what I can sell a piece for? The appraisal value does not determine the resale price. The secondary market for fine jewelry — auction, estate dealers, private sale — prices independently of appraisal values. A piece with an insurance replacement appraisal of fifty thousand dollars may sell on the secondary market for fifteen to twenty thousand dollars. This is not fraud or error; it reflects the difference between retail replacement value and fair market secondary value.

title: Men's Diamond Rings: Black Diamonds, Setting Styles, and What Actually Works
body:
Men's diamond rings are one of the least-guided purchases in fine jewelry. The conventions that govern women's rings don't transfer — and that's the first thing to get right.

Proportion First

Why Scale Decides Everything

The most common mistake in men's diamond jewelry is a mismatch between stone height, setting construction, and band width. A cathedral solitaire on a narrow band works in women's jewelry because every element is scaled for it. On a wide men's shank, the same configuration reads as borrowed — a component from one design grafted onto another.

Men's rings run from 4mm to 12mm wide. Most men find their proportional center between 6mm and 10mm, but the only reliable way to find the right width is to put rings on your hand. A 4mm band disappears on a wide hand. A 12mm band on a narrow hand reads as architectural armor.

Black Diamond

A Different Visual Language

Black diamond is opaque rather than transparent. Where a colorless diamond scintillates in prismatic flashes, black diamond absorbs light and presents a deep, graphic surface — matte to slightly lustrous depending on the cut and polish. That visual language translates naturally into men's jewelry.

The two dominant approaches: monochromatic (black diamond in blackened metal, the ring reads as a single tonal object) or contrasting (black diamond in platinum or yellow gold, where the boundary between metal and stone is the design). Both are valid — the choice is whether you want cohesion or contrast.

Most commercial black diamonds have been irradiated or fracture-filled. These treatments can make the stone marginally more brittle. For a ring worn daily in demanding conditions, bezel or channel setting provides better protection than prongs that leave the girdle exposed.

Metal Over Time

What Each Metal Costs Over Decades

Platinum is the right metal for a men's ring meant for decades of daily wear. It doesn't change color, requires no plating, and develops a wear patina most men prefer to periodic polishing. A wide men's ring in platinum has genuine heft — which reinforces the sense of permanence the piece is meant to carry.

White gold requires rhodium plating to maintain its white color. The plating wears through at high-contact points after months of daily wear. For an active man, the maintenance difference between white gold and platinum over five years is meaningful.

Titanium, tungsten, and cobalt chrome are harder than precious metals. They're also not resizable. Men's fingers change with age and fitness. A ring that can't be resized must be replaced. For a ring meant for a lifetime, that tradeoff matters more than the upfront cost savings.

Setting Construction

Bezel, Channel, and Flush

A bezel setting — continuous metal rim rather than prongs — is the most protective construction and one of the cleanest looking on a men's ring. The stone is fully secured, the girdle protected from impact. Particularly appropriate for black diamonds.

Channel setting places stones in a groove between two parallel walls with no prongs. Diamonds sit flush or near-flush with the band surface — a clean linear look without raised elements. Ideal for smaller diamonds, especially in a wide men's band.

Flush or gypsy setting places a single stone into a drilled seat, level with the surface. Only the table of the stone is visible. For men's rings, this delivers the stone as a quiet personal detail rather than a focal point — one or three flush-set diamonds across a plain band reads as refinement, not ornamentation.

Sizing and Service

What to Know Before You Commission

Men's ring sizing is more variable than women's because men's hands respond more dramatically to temperature and physical changes. Size to the larger end of your natural range — a ring sized for summer fits year-round. A ring sized for winter will be loose and at risk of loss in warm months.

Wide bands feel tighter than narrow ones at the same nominal size. A man sized at 10 in a 4mm band typically needs a 10.5 or 11 in a 10mm band. Ask explicitly about width compensation when sizing a ring above 8mm — some jewelers adjust for it automatically, others don't.

Know the service history of the piece before you buy it. A plain precious metal band is straightforward to resize at any point. A band with stones set across the full surface requires removal and resetting in the modified section. Tension-set rings may not be resizable at all without damaging the design.

title: Men's Wedding Bands: A Buying Guide That Skips the Cliches
body:
The men’s wedding band is worn on the same finger every day for decades — it is the most worn piece of jewelry most men will ever own, and the decisions around width, metal, finish, and thickness determine whether that experience is comfortable or not.

The Width

Why Width Is the First Decision and Not the Last

Band width is the dimension most men choose last and most regret first. Width is measured in millimeters across the band’s face — the distance from one edge to the other. Most men’s bands run from 4mm to 10mm, with 6mm and 8mm being the two most common selections. The width a band feels like on the hand is not always the width a band looks like in a display case, and this discrepancy is the most common source of post-purchase regret.

Wider bands — above 8mm — impose a structural constraint on finger movement. The wedding band sits at the base of the ring finger; a wide band extends up the finger away from the knuckle and can restrict the finger’s natural range of motion when the hand is closed into a fist. This is not a problem for every wearer, but it is a problem for men who work with their hands, play instruments, or are simply sensitive to the sensation of restriction. Try a wide band before committing.

The proportionality rule for band width is that the band’s visual presence on the hand should be calibrated to the wearer’s hand and finger size. A 4mm band on a wide hand with substantial fingers reads as a fine wire and provides almost no visual presence. A 10mm band on a narrow hand reads as disproportionately large. The target is a band that reads as intentional and resolved relative to the hand it is on — not so fine that it disappears, not so wide that it dominates. For most average adult male hands, 6mm to 8mm hits this proportional target.

The Metal

Platinum, Gold, and Alternative Metals — What Each Provides

Men’s bands are made in a wider range of metals than women’s fine jewelry, and the choice has genuine consequences for durability, comfort, and long-term appearance. The three categories to understand are precious metals (platinum, gold in various karats), contemporary metals (titanium, cobalt chrome, tungsten carbide), and mixed constructions that combine elements of both.

Platinum is the most appropriate metal for a men’s wedding band intended for lifetime daily wear. It does not change color, does not require plating, and is the most durable of the precious metals at equivalent gauge. Platinum develops a wear patina — a subtle surface texture that replaces the initial high polish — which many men prefer to the alternative of periodically polishing the band back to mirror finish. The patina is reversible; the band can be polished professionally at any time.

Gold in 14k or 18k is the traditional precious metal choice. Yellow gold reads richly and does not require surface maintenance other than occasional polishing. White gold requires rhodium replating to maintain its white color, which is a maintenance consideration for a band worn daily in demanding environments — workshop, kitchen, athletic training. Rose gold reads warmly and personally, and is the most distinctive of the three gold color options.

Titanium, tungsten, and cobalt chrome are marketed as durable alternatives that are harder than precious metals and available at significantly lower price points. They are genuinely harder than gold. They are also not resizable — resizing precious metal bands is a routine bench operation, but titanium and tungsten bands cannot be resized and must be replaced if the finger size changes. For a ring worn every day for decades, this is a significant practical constraint.

The Finish

Surface Treatment and What It Says About the Piece

A wedding band’s surface finish determines both its appearance and its maintenance requirements. High-polish finish produces a mirror surface that reflects light sharply and reads as formal and classic. Brushed or matte finish produces a directional satin texture that absorbs and diffuses light and reads as more understated and contemporary. Hammered finish creates an irregular, textured surface that catches light unpredictably and reads as handcrafted.

Combination finishes — polished edges with a brushed face, or hammered exterior with polished inner channel — add visual interest without the full visual commitment of an all-over texture. A polished center stripe on a brushed band is the most common combination finish and works well on bands from 6mm upward where there is sufficient width to separate the two surface regions clearly.

The maintenance implication of high-polish finish is that every contact scratch is visible against the mirror surface. Men who wear their bands through work, sports, or hands-on activity will accumulate visible scratches on a high-polish band within months. Brushed and matte finishes are more forgiving — incidental scratches blend into the existing texture rather than reading as disruptions to a smooth surface. For daily-wear bands in active use, the less reflective finish options age better and require less frequent professional polishing.

Comfort fit refers not to the surface finish but to the interior profile of the band. A standard band has a flat interior that sits with two sharp edges against the finger. A comfort-fit band has a domed or rounded interior that contacts the finger on a curved surface, reducing the pressure sensation at the band edges. For men who find rings uncomfortable or have not worn jewelry before, comfort-fit interior significantly reduces the adjustment period.

What People

Ask Us

Should the men’s band match the engagement ring? Coordination is more useful than matching. The bands should share at least one material characteristic — metal type, or at minimum metal color — to read as a set. They do not need to be identical or even close in design. A platinum men’s band with a brushed finish pairs well with a platinum diamond engagement ring, even if the two designs are completely different. The metal provides the visual connection.

What width is most practical for a man who works with his hands? For men who regularly work with their hands — construction, medical fields, cooking, athletic training — 4mm to 6mm is the most practical range. Narrower bands are less likely to catch on equipment, less likely to create a pressure point when the hand is gripped around a tool, and cause fewer heat management concerns in environments where metal rings carry thermal risk. Wherever thermal or physical catching risk is a genuine workplace issue, a band should be removed before work.

Can a men’s band include diamonds? Yes. Diamond-set men’s bands are more common than they were twenty years ago, and the design range has expanded significantly. A single row of channel-set diamonds across the band face is the most conservative option — clearly diamond but not overtly decorative. Channel-set baguette bands have a linear, architectural character that reads as masculine and minimal. Pavé-set bands are available and are appropriate for men who want significant sparkle in a band context.

Is platinum the right choice for a man who exercises regularly? Platinum handles exercise context well — it is the most corrosion-resistant precious metal, is not damaged by sweat, and its wear patina disguises incidental surface marks. The one consideration for active wearers is weight: platinum is significantly heavier than gold at equivalent dimensions, and some men find the extra weight noticeable during athletic activity. Trying the band at the intended weight before purchase matters.

How far in advance should we order the men’s band? For a custom or made-to-order men’s band, allow six to eight weeks from the design consultation to delivery. If the band is a standard design from existing inventory in the correct width and metal, allow two to three weeks for sizing and finishing. Do not leave the men’s band order until after the women’s engagement ring is finalized — the two pieces should be coordinated from the beginning, which means the men’s design conversation should happen at the same time as the engagement ring conversation.

title: Buying Fine Jewelry Online
body:
Online jewelry retail has matured substantially. Some categories of fine jewelry are genuinely well-suited to online purchase. Others are not. Knowing which is which saves money and prevents disappointment.

The case for buying jewelry online rests on price transparency, selection breadth, and comparison shopping efficiency. All three are real advantages in the right categories. The case against rests on the impossibility of evaluating a colored stone’s actual color from a photograph, the inability to assess a ring’s fit and feel without wearing it, and the difficulty of building trust in a transaction that involves thousands of dollars and a material you cannot inspect before paying.

Both cases are correct. The resolution is not online versus in-person as a general principle but rather knowing which specific purchases work online and which require a different approach.

What Works Well

Online

Certified loose diamonds are the category where online purchasing makes the most sense. GIA, AGS, and other major laboratory certificates establish the stone’s specifications with precision: cut grade, color grade, clarity grade, carat weight, and measurements. These specifications are consistent regardless of where you view the certificate.

A round brilliant in G/VS2 with an Excellent GIA cut grade is that stone regardless of whether you buy it from a New York wholesaler’s website or a Los Angeles atelier’s inventory. The certificate verifies the specification. The only remaining variable is price, and online comparison across multiple certified stones in the same specification gives you a genuine market baseline.

Simple gold and platinum jewelry, particularly chains, plain bands, and pieces without stones, also works well online. Metal purity is verified by hallmark; weight and dimensions can be specified; the product is what it is.

What Does Not Work

Online

Colored gemstones are the clearest case against online purchasing. A photograph of a sapphire can look completely different from the stone in person. Camera sensors do not render saturated colors accurately; the saturation is often enhanced or altered by the camera’s processing. A stone that looks vivid cornflower blue in a product photo can look grey-blue or dark in person.

The same problem applies to colored diamonds (pink, blue, yellow) and other gemstones where color is the primary value driver. For any stone where color is the point, an in-person evaluation is not optional.

Custom design is the second category that does not work online. Custom work requires conversation, sketches, model approvals, and iterative refinement. It requires a relationship with a maker. Online communication can supplement that process, but it cannot replace the physical component of evaluating materials, proportions, and finish.

High-value engagement rings in unusual sizes or with complex settings benefit from in-person evaluation of fit and proportion before purchase. A photograph does not communicate how a ring sits on the hand, which is a significant part of whether it works.

What to Look For

in an Online Jeweler

A clear, unambiguous return policy is the first criterion. A 30-day return window for an undamaged ring is the minimum standard for any reputable online jeweler. Without it, you have no recourse if the piece does not meet your expectations.

Third-party gemological documentation, typically a GIA certificate, for any significant diamond. The certificate number should be verifiable directly on the GIA website. Match the certificate to the stone using the GIA-laser-inscribed number on the girdle.

Real photography of the actual stone, not renders or stock photography. Renders show what the design is supposed to look like; real photography shows what this specific stone in this specific setting actually looks like.

Clear metal specifications: karat for gold, designation for platinum, rhodium plating disclosure for white gold.

Where Bez Ambar

Fits

Custom design and patented settings like the Blaze® are not available as commodity online purchases because they require specific conversations about stones, settings, and intentions. A Bez Ambar ring is a specific piece built for a specific client around specific material, not a product pulled from inventory in response to a click.

That said, initial conversations, pricing discussions, and design consultations can begin online. Contact us to begin.

What People

Ask Us

Is it safe to buy a diamond ring online? Safe if you have a GIA certificate for the stone, a verified return policy, and a reputable seller. Not safe without documentation or return rights. The risks are manageable if you verify the stone’s specifications independently and have a clear path to return the piece if it does not meet expectations in person.

How do I verify a GIA certificate is real? Go to gia.edu/report-check and enter the report number. The GIA database will confirm the report’s existence and the stone’s specifications. If the certificate number you were given does not appear in the GIA database, the certificate is not genuine.

Why does the stone look different in person than in the photos? Camera sensors, lighting, and image processing all affect how a stone looks in a photograph. Professional product photography is designed to make the stone look appealing; it is not designed to accurately represent the stone’s color under everyday lighting conditions. This is not necessarily deception; it is a limitation of photography as a medium for representing gemstones.

What return window is adequate for an online jewelry purchase? Thirty days is the industry minimum for a reputable seller. Some offer sixty or ninety days. The window should be calculated from delivery, not from purchase. Read the return policy carefully: some sellers offer refunds; others offer store credit only.

Can I get a custom ring made by Bez Ambar through an online consultation? Yes, as a starting point. Initial design consultations, discussion of stone options, and pricing discussions happen through email, phone, and video. Physical evaluation of materials and approvals of the ring at various stages of production may require either in-person visits or the shipment of samples and prototypes. Contact us to discuss.

title: Platinum vs White Gold: The Complete Comparison
body:
Platinum and white gold are different metals with different properties and different lifetime costs — the choice between them deserves more than a visual comparison.

The Materials

What Platinum and White Gold Actually Are

Platinum used in fine jewelry is typically 95 percent pure platinum alloyed with 5 percent iridium or ruthenium. The common stamp is PT950 or PLAT. Platinum is a naturally white metal — its white color does not come from any surface treatment and does not change with wear, exposure, or time. At the molecular level, platinum is dense, heavy, and extremely stable. It does not react with most common chemicals, does not oxidize, and does not corrode under normal wear conditions.

White gold is yellow gold alloyed with white metals — typically palladium, nickel, or a combination — to produce an alloy that is less yellow than standard gold. The resulting alloy in 18k white gold (75 percent gold, 25 percent white alloy metals) is not actually white — it is a light grayish-yellow. The white color you see in a white gold ring comes from a surface electroplating of rhodium, a dense, bright-white metal in the platinum group. That rhodium coating is not permanent. It wears at a rate determined by wear frequency, the wearer’s skin chemistry, and the thickness of the original plating.

The physical density difference between the two metals is significant and perceptible. Platinum is approximately 60 percent heavier than 18k white gold at equivalent dimensions. A platinum solitaire ring feels meaningfully heavier on the finger than an identical design in white gold. Some wearers prefer this heft; others find it uncomfortable for daily wear. This is a subjective factor with no right answer, but it should be experienced before the purchase decision is finalized.

The Durability

How Each Metal Wears and What That Means in Practice

Platinum and white gold do not wear the same way, and understanding the difference prevents unrealistic expectations about the condition of each metal type after years of daily wear.

Platinum is extremely resistant to material loss. A platinum ring worn daily for twenty years will have lost a negligible amount of metal from wear. However, platinum displaces rather than loses material under abrasion — scratches in platinum move metal to the side of the scratch rather than removing it. The result is a surface texture called a patina that develops over time as the polish is disrupted and the surface takes on a lower-gloss, satin-like quality. Some clients find this patina beautiful; others prefer high-polish and return the ring periodically for polishing. Both responses are valid, and polishing platinum to its original state requires professional equipment but is straightforward.

White gold loses material through normal abrasion — gold alloy is softer than platinum and scratches remove actual metal from the surface. The rate of material loss depends on the gold karat and the specific alloy composition, but over decades, high-wear areas of a white gold ring will show measurable metal reduction. In addition to this underlying wear, the rhodium plating coating the white gold wears through to the base alloy, revealing the grayish-yellow tone of the underlying white gold. Replating restores the white color and is necessary every two to five years for a ring worn daily, depending on the wear rate.

The Cost

Initial Price, Lifetime Maintenance, and True Total Cost

Platinum costs more than white gold at the time of fabrication. The reasons are the higher cost of the metal itself, the higher fabrication cost (platinum requires different bench tools and higher working temperatures than gold), and the higher per-unit cost of the denser material — a platinum ring of equal dimensions contains more metal by weight than a gold equivalent. Premium for platinum over white gold at comparable design complexity typically runs 25 to 40 percent.

The lifetime cost comparison changes when maintenance is included. White gold requires rhodium replating every two to five years for a ring worn daily. The cost of each replating session varies by studio, but typically runs between $50 and $150 per application. Over twenty years of daily wear, a white gold ring may require four to ten replating sessions, adding $200 to $1,500 to its total lifetime cost. Platinum requires no replating and its only maintenance cost is occasional polishing, which is less expensive than replating.

The break-even calculation depends on individual wear patterns and replating frequency, but for a ring intended for daily wear over decades, the platinum premium at purchase often becomes cost-neutral or advantageous when maintenance costs are fully accounted for. This is a useful calculation to complete before choosing between the two materials.

What People

Ask Us

Can I convert a white gold ring to platinum? Not directly — you cannot plate a white gold ring with platinum to achieve the same result as a platinum ring. The metals are fundamentally different, and the appearance and durability characteristics of platinum come from the metal throughout the piece, not from its surface. If you want your existing design in platinum, the ring must be recast or hand-fabricated from platinum. Stones from the existing piece can typically be reused in the new platinum setting.

Does platinum yellow with age? No. Platinum does not contain yellow gold and its white color comes from the metal itself rather than from any surface treatment. Platinum develops a patina from wear that reduces its surface gloss, but the underlying color does not change. The patina can be polished away to restore high-gloss at any time.

Is platinum hypoallergenic? Platinum jewelry is essentially inert and is the recommended choice for wearers with metal sensitivities. The nickel content in some white gold alloys is the most common cause of skin reactions to fine jewelry metals. 18k white gold made with palladium alloy (rather than nickel) is significantly less likely to cause reactions, but platinum’s complete absence of nickel and base metals makes it the safer choice for sensitive wearers.

Can platinum settings be repaired if damaged? Yes, platinum is highly repairable. Platinum’s malleability allows it to be reformed and welded without significant structural compromise, and the repair does not alter the color of the surrounding metal the way gold repairs can. A cracked or broken platinum shank is a routine bench repair. The repair is often stronger than the original at the repaired point because the welded area is fully consolidated.

Which metal is better for an engagement ring expected to last a lifetime? For a ring intended to be worn daily for fifty or more years, platinum is the superior choice from a purely material standpoint. It does not change color, does not lose significant metal through normal wear, and does not require periodic replating to maintain its appearance. The higher initial cost is offset by lower maintenance expense over the ring’s lifetime. For clients who value a lighter feel or a lower initial price point, white gold with an established replating schedule is a reasonable alternative.

title: Ring Enhancers and Wedding Band Guards: What They Are and When to Use One
body:
A ring enhancer is designed to frame and expand an existing ring without modifying the original piece. It solves problems that buying a new ring doesn't address.

What Enhancers Do

How an Enhancer Differs from a Matching Band

A ring enhancer wraps around or sits against an existing ring rather than stacking beside it. Where a matching wedding band sits alongside the engagement ring with a gap between them, an enhancer is shaped to fit the existing setting — contouring around the prongs, enclosing the stone's base, or framing the entire piece within a larger decorative structure.

The gap matters more than it seems. A straight band next to a cathedral or low-profile solitaire leaves a visible space between the band and the setting. Over years of daily wear, the two rings also migrate against each other and abrade the prongs. An enhancer eliminates both problems: it fits snugly without forcing the engagement ring into a fixed position.

Ring guards are a related but distinct category — bands designed to secure a ring that fits loosely. Where an enhancer is primarily aesthetic, a guard is primarily functional. In practice, many pieces serve both purposes: a fitted guard with pavé diamonds across its shoulders is simultaneously functional and decorative.

Main Configurations

What Each Enhancer Achieves

A V-notch or U-notch enhancer is the most common type. The center of the enhancer is shaped to receive the existing ring's setting — a prong solitaire sits in a V-cut, a bezel-set stone in a U-cut. The enhancer frames the engagement ring from below and to both sides, and its outer surface extends the ring's visual footprint.

A bypass enhancer runs on either side of the ring, with decorative elements arching alongside the center stone without a cutout. This works for rings that are already decorative enough that a cutout would interrupt the design.

A full frame surrounds the engagement ring completely within a larger setting. This transforms the original piece into a component of a new, larger ring. The most dramatic option — the frame can display the original stone in a halo configuration or shift its apparent shape by surrounding it with differently cut diamonds.

Permanent or Removable

Whether to Connect the Pieces

Soldering the enhancer to the engagement ring creates a single rigid unit. The two can't migrate against each other, no debris accumulates in the gap, and the composite piece wears cleanly. The cost is that the two pieces can no longer be worn separately.

For a woman who will always wear both rings together, soldering is the right choice. For a woman who wants the option of wearing the engagement ring alone — during pregnancy, during athletic activity, or simply when she wants a different look — keeping the pieces separate is the right choice.

A middle option is a small positioning notch on the enhancer's inner surface that locates the engagement ring precisely without permanently joining them. This reduces migration without committing to a permanent connection. Not all jewelers offer this — it requires a custom fit rather than a standard contour.

Commissioning

What to Bring to the Jeweler

An enhancer made to fit a specific engagement ring requires that ring to be physically present during design and fitting. The jeweler needs to measure the setting geometry, the shank profile, and the overall ring height. Photographs are insufficient for a precision fit. The engagement ring will need to be left with the jeweler for the duration of fabrication — typically four to eight weeks.

The metal should match the engagement ring or contrast deliberately. Mixing white gold and platinum is a common unintentional mismatch: platinum is a cool neutral white, rhodium-plated white gold is a brighter reflective white. On the hand together, the difference is visible as the rhodium wears.

Budget for the enhancer itself, the labor for the custom fit, and — if soldering — the cost of the join and finish. A well-made enhancer in precious metal with quality side stones typically runs $1,500 to $8,000 depending on scale and stone weight.

title: Ring Sizing Guide
body:
Ring sizing seems simple until it is not. A well-sized ring should slip over the knuckle with slight resistance and sit without rotating. Getting there requires knowing a few things most buyers do not.

A ring that fits correctly sits at the base of the finger without rotating freely or leaving a deep indent. It slips over the knuckle with slight resistance. It does not spin unless the finger is cold or extended straight up. These are the functional criteria, and meeting them requires measuring correctly rather than guessing.

Most people do not know their ring size precisely, and many people have never had their finger professionally sized. The result is rings that are either too loose to wear safely or too tight to remove comfortably. Neither outcome is acceptable for a piece of jewelry meant to be worn daily.

The US

Sizing System

Ring sizes in the United States are expressed as numbers from approximately 3 to 13, with half sizes (4.5, 5.5, 6.5, etc.) in between. Each full size represents a difference of approximately 0.8 millimeters in internal diameter and about 2.5 millimeters in internal circumference.

Women’s ring sizes typically fall between 5 and 8, with size 6 and 7 being the most common. Men’s ring sizes typically fall between 8 and 12, with sizes 9 and 10 being common. These are general patterns; actual finger sizes vary considerably across individuals.

How to Measure

at Home

The most reliable home method uses a strip of paper or thin string and a ruler.

Wrap the strip snugly around the base of the finger you are sizing, at the point where the ring will sit. Mark where the strip overlaps, then lay it flat against a ruler and measure the length in millimeters. This is the internal circumference.

Divide the circumference by 3.14 (pi) to get the internal diameter in millimeters. Compare that diameter to a ring size conversion chart to find your size.

Two important variables: finger size changes with temperature and time of day. Fingers are largest in the evening and when warm. Fingers are smallest in the morning and when cold. For a ring meant for daily wear, measure in the afternoon or evening when fingers are at their typical daily size.

If your knuckle is significantly larger than the base of your finger, size for the knuckle rather than the base, and accept that the ring will have some movement at the base. Alternatively, a jeweler can fit a sizing adjuster on the inside of the shank.

Width

Affects Sizing

A ring’s width changes how a given size feels on the finger. A wide band, more than 6mm, presses against more surface area of the finger and creates more friction. A ring that fits comfortably as a 6 in a 2mm band may feel tight in the same size in a 8mm band.

The practical rule: go up half a size for every additional 2mm of band width beyond your base size. If you wear a 6 in a 2mm band, order a 6.5 in a 5mm band and a 7 in an 8mm band. This is a general guideline; the best approach is to try the specific width on a ring mandrel at a jeweler’s before committing.

Professional Sizing

Is Worth It

For a significant piece of fine jewelry, a professional sizing by a jeweler with ring mandrels and proper tools is worth the ten minutes it takes. The mandrel measures both base of finger and knuckle in the same session, giving the jeweler what they need to make a specific recommendation for your finger’s particular combination of knuckle and base measurements.

If you are buying the ring as a surprise and cannot size the recipient, a standard starting point is size 6 for women and size 10 for men. These are the most statistically common sizes. A ring can always be resized after the fact.

What People

Ask Us

What is the most common ring size for women? Size 6 and 7 are the most common women’s ring sizes in the United States, with size 6 being the single most common. However, finger sizes vary considerably, and sizing assumptions based on statistics are less reliable than a proper measurement.

Does ring size change over time? Yes. Finger size changes with age, weight changes, pregnancy, and health conditions. A ring sized correctly at 25 may no longer fit at 45. Significant weight changes (gain or loss of 20 pounds or more) often require resizing. Annual inspection of fit is good practice for rings worn daily.

How much does it cost to resize a ring? Resizing by one or two sizes typically costs $30 to $100 at most jewelry shops. Eternity bands and rings with stones all around the shank are more difficult and expensive to resize, and some cannot be resized without damaging the setting. Confirm resizability before purchasing a ring with extensive stone settings.

Can I measure my ring size with an existing ring I already own? Yes. Place the ring on a flat surface and measure the interior diameter in millimeters using calipers or a ruler. Compare that measurement to a ring size conversion chart. This method is quite accurate if the existing ring fits the same finger correctly.

What if I am between ring sizes? Order the larger size. A ring that is half a size too large can be worn with a sizing adjuster (a small plastic or metal guard inside the shank that is removable). A ring that is half a size too small cannot be worn comfortably and will require resizing.

title: The Craft Behind Ring Sizing
body:
Sizing a ring is one of the most common jeweler’s services requested. What actually happens in the process, and when it is not possible, is worth knowing before you need it.

Most people have had a ring resized at some point. Fewer understand what actually happens during the process, which metals size easily versus which resist, and the specific situations where a resizing request will be turned down by any competent jeweler because the construction of the ring makes it genuinely impossible.

Knowing this in advance prevents a common disappointment: buying a ring that cannot be resized and only discovering it when the ring no longer fits.

Sizing Up

Adding Material

To make a ring larger, a jeweler cuts the shank at the bottom, pulls the two ends apart to create the needed gap, and adds a piece of matching metal to fill it. The addition is soldered in place and then the seam is finished and polished until it is invisible.

The process sounds simple and largely is, with the right materials. Yellow gold and rose gold in 14k or 18k are the most cooperative. They solder cleanly, the colors match well, and the finished seam is essentially undetectable to the naked eye.

White gold is slightly more complex because the added metal needs to match the rhodium-plated finish of the surrounding shank. The seam may be visible before replating but disappears after the rhodium is applied to the entire shank surface.

Platinum sizes very well: the metal is welded rather than soldered (different heat and technique) but the result is a seamless addition.

Sizing Down

Removing Material

To make a ring smaller, a jeweler cuts out a small section of shank, joins the two ends, solders them closed, and finishes the seam. This is slightly easier than sizing up because no new material is introduced.

The same metals that size up well size down well. The same limitations that apply in one direction apply in both.

One additional consideration when sizing down: removing metal from the shank changes the shank’s thickness slightly, particularly if the original shank is thin. Multiple rounds of downsizing can eventually weaken the shank if too much material is removed. A jeweler will advise when a shank is approaching the limit of further reduction.

When Sizing

Is Not Possible

Certain ring constructions cannot be sized without destroying what makes them what they are.

Eternity bands, where stones run continuously all the way around the shank, are the most common example. Cutting the shank to add or remove material necessarily destroys the continuous stone setting in that section. There is no clean way to add or remove metal without gaps or disruption in the stone pattern.

Tungsten carbide and titanium rings cannot be sized at all. These metals cannot be soldered with standard jewelry techniques; they require specialized machine tools to work with and the result is not a seamless, invisible repair. Many jewelers will not attempt it. These metals are not appropriate for rings that may need resizing.

Rings with delicate or elaborate surface decoration, such as milgrain edge patterns or engraving, are harder to resize because the sizing operation affects the surrounding area and the pattern may not match seamlessly after repair.

The Invisible

Sizing Adjuster

For rings that cannot be resized in the conventional way, or for wearers whose finger size fluctuates significantly across seasons, a sizing adjuster is an alternative. A small guard, made of metal or plastic, is added to the inner surface of the shank to effectively reduce the interior diameter without altering the ring itself. These are removable and adjustable.

They are not a substitute for a correctly sized ring in terms of comfort or aesthetics, but they provide a workable solution for eternity bands or other rings where conventional resizing is not possible.

The Right Size

from the Start

The most reliable solution is getting the ring sized correctly before it is made, or ordered at a size that allows for easy resizing within one or two steps after delivery. For engagement rings and wedding bands specifically, sizing is worth taking seriously before purchase because the alternative, resizing after the fact, is an additional step and expense that is avoidable.

What People

Ask Us

How many sizes can a ring be resized? Most rings can be resized by up to two full sizes up or down without issue. Beyond that range, the amount of metal being added or removed begins to affect the structural integrity or the visual proportions of the ring. The specific limit depends on the original ring’s construction and metal weight.

How long does resizing take? A standard resize with a reputable jeweler takes one to three business days. Rush service is often available at an additional cost. For rings with significant stone settings or unusual construction, more time may be required to assess and complete the work carefully.

Does resizing damage a ring? A properly executed resize by a skilled jeweler leaves no visible evidence of the work. The seam is polished smooth and the finish is restored. A poorly executed resize can leave a visible seam or affect the ring’s finish in the area of the work. Ask about a jeweler’s resizing experience before entrusting significant pieces.

Can a ring with gemstones all around it be resized? Not without disruption to the setting. Eternity bands with stones continuously around the shank cannot be conventionally resized. Half-eternity bands, where stones cover only the top half of the visible shank, can sometimes be sized by cutting in the plain section at the bottom. Confirm before purchasing any ring with extensive stone coverage that it can be resized to what you need.

What is the invisible sizing technique? Some jewelers offer a technique where the inside of the shank is built up slightly with additional metal, reducing the interior diameter without any external evidence of the work. This is appropriate for small adjustments, typically half a size. It does not involve cutting the shank and is useful for rings where shank integrity is critical.

title: Stretch Band Rings and the EasyFit Shank: Solving the Knuckle Problem
body:
A standard ring is sized to the finger's base circumference. Fingers are not cylinders. For many people, the joint is meaningfully larger than the base — and no standard size satisfies both requirements at once.

The Knuckle Problem

Why Standard Sizing Fails for Many Hands

The difference between knuckle and base circumference varies by person. For some hands it's minimal — half a size or less — and a standard ring works fine. For others, particularly those with joint changes from arthritis or age, the difference is substantial enough that no standard size works for both.

The conventional workarounds don't hold up. Sizing up to clear the knuckle leaves the ring spinning and migrating throughout the day. Sizing down means a struggle every time the ring goes on and off, with the knuckle abrading the metal over years. Neither is a solution — they're accommodations to a constraint the jewelry industry has accepted rather than solved.

The EasyFit Shank

How the Mechanism Works

The EasyFit shank is a patented ring construction by Bez Ambar. The mechanism replaces the continuous band of a standard shank with a flexible structure that opens under gentle lateral pressure and closes securely when released. From the outside, the ring looks like any other fine jewelry piece — the mechanism is entirely internal, visible only at the underside of the shank.

In the open position, the ring passes over a significantly larger diameter than the closed position — typically enough to accommodate the full difference between joint size and base size. In the closed position, it contracts to the base circumference, holding the ring in place without spinning. No springs, no pins, no small components that wear out. The mechanism relies on controlled metal elasticity.

Who It Helps Most

Candidates for a Stretch or EasyFit Ring

The most common candidate is someone whose knuckle circumference is one or more sizes larger than their ring base. This is particularly common in women over fifty, where joint changes — from arthritis or aging — progressively increase the difference between joint and base size.

Arthritis affects ring sizing in two ways: it enlarges the joint, and it makes forcing a tight ring over an inflamed joint painful. An EasyFit ring eliminates both problems — the joint is never stressed during entry, and the ring doesn't need to be sized to a compromised dimension.

Pregnancy and the temporary swelling it causes create the same problem in a shorter time frame. While an EasyFit shank is designed for permanent jewelry, the concept allows women to continue wearing meaningful pieces through periods when their fingers are temporarily enlarged.

The Extent Collection

The Same Mechanism at Bracelet Scale

The Extent bracelets apply the same engineering at wrist scale. The patented flex mechanism allows the bracelet to open wide for the hand and close precisely around the wrist. No clasp to manage, no box closure to align, no push-tab spring to break. It goes on and off with a gesture.

The collection runs round brilliant diamonds in 25mm and 30mm widths, Asscher-cut in a double-row configuration, and emerald-cut in a full edge-to-edge setting. The round models — Liquid Carat™ — present diamonds in an unbroken sequence with no visible structural interruption. The bracelet moves like fabric and returns to its shape.

What the Extent collection demonstrates is that the flex mechanism is compatible with serious fine jewelry construction: VS clarity stones, matched cuts, substantial carat weights. This is not a compromise. It's the same standard of construction as any other Bez Ambar piece, with the mechanism engineered in from the start.

Commissioning

How to Order a Ring With an EasyFit Shank

The process begins with establishing both measurements: knuckle circumference and base circumference. Both are needed to specify the mechanism's range of motion for the individual hand. The sizing consultation is more involved than for a standard ring — the jeweler needs to understand the full range, not just a nominal size.

The EasyFit shank can be added to most ring designs. Existing pieces can be retrofitted in many cases, and new pieces can be built with it from the start. Lead time is the same as for any custom fine jewelry piece — typically six to ten weeks depending on complexity.

title: The Los Angeles Diamond District
body:
The LA Diamond District on Hill Street in downtown Los Angeles houses nearly 5,000 jewelry businesses. What you can actually accomplish there, and what you cannot, is a useful distinction to have before you go.

Hill Street in downtown Los Angeles is one of the largest jewelry markets in the United States. The district runs primarily along Hill Street between 6th and 8th Streets, with overflow into adjacent streets and the jewelry exchanges that anchor the blocks. The buildings house dealers who work at multiple levels of the trade: cutters, wholesalers, setters, diamond dealers, estate buyers, and retailers all operating within a few blocks of each other.

For someone who knows what they are looking for and how the district works, it is a useful resource. For someone who does not, it can be disorienting and potentially expensive in the wrong direction.

How the District

Actually Works

The Diamond District is primarily a wholesale and trade market. Many of the dealers sell to the trade, meaning to other jewelers and retailers, rather than to the general public. Some will also sell to retail buyers, particularly for loose stones, but the experience is different from walking into a retail jewelry store.

Prices are negotiated. Unlike retail stores where the price is posted and fixed, most dealers in the district expect negotiation. The first price offered is often not the final price. Whether this benefits you depends on how much you know about what you are pricing.

The district is competitive. The same category of stone, a round brilliant in G/VS2, will be priced differently by different dealers in the same building. Comparison shopping across three or four dealers for the same specification produces a range that gives you a genuine baseline.

What the District

Is Good For

Loose diamond shopping is the district’s strongest application for retail buyers. If you want to compare multiple stones in the same specification across multiple dealers, the district allows you to do this efficiently in a few hours in a way that no single retail location can match.

Repairs and modifications are widely available and often less expensive than at destination retailers. Stone setting, chain repairs, prong work, and sizing can all be accomplished at competitive prices.

Appraisals from independent appraisers, some of whom have offices in the district, provide useful information about the value of pieces you already own.

Estate and vintage pieces appear regularly in some district shops, sourced from estate sales and consignment.

What the District

Is Not For

The district is not the right environment for custom design work. Custom work requires a relationship with a specific maker, multiple consultations, and the ability to evaluate sketches, models, and progress. The district is transactional by nature; it is not set up for the collaborative process that custom jewelry requires.

The district cannot offer the design vision that distinguishes fine jewelry from commodity jewelry. A diamond at a competitive price is available in the district. A ring conceived by a specific designer with a specific visual language and approach is not.

Authentication and documentation are worth scrutinizing. While many district dealers are reputable and provide GIA certificates for their stones, the volume of the district also creates conditions where misrepresentation can occur. Get documentation for everything. Ask for GIA reports on any significant diamond purchase and have any significant purchase verified independently before the return window closes.

Bez Ambar’s

Place in the LA Market

Bez Ambar has operated in Los Angeles for decades and has deep roots in the LA diamond and jewelry trade. The relationship to the district is one of a designer who sources material from the wholesale market but designs and makes finished pieces at a different level: not commodity jewelry at competitive prices but specific pieces conceived with specific aesthetic intentions.

A diamond from the district in a Bez Ambar setting is not the same product as the same diamond in a standard setting. The design is the work.

What People

Ask Us

Is the LA Diamond District safe? Yes. The district is a commercial business area with significant security infrastructure. Individual jewelry exchange buildings have controlled entry, security personnel, and cameras. Exercise the same common sense you would in any urban commercial environment.

Do I need to know anything before going? Know the four Cs (cut, color, clarity, carat weight) well enough to evaluate what dealers tell you. Have a GIA chart on your phone for size reference. Have a sense of what a fair price range is for what you want, either from research or from comparing multiple dealers. Go with specific criteria rather than browsing without a target.

Can I negotiate prices in the Diamond District? Generally yes for loose stones and finished jewelry. The extent of negotiation depends on the dealer and the specific piece. Some dealers post firm prices; most expect some negotiation. Starting at 10 to 15 percent below the asking price and settling in between is a common pattern.

Is it safe to buy a diamond there without a GIA certificate? No significant diamond purchase should be made without a GIA certificate from the current, current owner of the stone, not a photocopy of an old report. The certificate should include the stone’s cut grade, color grade, clarity grade, and measurements. Anything without documentation is a risk.

What is the parking situation? The district is in downtown LA. Parking structures are available nearby; street parking is limited. Many visitors take rideshare. Budget for parking costs and traffic on any trip to the district.

title: Traveling With Fine Jewelry: What to Bring and How to Protect It
body:
The right answer to how much fine jewelry to bring on a trip is almost always less than you are planning.

The Selection

How to Decide What Travels and What Stays Home

The most important decision in traveling with fine jewelry is made before you pack anything: which pieces are worth the risk of travel. Risk in this context has two components — the physical risk of loss, theft, or damage, and the stress of responsibility for pieces of financial and sentimental value in an environment you do not control. Both risks increase with every piece you bring.

The practical travel jewelry selection answers these questions for each piece: Will I actually wear this, or am I bringing it because I might want to? Can I replace it if it is lost? Does its value justify the cognitive overhead of worrying about it for the duration of the trip? A piece that answers no to the first question, yes to the second, and raises uncertainty on the third probably stays home. A piece that you will wear daily, that has irreplaceable sentimental value, and that is adequately insured for the travel context travels with you.

High-value heirloom pieces — pieces of significant financial value, pieces with irreplaceable stones, pieces with no insurance coverage or coverage that excludes travel — should stay home. The sentimental argument for bringing an irreplaceable piece on a trip is almost always outweighed by the sentimental consequences of losing it. A high-resolution photograph of the piece, plus the memory of wearing it, travels free.

For most travel purposes, a well-chosen three-piece selection serves better than a larger collection: one pair of earrings that works across multiple dress codes, one necklace or pendant, and one bracelet or additional ring. These three pieces, combined with the jewelry you are wearing when you arrive, cover most occasions and fit easily in a compact jewelry roll.

The Logistics

How to Carry Fine Jewelry Through Airports and International Borders

Fine jewelry must travel in carry-on luggage, not checked baggage. This is not a preference — it is a practical necessity. Checked baggage is the most theft-vulnerable environment in modern travel; insurance claims for jewelry stolen from checked bags are common and frequently contested. Keep every piece on your person or in your carry-on from door to door.

Airport security screening requires you to remove jewelry that may trigger metal detection. Most fine jewelry — rings, necklaces, bracelets — will trigger standard metal detectors if the total metal mass is above the threshold. Having a small compact container in your carry-on bag makes the removal and replacement of pieces during screening faster and lower-risk than carrying pieces loose in your pocket. A small zippered pouch in an accessible compartment of your carry-on works. The thirty seconds of organization during screening significantly reduces the chance of leaving a piece in a screening bin.

International travel with fine jewelry requires attention to customs regulations. Bringing personal jewelry in and out of most countries for personal use is not subject to duty, but the distinction between “personal jewelry” and “goods for sale” depends on quantity and value. Very large quantities of fine jewelry, or carrying pieces without wearing them, can invite customs scrutiny. Keep documentation of original purchase for any high-value piece traveling internationally, and be prepared to demonstrate that the pieces are for personal use.

The Hotel

The Highest-Risk Hours of Any Trip

Hotels are the most vulnerable environment for jewelry during travel. A hotel room that appears locked and private is accessed routinely by housekeeping, maintenance, and in theft scenarios, unauthorized entrants. Jewelry left on a bathroom counter, beside the bed, or on a dresser is accessible to anyone who enters the room during the day.

The hotel room safe is better than leaving pieces on open surfaces, but hotel safes have known vulnerabilities — standard override codes exist for most common models, and their use is well understood in the theft-for-hire communities that target high-value travelers. For any piece you cannot afford to lose, the safest storage during a hotel stay is on your person, in your secured carry-on bag with the room, or in the hotel’s main safe deposit facility at the front desk, which is separate from the room safes and carries a chain-of-custody log.

Do not leave fine jewelry in your hotel room overnight during beach or pool days, even in the room safe. The theft risk in resort environments is highest during daytime hours when guests are at the beach and rooms are accessible to staff. Either wear the jewelry to the beach (with the attendant risk of water, sun, and physical activity) or leave it at home. Most resort environments do not call for fine diamond jewelry, which is a useful frame for the selection decision before the trip begins.

What People

Ask Us

Will my home jewelry insurance cover pieces while traveling internationally? It depends on the policy. Standard homeowner’s jewelry riders often restrict coverage to losses within the home or within the United States. Dedicated jewelry insurance policies from specialty insurers typically cover pieces worldwide. Read the geographic coverage clause of your policy before any international trip with fine jewelry, and call your insurer if you are unclear.

Can I ship fine jewelry to a destination rather than carrying it? Yes, for high-value pieces that would create airport or customs complications. Shipping must be via a carrier that offers declared-value coverage (FedEx, UPS, and some specialty fine art shippers), with the piece insured for its full replacement value. Ship to a secure address — not an unattended hotel room — and use the fastest available service to minimize the time the piece is in transit. Never ship fine jewelry through standard postal services.

What should I wear through airport security to minimize delays? Wear pieces that you are not going to remove — embedded pieces, pieces with sentimental significance that you would not want to leave in a security bin. Put anything that you would be distressed to lose into your carry-on container before you reach the security lane. Plan for a sixty-second stop to reorganize after security rather than trying to remove and replace pieces at the conveyor.

How should I store jewelry when swimming or at the beach? Lock it in your carry-on bag in the hotel room and do not bring it to the beach or pool. Saltwater and chlorinated water are both actively damaging to fine jewelry — chlorine attacks gold alloys, saltwater promotes corrosion at metal junctions, and sand is abrasive enough to scratch gold surfaces. The only jewelry appropriate for beach or pool wear is specifically fabricated for water resistance using non-reactive materials.

What documentation should I bring when traveling with jewelry? Carry a digital copy of the insurance rider or dedicated policy coverage, photographs of each piece, and appraisal documentation. Store these documents separately from the jewelry — in your email or cloud storage — so that if the pieces are lost or stolen, the documentation remains accessible for the claim. A police report from the jurisdiction of the loss is required by most insurers.
